Higher term premia raise the price of exactly the public capital deepening that the bull case requires.

NEGATIVE TWO. The Hormuz deadlock hardened rather than resolved. Brent stood at $88.31 on 17 August 2026, down 0.24 percent on the day but up more than 5 percent across the week, as Iran and Oman failed to reach agreement on reopening the strait and Washington escalated. Bessent has said the US will impose unprecedented economic measures while maintaining the naval blockade of Iranian ports, with further announcements expected this week. Brent below $100 means trigger 6 still has not fired on price, but a week of rising prices on a failed deal shifts weight toward EY's closed-strait scenario, in which UK GDP grows 0.5 percent in 2026 and contracts 0.2 percent in 2027.

NEGATIVE THREE, structural and the most relevant to the 2030s. UK output per hour rose 0.9 percent q/q in Q1 2026 but only 0.4 percent year on year, after a 0.4 percent annual fall in the prior period. A 0.4 percent y/y trend run rate is less than half the OBR's 1.0 percent underlying assumption. Corroborating this, Bank staff estimates in the April 2026 Monetary Policy Report put potential supply growth at around 0.3-0.4 percent per quarter, and Bailey's 14 July 2026 Mansion House speech described post-crisis potential supply growth as having halved to around 1.25 percent a year from above 2.5 percent pre-2008. Both official supply-side anchors now sit below the 1.5 percent bar rather than straddling it. The ONS productivity flash estimate is due 18 August 2026, one day outside this window.

POSITIVE ONE. The Resolution Foundation's 13 August release confirmed the UK was the fastest-growing G7 economy in the first half of 2026, with combined growth of 1.0 percent across Q1 and Q2, and GDP per capita up 0.4 percent in Q2. That is real cyclical outperformance. But the same release put GDP per capita 6.6 percent below its pre-pandemic trend, which is a reminder of how large the level shortfall is and how little of it is being recovered. Net, this is a wash rather than an upgrade.

TRIGGER CHECK. (1) UP if the 28 October OBR forecast leaves trend productivity at 1.0 percent or higher, or IMF/OECD lift potential above 1.5 percent: DID NOT FIRE. The OBR forecast commissioned for 28 October 2026 remains pending; the IMF Article IV concluded 16 July still holds potential at 1.4 percent. Reporting continues to point to downgrades across every forecast year to 2030 on trend productivity revisions. (2) UP if AI productivity contributions broaden beyond AI-producing sectors, or ONS adoption depth exceeds 1.6 tools per adopter: DID NOT FIRE. No new ONS or BoE industry evidence in the window. The large headline numbers in circulation, Microsoft-commissioned GBP 550bn by 2035, PwC's 10 percent higher GDP by 2030, the AI Opportunities Action Plan's GBP 400bn by 2030, are all commissioned scenario work, not measured outturns, and none is new. (3) UP if business investment posts a second consecutive quarter of 1.5 percent or better, or BCC capex intentions recover above 25 percent, or the 10-year gilt falls below 4 percent: DID NOT FIRE. Q3 business investment is not published until late 2026; BCC intentions remain at 17 percent from fieldwork of 11 May to 8 June; the gilt went the wrong way to 5.04 percent. (4) DOWN if Q3 2026 GDP comes in at 0.1 percent q/q or lower: NOT YET TESTABLE, the July monthly print lands 11 September. (5) DOWN if the 10-year gilt exceeds 5.5 percent or the Budget delivers capital-led consolidation: DID NOT FIRE but MOVED ADVERSELY, 5.04 percent on 14 August is a fresh high, and Budget reporting still points to business-rates rebalancing toward smaller firms rather than capital cuts. (6) DOWN if Hormuz stays disrupted into 2027 with Brent sustained above $100, or labour demand keeps deteriorating: PARTIALLY FIRED, unchanged from the prior. Hormuz remains closed with talks stalled and Brent up 5 percent on the week, but at $88.31 it is far below $100.

NET REASONING. The arithmetic is unchanged and remains the whole question. Roughly 1.0 percent trend productivity, and arguably nearer 0.4 percent on the latest y/y outturn, plus roughly 0.3-0.5 percent labour supply growth as natural change turns negative from 2026 and net migration settles near the ONS 230,000 long-run assumption, gives potential in the 1.3-1.5 percent range with the central point just under the bar. A decade arithmetic mean is then dragged asymmetrically by recession years. What moved in this window was not the central arithmetic but the tail: a fresh gilt high raises the cost of the investment-led upside path, a failed Hormuz negotiation raises the odds of a 2027 contraction feeding into an early-2030s starting base, and the productivity y/y print at 0.4 percent sits below rather than at the OBR anchor. One point down is the right size for two days of thin, directionally consistent news on a fourteen-year structural question. The CI shifts down by one point and keeps its 27-point width, since nothing in the window resolved any structural uncertainty. The 18 August productivity flash and the 20 August Blue Book 2026 GDP impacts article are the next scheduled tests.

question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?

First-half fiscal 2026 revenue was $408.8m with non-GAAP EBITDA of $49.7m, a 12.2% margin, described as the highest first-half performance in CRA's history. The only publicly listed pure-play in the economic consulting reference class is therefore raising revenue guidance, guiding headcount up, and actively absorbing a graduate intake. On a narrow reading of 'economic consultancy' this is close to dispositive against the resolution for the near term. (2) NEXIA GLOBAL GROWTH INSIGHTS SURVEY 2026 (Consultancy.uk, 17 August 2026), n=179 predominantly mid-sized companies: 61% expect 5-20% revenue growth over the next twelve months, 83% are confident of hitting growth targets, 54% call their strategy 'ambitious', and 48% of European growth leaders plan or are considering entering new territory versus 46% in Asia-Pacific and 20pp above North America. (3) GRANT THORNTON / UNIVERSITY OF LEEDS 'TALENT TRACK' (Consultancy.uk, 17 August 2026): a four-year accounting and finance professional degree, first cohort September 2026, multiple paid placements, a 15-month third-year placement, a permanent role with an ACA training agreement on completion, and stated plans to expand in following years. (4) BHM CAPITAL launched a Consulting and AI-Enablement practice on 17 August 2026 (Consultancy-me.com), advising governments, institutions and corporates on AI-driven transformation - capital entering the consulting pool to sell AI advice, not exiting it. (5) ONS GRANULARITY: in the three months to May 2026, 'activities of head offices and management consultancy activities' grew 3.1%; in the three months to June 2026, professional, scientific and technical activities grew 1.7%, with advertising and market research up 4.3%, scientific R&D up 3.9% and legal activities up 2.5%. Trigger 1 (pure-play economic consultancy revenue decline attributed by management to AI fee compression; next test CRA Q3 FY2026 in late October): DID NOT FIRE, and moved sharply further away - CRA raised guidance and guided headcount up. Trigger 2 (Big 4 or MBB annual revenue down >10% on AI, or client-facing headcount -15% at 2+ firms): DID NOT FIRE. The only new item is secondary-source reporting that KPMG cut roughly 400 US advisory positions, which is an order of magnitude below the 15% bar and is carried forward UNVERIFIED at primary-source level. Standing picture unchanged: McKinsey toward 40,000 from 45,000-plus, Accenture 11,000-plus exits under an $865m charge with stated intent to hire more next year, BCG 2025 revenue $14.4bn up ~7%. Source's position is unchanged and demand-positive - cautious-on-AI buyers down from 50% in 2025 to 23% in 2026, deployed-or-eager up from 15% to over 40%, technology consulting above $400bn in 2026 with growth rising to 7%. Trigger 5 (positive FY growth across Big 4 and MBB, or graduate intake recovery toward 2024 levels): PARTIALLY FIRED, and strengthened for the first time in weeks. Three new demand-and-capacity-positive items landed and one of them - CRA's simultaneous revenue upgrade and headcount expansion at the archetypal firm in the reference class - is materially diagnostic rather than merely confirmatory. There is also a mechanical arithmetic point that strengthens each day the sector fails to start contracting: the resolution measures a 33% fall from a 2024 baseline by 31 December 2030, and with 2025 and 2026 both growing, the annualised decline now required from 2027 onward has risen well above what any credible forecaster is projecting. That argues for lowering the central estimate and narrowing the upper bound rather than the lower one. I hold the floor at 8 because four-plus years of model-capability uncertainty remains genuinely open and the credential-and-liability bundle is not provably safe to 2030. Central to 14, upper to 25.

question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
key_change: HOLD: 1 to 1. Central stays at 1% with an 80% CI of [0, 2]. The estimate is already at the practical floor for an integer forecast, so a hold is the only honest arithmetic outcome, but the direction of travel in the 17-18 August window was clearly and materially NO-favourable, and the residual probability mass has thinned further. NOT YET PUBLISHED: the ONS July 2026 CPI print is NOT out. The ONS release page for Consumer price inflation, UK: July 2026 (checked 18 August 2026) states 'Release date: 19 August 2026 7:00am' and 'This release is not yet published'. Nothing below is a reported July figure. THE ARITHMETIC. June 2026 CPI was 2.6% (ONS, published 22 July 2026). Exactly five reference months can publish before 1 January 2027: July 2026 (release 19 August), August (mid-September), September (mid-October), October (mid-November) and November (mid-December). December 2026 CPI publishes mid-January 2027 and cannot resolve the question. From the 2.6% June base, YES requires at least one of those five prints below 1.95% on ONS rounding, a fall of at least 0.65pp. If the consensus 2.9% lands tomorrow, the window shrinks to four months and the required fall grows to at least 0.95pp, at a time when the Ofgem cap rises again in October and services ran 3.6% in June. NEW DATED ITEMS. The easing I logged yesterday has been undone and NBP is now within 6p of the 160p downside trigger. (3) Brent rose to USD 90.97/bbl on 18 August 2026, up 0.11% on the day (Trading Economics), against USD 88.31 on 17 August: about USD 21 above the USD 70 level that would reopen the question. (4) Geopolitics deteriorated sharply. The 60-day US-Iran MoU deadline expired on 17 August with no extension (CNN live, 17 August 2026); Trump ruled out extending in the near term and threatened to attack Oman if it interfered in the Hormuz crisis. Al Jazeera (12 August) recorded five commodity vessels transiting on the Saturday and none on the Sunday, against 31 the previous weekend. (5) Rate expectations turned hawkish: futures price roughly a 52% chance of a hike at the 17 September MPC, a Reuters poll of 65 economists has nearly 40% expecting at least one hike by year-end, and Interactive Investor's Victoria Scholar expects one 25bp hike to 4.0% with inflation 'peaking above 3% later this year'. (6) Food risk rose: the Food and Drink Federation warned this week that heatwaves and drought across the UK and Europe are hitting 'fruit, vegetable and grain supply', with upward pressure on food inflation into 2027; BRC-NIQ June data had food at 2.4% y/y and shop prices at 1.2%, still soft but with retailers saying they cannot absorb energy and Iran-related costs indefinitely. That is an increase. Trigger 3 (revise UP if the Hormuz agreement is implemented with the blockade lifted and Brent holds below USD 70 with NBP below about 100p for two weeks before end-September) DID NOT FIRE and moved decisively away: the ceasefire lapsed, Trump ruled out extension and threatened Oman, and a vessel was hit today. Trigger 4 (revise UP if September or October prints come in at or below 2.4% with services below 3.0%) DID NOT FIRE: no such prints exist. First, the resolution-mechanics technicality: no Q4 2026-dated figure yet exists for either firm, and a strict resolver could in principle demand one for each. That risk is falling as Anthropic's October listing would force public quarterly disclosure inside the window, and it is further reduced because a $100-120bn Anthropic exit would clear the bar single-handed. Second, the comparability caveat Bloomberg now attaches explicitly to any OpenAI-versus-Anthropic run-rate comparison: a resolver insisting on a like-for-like net basis for both would need to do work no published source has yet done. The one genuinely adverse item, the further hardening of OpenAI's 2027 lean with Friar now named as advocating it, attacks a redundant disclosure channel: Bloomberg has printed OpenAI's run rate three times in 2026 without any prospectus. Holding at 99 rather than moving higher reflects the discipline of never assigning near-certainty to a question whose resolution still depends on a future publication event, not any doubt about the underlying arithmetic.

question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
key_change:
Move: 33 to 34. A one-point move back up, reversing yesterday's cut. The driver is not a news event but a measurement correction to the prior's own inside view, discovered while chasing today's scheduled release. Two items push up, three push down, and the up items are the more structural.

UP ONE, and the important one. The prior's single strongest negative was that UK output per hour rose only 0.4 percent year on year in Quarter 1 2026, described as less than half the OBR's 1.0 percent underlying assumption. That reading is the Labour Force Survey-based flash. The same ONS bulletin (Productivity flash estimate and overview, UK: January to March 2026 and October to December 2025, released 19 May 2026) reports a second estimate built from PAYE Real Time Information: output per hour up 2.1 percent year on year in Quarter 1 2026, and 5.5 percent above the 2019 average versus 3.5 percent on the LFS basis. Critically, a notice carried in that bulletin, following the ONS blog of 16 June 2026 on how the ONS measures productivity, states that because historic low LFS response levels still contaminate annual growth rates in the headline series, 'the ONS therefore recommends, at the current time, that users focus on the experimental RTI approach as the best estimate of how productivity is changing in the UK economy.' The prior leaned on the measure the producing statistical agency explicitly recommends against. On the recommended measure, realised productivity is running above, not far below, the OBR's 1.0 percent anchor. That does not resolve the question, since the RTI series is official statistics in development, is a hybrid of RTI worker counts and LFS average hours, and has diverged from the LFS since 2022 for reasons ONS itself says users should not overinterpret. But it removes the sharpest edge of yesterday's downgrade.

UP TWO. Reuters, 13 August 2026, on the ONS Quarter 2 first estimate: information and communications supplied close to half of Britain's 0.4 percent second-quarter growth, the largest single industry contribution. Output in computer programming and consultancy rose 3.7 percent on the quarter after 3.8 percent in the preceding quarter. Investment in plant and machinery reached GBP 22.1bn, just short of the distorted early-2022 peak, which ONS attributed largely to ICT equipment and computer hardware alongside government weapons purchases. Manufacturing output in computing, optical and electronic products rose 10.7 percent year on year, ahead of the other twelve sub-sectors for the first time since early 2017. This is the AI compute build-out arriving in the national accounts rather than in survey sentiment. The honest caveat, which the reporting itself makes, is that hardware purchases are investment in capacity, not yet output per worker.

DOWN ONE. The 10-year gilt rose to 5.07 percent on 17 August 2026, up 2 basis points on the session, up 3 basis points on the month and 32 basis points on the year, and was quoted around 5.09 percent intraday on 18 August. That is another fresh high after 5.04 percent on 14 August, extending the adverse drift and raising the cost of the public capital deepening the bull case needs.

DOWN TWO. Brent stood at 90.89 dollars on 18 August 2026, having climbed above 91 dollars for a third consecutive session as the June memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran expired on Monday 17 August and Trump said he was not interested in extending the interim deal. Iran and Oman continue talks on Hormuz shipping without US participation. Trading Economics puts Brent at 104.28 dollars in twelve months. Prices are up 38 percent on the year and 2 percent on the month.

DOWN THREE. Today's labour market release (ONS, 18 August 2026, 7:00am) continues the demand deterioration: vacancies 707,000, unemployment 4.9 percent, employment up 83,000 after 147,000, payrolled employees down 12,850 in July after down 13,490, total pay growth easing to 4.1 percent from 4.4 percent, and average weekly hours up to 32.10 from 31.90. Rising hours against 0.4 percent quarterly GVA growth points to a soft Quarter 2 productivity flash.

TRIGGER CHECK. (1) UP if the 28 October OBR forecast leaves trend productivity at 1.0 percent or higher, or IMF/OECD lift potential above 1.5 percent: DID NOT FIRE, forecast still pending, IMF Article IV of 16 July 2026 still 1.4 percent. (2) UP if the 18 August 2026 ONS productivity flash shows output per hour accelerating to 1.0 percent y/y or better: DID NOT FIRE, NOT YET OBSERVABLE. As of checking, the ONS labour productivity landing page, the LZVD and LZVB series pages, the release calendar and the 'latest' article all still resolve to the 19 May 2026 bulletin covering Quarter 1 2026 and Quarter 4 2025, and Trading Economics' productivity calendar still lists 19 May as the last entry. The 18 August release remains scheduled (an ONS notice of 31 July 2026 confirms corrected manufacturing unit wage cost data 'will be published in our Productivity flash estimate and overview, UK release on 18 August 2026'). It has published or will publish later today; it is not yet readable. (3) UP if AI productivity contributions broaden beyond AI-producing sectors, or ONS adoption depth exceeds 1.6 tools per adopter: DID NOT FIRE. The 13 August GDP composition is concentrated precisely in the AI-producing bracket, computer programming and consultancy plus hardware manufacture, which is the same narrowness the Bank Underground post of 6 August 2026 identified. ONS adoption remains 35 percent of firms at 1.6 tools each, with large language models used by 18 percent of firms in June 2026 and under one in five adopters using AI for new products, services or markets. (4) UP if business investment posts a second consecutive quarter of 1.5 percent or better, or BCC capex intentions recover above 25 percent, or the gilt falls below 4.5 percent: DID NOT FIRE. Quarter 2 business investment was 1.7 percent but Quarter 1 was 0.9 percent, so the two-quarter test is unmet and Quarter 3 is not published; the BCC Quarterly Economic Survey for Quarter 2 2026 has investment intentions at 17 percent, DOWN from 21 percent in Quarter 1 with 26 percent planning cuts, a post-pandemic low, with inflation now the top concern at 66 percent against 50 percent in Quarter 1; the gilt went the wrong way. (5) DOWN if the gilt exceeds 5.5 percent or the Budget delivers capital-led consolidation: DID NOT FIRE but MOVED ADVERSELY AGAIN, 5.07 to 5.09 percent. (6) DOWN if Quarter 3 2026 GDP comes in at 0.1 percent q/q or lower: NOT YET TESTABLE, July monthly print 11 September. (7) DOWN if Hormuz persists into 2027 with Brent above 100 dollars, or labour demand keeps deteriorating: PARTIALLY FIRED and hardening. Brent at 90.89 is below 100, but the peace-deal window has now formally lapsed, and the labour demand leg of this trigger fired outright today on vacancies, payrolls and pay.

NET REASONING. The arithmetic remains the question. Potential growth equals trend productivity plus trend labour input. On labour input, ONS 2024-based projections have natural change negative from 2026, net migration at 138,000 in 2026 stabilising at a long-run 230,000 from 2028, and the population up 2.3 million between 2025 and 2039 with migration accounting for essentially all of it: roughly 0.3 to 0.5 percent a year of working-age growth across the 2030s, with today's vacancy, payroll and pay data arguing the lower half of that if participation keeps slipping. On productivity, the anchors now bracket the threshold more widely than yesterday's write-up allowed. The pessimistic anchor is the outturn record: ONS series LZVD gives annual whole-economy output per hour growth of minus 0.4 percent in 2023, minus 0.8 percent in 2024 and plus 0.1 percent in 2025, and a decade mean of exactly 0.60 percent for both 2010 to 2019 and 2016 to 2025, with the index at 99.1 in Quarter 4 2025 against a 2023 base of 100. The optimistic anchor is the ONS-recommended RTI measure at 2.1 percent year on year. The official judgements sit between: OBR 1.0 percent, Bailey's 14 July 2026 Mansion House figure of about 1.25 percent, IMF potential 1.4 percent, Bank staff 0.3 to 0.4 percent per quarter in the April 2026 Monetary Policy Report. Take 1.0 to 1.2 percent productivity plus 0.3 to 0.5 percent labour and potential lands at 1.3 to 1.7 percent, straddling the bar with the central point a shade under it. Then apply the shape of the question: a ten-year arithmetic mean is dragged asymmetrically by bad years, and a single minus 1.5 percent recession year subtracts about 0.3 points from the decade average on its own, while the 2030s carry non-trivial odds of at least one recession, energy shock, climate event or fiscal accident. That asymmetry, not the central potential estimate, is why this sits in the low thirties rather than near fifty. What changed today is the width and centre of the productivity input, not the structure: the strongest single negative in yesterday's file turned out to rest on the measure the ONS tells users not to use, and the AI capital build-out is now visible in official output and investment data rather than only in commissioned scenarios. Against that, three separate stress indicators, gilts, oil and labour demand, all moved the wrong way in twenty-four hours. One point up is the right size. The CI shifts up one point and keeps its 27-point width, since nothing resolved. The immediate tests are the delayed 18 August productivity flash, the 20 August Blue Book 2026 GDP impacts article, the 11 September monthly GDP print, the 17 September MPC, and the 28 October Budget forecast.

question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
key_change: Move: 14 to 13. The 18-19 August 2026 window produced one genuinely new piece of official, resolution-relevant statistics and a set of dated sector items that, on balance, cut against the YES side while adding one real capability datapoint on the YES side. The single most important item is the Office for National Statistics release of 18 August 2026, "Vacancies and jobs in the UK: August 2026" (release date 18 August 2026, next release 15 September 2026). Its workforce-jobs section for March 2026 records professional, scientific and technical activities at 3,492,000 jobs, up 43,000 (1.3%) on the quarter and the second-largest volume increase of any of the twenty industry sectors, behind only human health and social work (up 61,000). The sectors with the largest annual falls were information and communication (down 3.6%) and manufacturing (down 3.2%, down 81,000 jobs); professional services was not among the eight sectors that fell on the year. On vacancies, total UK vacancies fell 6,000 (0.8%) to 707,000 in May to July 2026, down 19,000 (2.7%) on the year and 81,000 (10.3%) below the January-March 2020 level, the lowest outside the pandemic since September-November 2014. But the falls were concentrated elsewhere: the largest quarterly declines were human health and social work (down 5,000) and education (down 4,000, or 7.3%), and the largest annual percentage declines were arts, entertainment and recreation (down 17.0%) and water supply (down 11.3%). Professional and scientific services did not feature in either list. The unemployment-to-vacancy ratio held at 2.5, unchanged since July-September 2025. This is a cooling labour market in which professional services is conspicuously not the epicentre. That matters directly: with 2026 sector employment above its 2024 level, a 33% decline from a 2024 baseline by 31 December 2030 now requires a steeper peak-to-trough collapse inside a shorter remaining window than it did a year ago, and the arithmetic tightens with each such print. The Credit Protection Association's 18 August 2026 daily business round-up corroborated the macro picture from the same release: vacancies 707,000, a five-year low; unemployment 4.9%; private-sector wage growth 2.8%, the weakest for almost six years; CIPD private-sector employment intentions at a record low reading of +11 with only 57% of employers planning to recruit in the next three months; and S&P Global's UK consumer sentiment index down to 42.9 in August from 43.4 in July. It also reported the Lloyds Business Barometer survey of 1,200 companies, in which 54% said AI had resulted in job creation, 25% said they were hiring more candidates with AI skills and 20% were creating dedicated AI roles, alongside the caveat that hiring for some AI-exposed occupations has weakened since 2022. The same round-up's insolvency list for 18 August named Clancy Consulting Ltd and Pearson Ham Consulting Ltd among six administrations and GTL Consulting Ltd among thirteen liquidations, but none of these is an AI story: Clancy's notice (reported by Consultancy.uk on 14 August 2026) was attributed to the building services market, and Pearson Ham's appears to be the administrative leg of its 13 August acquisition by CIL Strategy Consultants, which is rebranding it CIL Pearson Ham. On Consultancy.uk itself, the news index on 19 August carried four items dated 18 August and four dated 19 August, an unchanged publication cadence from the four 17 August datelines noted yesterday. The substantive AI-related pieces were: "AI bubble talk will 'not stop the underlying shift in how work gets done'" (18 August 2026), in which Elixirr partner Adam Hofmann responds to Russ Mould's Telegraph comparison of AI-market valuations to 1929 conditions (S&P 500 at 41 times ten-year average earnings, Shiller CAPE at its widest since 2000). Hofmann argues the bubble is in circular financing rather than in demand, that the companies driving the build are profitable rather than debt-financed, and that a correction "would not stop the underlying shift in how work gets done" — an explicit statement that even a valuation reset does not reverse the task-level substitution. Second, "Why financial services AI pilots are still stalling, three years into the hype" (19 August 2026), by Ilia Prokashev of Alpha FMC. It is genuinely two-sided evidence. On the down side, it reports Valliance research from mid-2026 finding 48% of mature organisations with established AI programmes still have initiatives stuck at pilot stage, and that a year after two-thirds of financial services CEOs expected to move past piloting, 60% were still in it — a slow-diffusion finding that pushes any displacement date out. On the up side, it contains the sharpest capability datapoint of the window: Alpha's Concord fund-compliance engine, launched June 2026, achieved 99.8% accuracy on compliance checks against 92.5% on manual review of the same population, reviewed 100% of documents rather than the typical 2-10% sample, and did so at eight times the speed of a human review team. That is a document-review workload directly analogous to the junior-analyst layer in economic consulting, and it is being sold by a consultancy rather than replacing one. Third, "How to move AI plans from paper to practice" (18 August 2026), another advisory-demand piece. The remaining 18-19 August items were routine expansion news: WSP winning Wiltshire Council's six-year highways consultancy contract (18 August), First Actuarial promoting four new partners "amid ongoing growth" (18 August), Unit4 adding two senior public-sector hires (19 August), Leonard Curtis appointing Mark Hickford as restructuring director (19 August). No layoff, fee-compression or headcount-reduction story appeared. On listed firms, I found nothing dated 18-19 August. CRA International's Q2 FY2026 release and its $400m credit-facility increase and extension (a $75m term loan plus a $325m revolver, six lenders, five years) both date to 6 August 2026 and were already in the prior. That is AI acting as a demand generator, not a substitute, at a mid-cap consultancy. Finally, the DisplaceIndex AI-layoff tracker, fetched live on 19 August 2026, showed 373,784 AI-attributed job cuts since January 2023 across 56 distinct events, with technology accounting for 247,828 and the AI displacement ratio (AI-attributed cuts divided by FRED JTSLDL total US layoffs) at 1.2% in the latest month. Sources I could fetch directly: consultancy.uk news index and two articles, cpa.co.uk 18 August round-up, the ONS August 2026 vacancies and jobs bulletin, displaceindex.com. Sources I could not fetch: consulting.us (blocked, not in provenance set), Financial Times, Source Global Research primary, Bloomberg's 6 August "McKinsey and Consulting Rivals Bet on Experts to Ride AI Wave", learningnews.com (404). question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?

Fourth, one aggregator did move: BritPolls' headline poll-of-polls now reads Reform 23.8, Labour 25.2, Conservative 19.6, against Reform 24.4, Labour 25.0, Conservative 20.4 in the version cached earlier in the week - Labour's lead widening from roughly 0.6 to 1.4 points as older, weaker Labour polls roll out of the window. That is a rolling-window artefact more than a signal, but it points the same way as everything else. Fifth, the substantive political news. Reform UK's £50bn-a-year welfare package, trailed by Robert Jenrick in the Sunday Times on 16 August and set out at a press conference on 17 August with further detail on 17-18 August, is the largest policy event of the window. Labour called it "fantasy economics, built on stripping support from disabled people"; the Conservatives called it "half-baked" and a distraction from Farage's £5m gift. The Week UK's 18 August piece, "Are welfare cuts Reform's stumbling block?", collects the expert reaction: Ben Chu on BBC Verify calls it "extremely ambitious" but a "political risk"; John Curtice tells The Independent it fits Reform's current ideological appeal but has limits to wider appeal and potential to backfire with their base; Fraser Nelson notes that "every Reform MP sits on more Pip claimants than the majority that elected them", that Jenrick's own Newark seat has 6,011 PIP claimants against a 3,572 majority, and that Jenrick risks entering the next election as "the Pip-snatcher"; the Times editorial calls the foreign-national element largely "pointless" given no-recourse-to-public-funds rules; even the Telegraph's supportive editorial concedes "flaws". This is a genuine, dated deterioration in Reform's positioning in precisely the northern and coastal welfare-dependent seats it must win to be largest party. Sixth, Reform's organisational bleeding continued on 18 August: the party suspended Conservative defector Tim Montgomerie after he criticised Farage and Zia Yusuf, and Helen Butler resigned as Reform councillor for Shepshed on Leicestershire County Council, following a South Tyneside resignation on 12 August, a Kirklees suspension on 13 August, and earlier defections to Restore Britain and the SDP. Labour is now the favourite, having overtaken Reform after Burnham's accession and Farage's resignation, but 40% is well below both Electoral Calculus's 58% and my prior 54. The gap is explicable: Electoral Calculus's figure is conditional on an election held on current polling and prices none of the three-plus years of decay to come, whereas the question resolves by December 2029. Polymarket carries no live most-seats market, but its UK election-timing series prices an election called by 31 December 2026 at 15% and by 30 June 2027 at 32%, so the modal case remains a late-parliament contest in 2028-29, long after any honeymoon has expired. Weighing an unconditional decomposition - roughly 25% chance of an early contest at about 62% Labour-largest, 75% chance of a 2028-29 contest at about 46% - lands near 50. I move to 51 rather than lower because the day's genuine news, the welfare-policy backfire risk, Reform's continued fragmentation and Pack's polling-error evidence, all point Labour's way, and because bookmaker prices on long-horizon political markets carry a favourite-longshot bias that overstates the field.

question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2035?
key_change:
HOLD: 85 to 85. Nothing in the 18-19 August 2026 window moves a question whose resolution horizon is more than eight years away and whose bar is loose. The single most directly relevant observation is that the Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard, fetched successfully today at agi.goodheartlabs.com, still reads "Our combined forecast estimates AGI will arrive in 2031, as of August 18, 2026," with an unchanged 80 percent confidence band of 2027 to 2043. That is the identical median and identical interval used in the 18 August prior. The dashboard aggregates the Metaculus weakly-general question, the Metaculus strict general-AI question, the Metaculus long adversarial Turing test question, the Manifold "AGI When? [High Quality Turing Test]" distribution, and the Kalshi "AI passes Turing test before 2030" contract, so a flat reading across the day is a genuine multi-source null rather than a stale single feed. The Metaculus strict general-AI community median remains January 2033 with roughly 25 percent by 2029 across about 1,800 to 1,900 forecasters, and the weakly-general variant remains June 2028; I could not retrieve the live Metaculus pages themselves and am relying on secondary aggregators (AIToolsReview, veracalloway, the dashboard) reporting those figures as of August 2026, so treat the precise medians as approximately rather than exactly current.

The substantive news flow in the window was safety-and-governance heavy rather than capability-declaration heavy. OpenAI published "Pacing model development in an era of cyber-critical capabilities" on 18 August 2026. It confirms that the company paused reinforcement-learning training on deployment-bound models for two weeks, is holding its largest planned frontier RL run, and has left a substantial set of Astra and cyber-related workloads paused pending stronger isolation, continuous security testing and multistage monitoring. This follows the 7 August Axios exclusive that OpenAI was slowing release of Astra because internal evaluations could not rule out Critical cyber capability under its Preparedness Framework, with the blog wording implying months rather than weeks of delay. Cutting in the other direction, on 1 August OpenAI disclosed that Astra had solved ten long-open mathematics problems, including three Erdos problems, at roughly $2,000 of API cost. For the 2035 question this pair is close to a wash, and if anything mildly positive: a two-week RL pause and a months-long release delay are noise on an eight-year horizon, whereas evidence that a not-yet-released model is autonomously producing novel mathematics and plausibly crossing a Critical cyber threshold is a real capability datapoint. It does, however, establish an important structural fact - that labs are now willing to voluntarily decelerate - which matters more for near-term variants than for this one.

Anthropic's second company-wide Risk Report, published 14 August and heavily discussed on 18 August via Zvi Mowshowitz's substack write-up and secondary coverage at Unite.AI, TechTimes and Techi, raised the catastrophic-misalignment-in-high-stakes-settings rating from "very low" (February 2026) to "low". Anthropic is explicit that this reflects increased uncertainty, partly downstream of the cyber-evaluation incident disclosures, not a specific failed test or a conclusion that models became more dangerous. Two details bear on capability trajectory. First, Anthropic disclosed an unreleased internal model, "Model 2", described as somewhat more capable than frontier Mythos 5, with no current plans for external release - a second confirmation, alongside Astra, that the deployed frontier now materially lags the internal frontier. Second, and more interesting, the internal benchmark Anthropic built to detect whether its most dangerous capability threshold has been crossed has saturated and can no longer register incremental gains, at the same time as the company reports early signs of acceleration. Benchmark saturation at the safety-critical end is a modest positive for capability timelines and a clear negative for measurability, which is one reason I do not treat it as worth more than a fraction of a point.

On capability benchmarks generally, the picture in August 2026 is bifurcated and unchanged in the window. ARC-AGI-2 is effectively falling: as of 7 August GPT-5.6 Sol leads at 92.5 percent, Claude Opus 5 at 90.4 percent and GPT-5.5 at 85 percent, against average individual human performance of 66 percent and an 85 percent grand-prize threshold. ARC-AGI-3, by contrast, still has frontier systems scoring under 1 percent. Google shipped Gemini 3.7 Flash on 13 August with FrontierCode 1.1 Main at 43.6 percent (up from 34.4 percent for 3.6 Flash three weeks earlier), Terminal-bench 2.1 at 85.8 percent, DeepSWE v1.1 at 65.3 percent and AutomationBench at 30.4 percent. Rapid gains on coding and agentic benchmarks alongside near-zero performance on novel fluid-reasoning tasks is exactly the pattern that keeps the strict-definition distributions wide and is the main reason my central estimate is not higher.

The one arguably negative dated item is compute. Fortune reported on 18 August 2026 that the OpenAI-Nvidia Ohio arrangement "comes in $145 billion lower than reported", framing it as a signal of concerns about artificial demand for chips. The confirmed structure, per the 17 August securities filing covered by CNBC, Bloomberg, Axios and UPI, is a backstop of up to $105 billion of OpenAI lease and power obligations to SB Energy at the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Pike County over a 20-year lease, supporting an initial 4.25 GW with an option for a further 3.75 GW, phased online from 2028, plus a $1.5 billion Nvidia equity investment in SB Energy. Nvidia had previously discussed a backstop of up to $250 billion for a 10 GW buildout, and reports on 10 August already indicated a cut below $120 billion. So the news is that a very large buildout got somewhat smaller, not that it was cancelled: 4.25 GW firm with an option to roughly double is still one of the largest single compute commitments ever, and it is a guarantee rather than cash, which is precisely why the headline number is elastic. Against a 2035 horizon, a step-down from a speculative $250 billion figure to a contracted $105 billion is worth well under a point.

I also checked for the two things that would actually move this question - a lab announcing AGI, or three or more leading researchers stating AGI has been achieved - and found nothing new on 18 or 19 August. The standing precedent remains Jensen Huang's March 2026 "we've achieved AGI" remark, which Fortune covered on 30 March 2026 alongside the observation that nobody agrees what the term means, and which was publicly contested by researchers proposing new measurement schemes. That episode is informative for the resolution criteria: the announcement bar here is genuinely low, and definitional drift is a live pathway to YES independent of any strict capability threshold. On the timeline-revision side, the most recent systematic tracker I could fetch is FutureSearch's, last modified 12 April 2026, which reports that every forecaster who updated between January and April 2026 moved sooner, after a 2025 period in which Kokotajlo, Lifland, Amodei, Wildeford and the Metaculus community all moved later. No update to that tracker appeared in the window. Sources I could not fetch directly: Metaculus question pages, Kalshi and Polymarket order books, and llm-stats.com (bot check). Kalshi's OpenAI-AGI-by-2030 contract is reported at roughly 55 percent and Polymarket's OpenAI-AGI-by-2027 at roughly 9 to 11 percent, both from secondary summaries rather than live quotes.

question: Will China initiate a military blockade or invasion of Taiwan before 1 January 2030?
key_change:
HOLD: 7 to 7. The 18-19 August 2026 window produced a moderate volume of dated, checkable material, but nothing that changes the structural picture of a coercion campaign that remains intense, expanding in the maritime-legal domain, and still entirely below the threshold this question asks about. Taking the items in order. Taiwan's Ministry of National Defense reported, in its post to X on 19 August 2026, 20 sorties of PLA aircraft, 7 PLAN vessels and 6 official (coast guard/maritime) ships around Taiwan up to 0600 UTC+8, with 15 of the 20 sorties entering the northern, central, southwestern and eastern ADIZ. That is a four-fold jump on the 18 August figure carried in the prior forecast (5 sorties, 8 PLAN vessels, 7 official ships, 3 sorties into northern/eastern ADIZ) and a twenty-fold jump on 17 August (1 sortie, 9 PLAN vessels, 7 official ships). Read against the wider mid-August series, the 19 August number is unremarkable: MND logged 11 aircraft and 8 PLAN vessels on 16 August with 7 median-line crossings, 4 aircraft and 8 vessels on 15 August, and 9 aircraft and 12 vessels on 14 August. The August 2026 range is roughly 1 to 20 sorties per day against a 2024-25 baseline that frequently exceeded 20-30 and spiked above 40. A single 20-sortie day is inside the noise band and I have deliberately not updated on it. Notably, the 19 August MND text does not describe a median-line crossing count separately, only ADIZ entries, so I cannot confirm from the ANI relay whether crossings rose in proportion.

The most substantive analytical input in the window is the joint AEI-Institute for the Study of War China & Taiwan Update dated 18 August 2026 (data cutoff 17 August), which I fetched in full. Its three toplines are the Legislative Yuan's passage on 14 August of the NT$2.99 trillion (US$93bn) 2026 general budget after a record 350-day delay, including the full NT$44.2bn (US$1.38bn) drone-industry budget and NT$19.2bn (US$600m) in procurement, with a 2.5 percent cut to military equipment and facilities; Philippine President Marcos's 14 August statement that "there will be no attacks on anyone from the Philippines" during a PRC invasion of Taiwan, alongside a sought "reset" with Beijing and possible joint South China Sea oil and gas exploration; and an assessment that the PRC will use Taiwan's 2026 local elections, especially the Kaohsiung mayoral race, as a testing ground for interference operations, citing Liberty Times reporting of 10 August that the CCP's Beidaihe retreat (begun 3 August) set electing "patriotic forces" in Taiwan in 2026 as a near-term objective. Crucially, the ISW-AEI update contains no invasion or blockade warning indicators: no mobilisation, no reserve call-up, no shipping or NOTAM closures, no announced named exercise. Its other items are a suspected PRC AI-agent cyberattack that mapped 21 Taiwanese government systems in early July, compromised 85 accounts and extracted 2,500 personnel records; a Vatn Systems-NCSIST memorandum of 11 August on S12 autonomous UUVs; a US-Taiwan coast guard training course running 10-21 August; and PRC seabed "lawnmower" surveying near Palau and Guam.

Three further dated items matter more for the tails. First, and most consequential: between 15 and 16 August 2026 the United States began redeploying USS George Washington, its last carrier in Asia, from Japan through the Singapore Strait (entered 13 August) to the Middle East to relieve USS Abraham Lincoln in the Iran campaign, leaving the western Pacific without a US carrier. Axios covered this on 17 August; TWZ's carrier tracker of 17 August and Forbes on 13 August corroborate. Global Times ran a triumphalist piece framing it as "the bill for overstretch." This is a genuine, if temporary, window-of-opportunity signal and the strongest upward item in the window. I weight it modestly: carrier gaps in Asia also occurred in 2024 without incident, a Taiwan campaign requires months of observable preparation that has not begun, and the gap is expected to be measured in weeks. Second, the Iran war itself (Strait of Hormuz closure prompted a Philippine energy emergency on 24 March 2026) is absorbing US naval capacity and is the main structural reason for the gap. Third, on the de-escalatory side, the White House and Secretary of State Rubio have confirmed Xi Jinping's state visit to the United States on 24 September 2026, the third Trump-Xi meeting of the term, following the May 2026 Beijing summit at which Xi called Taiwan "the most important issue" and warned of collision. Nations do not typically initiate blockades five weeks before a state visit they are actively preparing.

On the coercion-infrastructure side, the trend continues to build without crossing thresholds. Guangdong Maritime Safety Administration announced new Taiwan Strait traffic-control measures on 14 August, nominally typhoon-related but read by analysts as a jurisdiction test. PRC state media on 14 August framed a 12 August PRC-Indonesian naval passing exercise east of Taiwan as demonstrating PRC jurisdiction over Taiwan's eastern EEZ; Jakarta publicly downplayed it on 16 August as a routine goodwill engagement in international waters, which is a meaningful rebuff. China Coast Guard has run regular patrols east of Taiwan since June-July 2026, condemned by Rubio. Taiwan ran an anti-blockade merchant-escort drill on 13 August during Han Kuang, which concluded 14 August. Set against this, SCMP reporting notes PLA fighter sorties near Taiwan fell to a three-year low in H1 2026 and that the PLA staged no large-scale named drills around the island in that period, the first such stretch since 2022 — a materially dovish operational-tempo datapoint that offsets the maritime-legal escalation.

Market and forecast-community evidence: Polymarket's "invade Taiwan by 30 September 2026" market sat at roughly 98.8 percent No on about US$1.86m volume as of 12 August 2026, and end-2026 at roughly 96 percent No. I could not directly fetch Metaculus or Polymarket pages (the Metaculus API URL was outside the fetch provenance set), so these figures come from search summaries and secondary crypto-press aggregation and should be treated as indicative only. Search-surfaced Metaculus figures for 2030-horizon invasion questions ranged from 22 to 43 percent, but those questions are differently worded (some include any armed conflict or partial control) and I do not treat them as comparable to this resolution criterion. Sources I could fetch directly and rely on: AEI/ISW 18 August, ANI relay of MND 19 August, SecurityStudies.info Asia-Pacific briefing of 16 August, GlobalSecurity/Global Times of 11 August, armedconflicts.org tracker refreshed 19 August. Sources I could not fetch: Metaculus, Polymarket, Reuters and Taipei Times originals, PRC MND and Taiwan Affairs Office primary transcripts. Net: one modest upward item (carrier gap), one modest downward item (September summit on track, low PLA sortie tempo), and a large volume of confirmatory gray-zone noise. Hold at 7.

question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
key_change: HOLD: 1 to 1, with the 80% interval narrowed from [0, 2] to [0, 1]. The July 2026 print published on schedule at 7:00am today, 19 August 2026, and it did not surprise to the downside. It surprised, mildly, to the upside of the Bank of England's own path and squarely in line with the economist consensus: UK CPI rose 2.9% in the 12 months to July 2026, up from 2.6% in June, the highest annual rate since March 2026 and 0.9 percentage points above the level this question requires. Consensus going into the print was 2.9% (Pantheon Macroeconomics and Deutsche Bank both published 2.9%), so the headline came in as expected, but the Bank of England's own July Monetary Policy Report profile had implied around 2.8%, meaning the outturn was a touch hotter than the official forecast. Core CPI held at 2.6% year on year, against a consensus of 2.5% and a Deutsche Bank call of 2.5%, so the underlying picture was firmer than expected too. Core CPIH rose to 2.9% from 2.8%. The composition is exactly what was anticipated in yesterday's reasoning: the largest upward contribution came from housing and household services, whose annual rate jumped to 4.1% from 2.7% in June, driven by gas prices up 14.7% and electricity up 3.6%. That reflects Ofgem's energy price cap rising 13% on 1 July, which lifted the typical dual-fuel direct-debit bill by GBP 221 to GBP 1,862. The one genuinely disinflationary element was services: the CPI services annual rate eased to 3.4% from 3.6%, matching Pantheon's call, and that easing was driven largely by an air-fares base effect, with fares up 11.7% between June and July 2026 against 30.2% in the same window of 2025. Robert Wood at Pantheon explicitly flagged that the services softening reflects temporary factors that will unwind over the summer, so it is not evidence of a durable disinflationary turn. The arithmetic of what remains is now considerably worse for YES than it was yesterday. With the July print banked, only four reference months can still publish before 1 January 2027: August (due mid-September), September (due 21 October 2026), October (due 18 November 2026) and November (due mid-December 2026). December 2026 publishes in January 2027 and is out of scope. Working in index terms using the ONS series, CPI stood at 138.9 in June 2025, 139.0 in July 2025, 139.3 in August and September 2025, 139.8 in October 2025 and 139.5 in November 2025; June 2026 was 142.5, and a 2.9% annual rate in July 2026 implies an index of roughly 143.0. To print an annual rate that rounds below 2.0%, the index would need to fall below about 142.0 in August or September, below about 142.5 in October, and below about 142.2 in November. From 143.0 that means the price level would have to fall by roughly 0.7% over one to two months, or by roughly 0.3% to 0.6% cumulatively over three to four months, at a time of year when the index normally rises. Nothing in the forward calendar points that way. Cornwall Insight's latest October cap forecast, published after the government's VAT announcement, is GBP 1,699.59 for October to December 2026, revised down from GBP 1,906.27, but the revision reflects the removal of 5% VAT on domestic electricity plus Ofgem's rebasing of typical household consumption, and Cornwall still expects the October cap to sit about 2% above the current level on a like-for-like basis because of Middle East-driven wholesale gas strength. Ofgem confirms the October cap by 26 August 2026. The VAT measure itself, announced on 21 July 2026 as one of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's first acts and effective 1 October 2026, is the single largest genuinely disinflationary event in the window, and the government's own costing puts its effect at roughly 0.10 percentage points off CPI, worth about GBP 45 off the annual cap. That is one-ninth of the gap that would need to close. Official and market forecasts point the other way entirely. The Bank's July 2026 Monetary Policy Report, published 30 July, has CPI peaking at around 3.2% in 2026 Q4, with the MPC noting risks to that projection tilted to the upside. HM Treasury's panel of independent forecasters averaged 3.7% for Q4 2026 in the 17 June survey and around 3.5% in the May survey. Deutsche Bank sees a 3.3% to 3.5% peak in Q4. In other words, the modal published path for every one of the four remaining reference months is materially above July's 2.9%, not below 2.0%. The policy signal is consistent: the MPC held Bank Rate at 3.75% for a fifth consecutive meeting on 30 July on a 6-3 vote, more divided than the 7-2 expected, and Governor Bailey said explicitly that if the Middle East conflict persists and second-round effects emerge the Bank will likely need to raise rates. Market commentary today frames the September 17 meeting as a live hike risk, not a cut. A central bank contemplating tightening is not a central bank that expects sub-2% prints within four months. Genuine offsets exist but are small relative to the gap. Grocery inflation, per Worldpanel by Numerator, slowed to 2.1% in the four weeks to 9 August 2026 from 2.6% in the four weeks to 12 July, the lowest since October 2024 and a fifth consecutive monthly deceleration; food carries roughly an 11% CPI weight, so even a full percentage point of further food disinflation is worth around 0.1pp. The goods annual rate had slowed to 1.7% in June. Labour market data released ahead of today's print was described as soft, which over time compresses services inflation. But these are 2027 stories on the published paths, not 2026 ones. Set against them, oil rose about 22% on the renewed Middle East hostilities, Brent was around USD 87 as of mid-August, and President Trump has ruled out extending the Iran ceasefire, keeping the energy impulse live into the autumn assessment window that determines the January 2027 cap. The net effect of today is not to change the direction of the forecast but to remove the last plausible route to YES. Yesterday the question was whether five prints starting from 2.6% could deliver 0.65pp of disinflation. Today it is whether four prints starting from 2.9% can deliver 0.95pp, with the October cap rising, oil elevated, the BoE forecasting a Q4 peak above 3%, and consensus above that. My unrounded point estimate has moved from roughly 0.8% to roughly 0.3%. That still rounds to 1 at integer resolution, and I am holding at 1 rather than dropping to 0 because four unobserved prints remain and a zero would assert impossibility: a sudden Middle East de-escalation collapsing gas, a large emergency energy or VAT package at the Autumn Budget, or an ONS reweighting or data incident are each individually improbable but not excluded. The substantive update is in the interval, which I am cutting to [0, 1]: a 2% upper bound is no longer defensible now that the starting point is 2.9% and the official central path is 3.2%.

question: Will Spider-Man: Brand New Day gross over $1.5B worldwide by 31 December 2026?
key_change:
HOLD at 100. Both resolution sources were reachable today and both report the identical cumulative worldwide figure, which sits roughly 35 percent above the $1.5B threshold. The Numbers (https://www.the-numbers.com/movie/spider-man-brand-new-day-(2026)), retrieved 19 August 2026, reports Domestic $794,051,866, International $1,236,000,000 and Worldwide $2,030,051,866, with the tracked report date on the domestic daily table advancing to 8/18/2026. Box Office Mojo (https://www.boxofficemojo.com/title/tt22084616/), retrieved 19 August 2026, reports the same three numbers to the dollar: Domestic $794,051,866, International $1,236,000,000, Worldwide $2,030,051,866. Note that Box Office Mojo's summary figures did not render through the plain page-extraction path (the aggregate table returned em-dashes, and the release-level page rl2299756545 returned "There is no data to display"), so the figures above were pulled from the raw title-page HTML via a direct request with a browser user-agent. That is a rendering artefact of the extraction method, not a data outage; the underlying page carries the numbers. I flag it because a naive retrieval on a future day could produce a spurious "source unreachable" or "source blank" reading, and the correct interpretation in that event is instrument failure rather than a restatement.

The delta since the 18 August snapshot is +$7,219,866 worldwide, from $2,022,832,000 to $2,030,051,866. Every dollar of that movement is domestic: the domestic line moved from $786,832,000 to $794,051,866, exactly +$7,219,866, while the international line is unchanged at $1,236,000,000. That pattern is the expected one. The Numbers refreshes domestic daily and international on a weekly-ish cadence tied to studio international reporting, so a flat international line on a Wednesday carries no information about foreign performance; it simply means the overseas cume has not been restated since the last international update. The domestic increment is consistent with a film in its third full week posting mid-week grosses in the $7M range against a $794M cume, which is a normal decay profile and irrelevant to resolution either way. It is also worth noting that the prior day's figures as recorded were round to the nearest thousand on domestic and worldwide, whereas today's are dollar-exact on both sources; the small apparent tidiness of yesterday's numbers reflects how they were transcribed, not a change in source precision.

The residual risk analysis is unchanged in structure and, if anything, marginally tighter than yesterday. Resolution requires the published worldwide cumulative on Box Office Mojo or The Numbers to exceed $1.5B at some point on or before 31 December 2026. That condition is already satisfied and has been continuously satisfied since roughly 13-14 August, when the film crossed $2B. The question does not require the figure to still be above $1.5B on 31 December; it requires the gross to have exceeded $1.5B by that date, and a cumulative gross is monotonically non-decreasing in normal accounting. So the only paths to NO are (a) a catastrophic downward restatement of about 26 percent of the published worldwide total, sustained through year end and reflected on both sources, or (b) a resolution-mechanics failure in which neither source is consultable or a resolver reads the question in some perverse way. Neither is a live concern. On (a), major-studio worldwide cumes are compiled from Comscore domestic actuals and studio-reported international actuals; downward revisions do occur, but they are of the order of hundreds of thousands to low single-digit millions, typically when an estimate is trued up to actuals or a territory is reclassified. A $530M haircut has no precedent for any wide release, let alone one whose milestones have been independently confirmed by Variety, Deadline and The Hollywood Reporter trade reporting. The redundancy in the resolution clause helps further: the question resolves YES on either source, so a data error confined to one aggregator cannot flip it. Today both sources agree to the dollar, which is itself weak evidence that the underlying feed is clean rather than one site carrying a stale or mis-keyed figure.

On (b), the extraction friction on Box Office Mojo noted above is the only observable that moved at all today, and it points at my retrieval method rather than at the source. The Numbers resolved cleanly on the first attempt. Even in a scenario where Box Office Mojo went dark permanently, The Numbers alone satisfies the resolution criterion, and vice versa. Trade press has independently and repeatedly recorded the $1B international and $2B worldwide milestones, so the factual record would survive the loss of both aggregators for any reasonable adjudication.

The forecast therefore stays at 100 with an 80% CI of [100, 100]. As stated yesterday, 100 here is a rounding of a probability above 99.9%, not a claim of logical certainty. The skill's guidance against extreme probabilities without extreme evidence is satisfied: the evidence is that the outcome has already occurred and is published on both named resolution sources with a 35 percent margin over the threshold, cross-confirmed by three independent trade outlets. Holding anything meaningfully below 100 would be a failure of calibration in the other direction, paying a scoring penalty for a hedge against an event with no reference-class instances. The only remaining function of continued daily monitoring is to catch a resolution-mechanics anomaly, not to track box office performance, which has been irrelevant to this question for about a week.

question: Will OpenAI and Anthropic have a combined ARR exceeding $70B by 31 December 2026?
key_change:
HOLD: 99 to 99. Nothing in the 18-19 August window moves the combined run-rate arithmetic below the $70bn bar; the day's biggest story was about the split between the two companies, not the total. Dated items follow. First, the Wall Street Journal, 18 August 2026, "OpenAI's Second-Quarter Sales Show Tepid Growth Compared With Anthropic": OpenAI generated $6.7bn of revenue in the three months to June, up from $5.7bn in Q1, an 18% sequential increase, while its operating loss including stock-based compensation widened to $12.3bn from $9.3bn. The same report puts Anthropic's Q2 revenue at $11.6bn with an operating profit of $559m, the first quarter in which Anthropic's sales exceeded OpenAI's. I could not fetch the WSJ piece directly (hard paywall); I verified the figures through SiliconANGLE's full-text write-up (Mike Wheatley, published 19 August 01:25 UTC, which links and quotes the WSJ story), plus Investing.com, PYMNTS and a KuCoin newswire flash, all consistent on $6.7bn, $5.7bn, 18%, $12.3bn, $9.3bn, $11.6bn and $559m. Second, SiliconANGLE adds that OpenAI told investors privately its growth rate has accelerated since the July model generation launched, without supplying numbers, and notes chief revenue officer Denise Dresser's departure after less than a year, following Brad Lightcap and Fidji Simo. Third, Forbes (Jon Markman, 18 August) and Fortune (18 August) both published follow-ups on Anthropic's $65bn run rate; neither carries a new figure. Fourth, Bloomberg Television ran "Anthropic's $65 Billion Surge, OpenAI's Teen Push" on 18 August, again a restatement. Fifth, I fetched the Axios piece (Madison Mills, 17 August, free) in full: it confirms Anthropic's preliminary Q2 revenue above $11.5bn per documents seen by Bloomberg, Q1 of $4.73bn implying a sequential increase above 140%, the $65bn run rate reached at end-July, and OpenAI's $40bn run rate per Greg Brockman's internal message. Axios explicitly flags that the two companies may not measure revenue the same way, and reports Anthropic meeting new investors ahead of an IPO expected September or October with Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan, and OpenAI on track to draw over half its revenue from enterprise by year end. Sixth, no public S-1 exists for either company as of 19 August; Anthropic's confidential draft was submitted 1 June 2026 and OpenAI's in early June, with reporting since late June that OpenAI may push its listing to 2027 rather than accept below a $1trn valuation. Seventh, the other OpenAI items dated 18 August are non-financial: the guardrailed junior version of ChatGPT launched, some training runs were paused over cybersecurity concerns, and on 17 August it leased a 10GW data centre campus from SoftBank's SB Energy.

The arithmetic is unchanged. On exit run rate, the measure the resolution language points at when it says ARR, Anthropic is above $65bn as of end-July (Bloomberg, 17 August) and OpenAI is above $40bn as of mid-August (Bloomberg, 13 August, sourced to Brockman's internal note that monthly run rate grew more than 20% in July alone). Combined, roughly $105bn against a $70bn threshold, a cushion of $35bn. For NO, the pair would have to shed a third of their combined run rate in the four and a half months to 31 December while both are mid-IPO-process and both are still growing. That is not a forecastable event; it is a discontinuity.

The one genuinely new consideration from 18 August is the gap between recognised revenue and claimed run rate at OpenAI. Four times Q2 revenue is $26.8bn, well short of the $40bn run rate, which tells you the $40bn is an exit-month annualisation rather than a trailing figure. Anthropic shows the same pattern less severely: four times $11.6bn is $46.4bn against a $65bn end-July run rate. If a resolver perversely used trailing-quarter-annualised revenue instead of ARR, the Q2 combined figure would be $18.3bn times four, or $73.2bn, still above $70bn but with only about 4.5% headroom. That is worth naming, but it cuts the right way over the remaining horizon: the question resolves on Q4, not Q2. For a Q4-actual-annualised reading to fail, combined Q4 revenue would have to come in below $17.5bn, against $18.3bn already booked in Q2 and with Anthropic having grown 140% sequentially into that quarter. Anthropic alone at roughly $16-18bn in Q3 would annualise to $64-72bn. So both the run-rate reading and the recognised-revenue reading point YES, the first with an enormous margin and the second with a comfortable and widening one.

Downside items I actively looked for and found: Ed Zitron's "Anthropic's Profitability Swindle" and institutional commentary on gross-versus-net treatment, front-loaded annual commitments, and the timing of the SpaceX compute contract, all arguing Anthropic's reported revenue and its Q2 operating profit flatter the underlying business; the WSJ's evidence that ChatGPT growth has stalled and that OpenAI cut prices on two recent models as enterprises shifted workloads to cheaper open-source and Chinese systems; and OpenAI's IPO slippage. None of these plausibly removes a third of the combined figure. Stress test the worst credible version: if a public S-1 forced Anthropic onto a strict net basis and halved its reported number to $32.5bn, adding OpenAI's $40bn still yields $72.5bn and the question still resolves YES. Halving both is the only path to NO, and no source suggests anything of the kind. Residual probability mass sits with resolver ambiguity, a restatement of both companies simultaneously, and genuine catastrophic tails, which together I keep at roughly 1%. Holding at 99 with the interval at 98 to 99.

question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
key_change:
Move: 34 to 32. The 18-19 August 2026 window contained one genuinely question-relevant release and several pieces of context, and on balance it removed the single most optimistic anchor in yesterday's reasoning. The decisive item is the ONS Productivity flash estimate and overview, UK: April to June 2026 and January to March 2026, published 18 August 2026 at 09:30 (I fetched this bulletin in full, plus the superseded 19 May 2026 edition, and the GOV.UK statistics landing page which confirms first-published-at 2026-08-18T09:30:01+01:00). Yesterday's forecast leaned explicitly on the 19 May release, in which the RTI/PAYE-based experimental measure showed output per hour up 2.1% year on year in Q1 2026 and 5.5% above the 2019 average, against a much weaker LFS-based headline of 0.4% year on year and 3.5% above 2019 — with ONS explicitly recommending users focus on the RTI approach. That optimistic anchor has now been overwritten by its own successor. In the 18 August print, the RTI-based flash estimate shows output per hour just 0.7% higher in the year to Q2 2026 (down from 2.1% in Q1), and minus 0.8% quarter on quarter, with the level 4.6% above the 2019 average — down from 5.5% a quarter earlier. Output per worker on the RTI basis is 1.4% higher year on year, versus 1.4% in Q1 and 1.9% in Q4 2025. ONS also quantifies the distortion from an operational error in LFS telephone collection between 3 May and 10 June 2026 (residual effects to 17 June): its best estimate is that without the issue, RTI-based output-per-hour growth would have been 0.6% rather than 0.7% in the year to Q2 2026. So the adjusted number is, if anything, slightly worse. The LFS-based measure is now outright negative: output per hour down 0.2% in the year to Q2 2026, and 2.3% above the 2019 average (down from 3.5% in Q1), with output per worker up 0.4%. Both series now converge on a picture of essentially stagnant productivity, whereas a day ago the two series told materially different stories and the ONS-preferred one was the good one.

The arithmetic matters more than the headline. Taking the RTI measure at face value, output per hour is 4.6% above the 2019 average as of Q2 2026 — roughly seven years — which compounds to about 0.64% a year. On the LFS measure, 2.3% over the same span is about 0.32% a year. Even ONS's preferred, more flattering series therefore implies a realised trend well below the roughly 1.0% underlying productivity growth the OBR assumes, and far below the 1.5%-plus that a decade average of GDP growth above 1.5% would require given demographics. The same bulletin reports whole-economy GVA up 7.1% versus the 2019 average, i.e. about 1.0% a year of actual realised GDP growth over the past seven years — a direct, ONS-sourced read on the very quantity this question is about, and one comfortably below the resolution bar. ONS also flagged that it is developing a new component-based approach to labour productivity, more closely aligned with RTI-based employment, with a methods article due in September 2026; and that initial findings from linking RTI to LFS and TLFS, which reconfirm that LFS recovery activity has reduced survey bias, will be published in autumn 2026. Those are scheduled resolution-relevant events, not evidence today, but they mean the measurement question that has been doing a lot of work in this forecast may be partially settled within two months.

The second item is the ONS Labour market overview, UK: August 2026, also released 18 August 2026 (I could not fetch the ONS bulletin page directly — provenance restrictions blocked it — so these figures come from search summaries of the ONS page and from the productivity bulletin's cross-references). Payrolled employees fell 78,000 (0.3%) in the year to June 2026 and were roughly flat on the month; the early July estimate was down 94,000 (0.3%) on the year at 30.3 million. The unemployment rate was 5.0% in April-June 2026, against 5.1% the previous quarter and 4.8% a year earlier. Around 3.9 million people are out of work and say they want a job, up 600,000 on two years ago, with 1.3 million young people not in work or full-time education. Annual regular pay growth was 3.5% and total pay 4.1% in April-June 2026, real regular pay up 0.5% on CPIH; public sector regular pay grew 6.1% against 2.8% in the private sector. This is a soft labour market, which is mostly cyclical and carries little direct information about the 2030s — but the scale of labour market detachment among the young is the kind of scarring that does show up in 2030s potential output, and the public-private pay wedge is a mild negative for aggregate measured productivity given the public sector's weaker measured output.

Third, ONS published Consumer price inflation, UK: July 2026 on 19 August 2026: CPI up 2.9% year on year (from 2.6% in June), CPIH 3.1% (from 2.8%), core CPI 2.6%, monthly CPI 0.3%, with the Ofgem cap rise of 13% on 1 July driving the housing and household services contribution and lower diesel prices offsetting through transport. The Bank's 30 July projection had CPI peaking near 3.2% in Q4 2026, so this is roughly on track and not itself a supply-side signal. It does, however, keep energy costs — a persistent structural drag on UK industrial competitiveness that the OECD flagged in its July 2026 UK survey — squarely in the picture. On 18 August the 10-year gilt yield was around 5.08%, its highest since 23 July, with 30-year around 5.7%, on a global bond selloff tied to Iran-related oil price pressure; the rise was capped by the weak labour market data. Elevated long-run real rates are a genuine 2030s headwind through the investment channel and through debt interest crowding out public capital spending.

Fourth, context just outside the window but bearing on interpretation: the ONS first quarterly estimate published 13 August 2026 put Q2 2026 GDP at plus 0.4% (after 0.6% in Q1), 1.2% higher year on year, with services up 0.5%, construction up 0.3% and production flat; June was plus 0.3%, May revised to zero, April minus 0.1%. Commentary around that release attributed nearly half of Q2 growth to information and communication and a surge in computer hardware spending — AI capex is now visible in the GDP accounts. The productivity bulletin corroborates the sectoral story: information and communication made the largest upward contribution to output per hour versus 2019 (plus 2.8 percentage points in Q1 2026), while human health and social work made the largest negative contribution (minus 0.9). This is the live bull case for the 2030s, but it is also the case that AI capex is capacity, not yet productivity, and the aggregate numbers released on 18 August show no economy-wide dividend yet.

Nothing in the window changed the fiscal or political backdrop, which is already priced: Andy Burnham became Prime Minister in July 2026, John Healey is Chancellor with a "growth in every postcode" framing and fiscal control as his "first duty", and the Budget is set for 28 October 2026. There was no new OBR, Bank of England, IMF or OECD publication on 18-19 August that I could locate; the most recent relevant supply-side statement remains Bailey's 14 July 2026 Mansion House speech. So the move is small and driven by one release. I take 2 percentage points off rather than a token 1, because the productivity flash is the flagship quarterly read on the exact variable that determines this question, it directly superseded the specific figure the prior forecast cited as its main upside anchor, and it moved that figure by 1.4 percentage points in the wrong direction while pulling the level series down 0.9 points. Two points is still a deliberately modest response to one noisy quarter.

On news, the window was busy but produced nothing resembling an AGI declaration. The AI Weekly index for 21 August records 179 tracked stories this week, down 42 percent on the prior week - a quiet week by volume, with the mix dominated by chips, funding and regulation rather than capability. The genuinely relevant items are two, and they point in opposite directions. First, on 20 August Anthropic published lab-validated results (anthropic.com/research/Claude-accelerates-protein-design) showing Claude designed protein binders that hit against 14 of 15 targets, independently produced and tested by Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience. Second, and cutting the other way, the 'Reconstruction' benchmark (arXiv 2608.16645, written up 19 August by TechTimes) uses a time-cut anti-leakage protocol to test whether models can recover what a paper proposed given only its pre-publication bibliography, across ML and five Nature-family domains. The braking evidence hardened slightly.
