question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
key_change:
Move: 13 to 12. The 19-21 August 2026 window produced almost nothing new that bears directly on resolution. I ran thirteen distinct searches and fetched five primary or near-primary sources, and the honest summary is that this was a quiet window in which the only genuinely load-bearing item is one I verified myself from official data rather than one that broke in the news. I am therefore making a small downward move rather than a hold, and the reason is arithmetic rather than headline.

The substantive item is the US Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Employment Statistics series CES6054160001, All Employees, Management, Scientific, and Technical Consulting Services, which I pulled in full from FRED today. The series was last updated 7 August 2026 at 8:33am CDT and the next release is 4 September 2026, so the print itself is not new to the window; what is new is that I have now checked the whole series and can state the resolution arithmetic exactly rather than approximately. July 2026 stands at 1,886,600 employees, seasonally adjusted. June 2026, at 1,888,100, is the highest monthly figure in the entire history of the series, which runs from January 1990. May 2026 was 1,878,000, April 1,879,500 and March 1,875,200. The twelve monthly values for 2024 average 1,860,500. So US consulting employment in July 2026 sits 1.4% above the 2024 baseline and 1.5% above July 2025 (1,859,000). A 33% fall from the 2024 average implies an end-2030 level of about 1,246,600. From the July 2026 level that is a fall of roughly 640,000 jobs, or 33.9%, in the fifty-three months from August 2026 to December 2030. Compounded, that is about minus 9.0% a year sustained for four years and five months, with no interruption. Against that, the deepest peak-to-trough drawdown this series has ever recorded is the pandemic shock: 1,569,000 in February 2020 to 1,474,100 in April 2020, a fall of 6.0%, fully recovered inside about ten months. The 2001 dot-com bust took it from 743,800 in March 2001 to 721,800 in July 2002, a fall of 3.0%. The global financial crisis took it from 1,048,000 in September 2008 to 1,016,100 in May 2010, again 3.0%. In thirty-six and a half years of monthly data covering two recessions and a pandemic, this series has never fallen more than about 6%, and never for more than about eighteen months. The question asks whether it falls by a third, over more than four years, and whether that fall is then attributed primarily to AI by two or more credible analyses. Having the numbers in front of me rather than in summary makes the required discontinuity look larger than I had been carrying it, and that justifies a further small step down.

On the news flow itself. I fetched the Consultancy.uk news index directly on 21 August. It carried five items dated 20 August and five dated 19 August, and no items dated 21 August were indexed at time of fetch. The 20 August set: Capital Economics publishing a paper arguing the new administration may shift the tax burden from businesses toward capital, wealth and income; environmental consultancy ECL joining private-equity-backed Celnor Group's safety and compliance division; TCS collaborating with Rolls-Royce on hydrogen-powered flight engineering; an advisory piece headlined "Five hard AI questions most boards are ignoring", whose framing is that AI transformation is a human capital discipline; and BDO appointing Justin Rodrigues and Owen Burn as partners. The 19 August set: research on sales and marketing misalignment reporting that fewer than one in ten B2B leaders are highly confident of hitting growth targets; Mark Hickford joining Leonard Curtis restructuring as a director; a Kotter's-eight-steps change management piece; the Alpha FMC article on stalling financial services AI pilots that I logged yesterday; and Unit4 adding Christoffer Crona and Ian Owen. Not one of these is a headcount reduction, a fee compression disclosure, a guidance cut or a contraction story. Two are new partner appointments and one is an acquisition. The Capital Economics item is a small but real NO-side signal in its own right: a UK economic consultancy publishing branded macro-fiscal analysis that a trade outlet picks up as news is exactly the activity the YES case says AI is eroding, and the market for it looks intact.

I fetched the Credit Protection Association's daily UK business round-up for 20 August 2026, published 07:43 UTC and modified 09:51. UK CPI rose to 2.9% in July from 2.6% in June, a four-month high and slightly above the Bank of England's July projection of 2.8%, with the household energy price cap up 13%. KPMG chief economist Yael Selfin expects inflation to drift towards about 3.5%; ICAEW's Suren Thiru called inflation one of the biggest threats to UK growth. Cornwall Insight forecasts a further 4% cap rise in October. On the other side, the British Retail Consortium's confidence index rose eight points to minus 28, its best since the start of the Iran conflict, and GfK improved at its fastest pace since November 2023. JD Sports cut full-year adjusted pre-tax profit guidance to 700-800 million pounds from 750-850 million, with comparable sales down 3.1%. Markets: the 30-year US Treasury yield reached a 19-year high of 5.34% before the Treasury doubled long-dated buybacks to at least 4 billion dollars per operation, pulling it back to roughly 5.18-5.22%; Brent crude was 93.08 dollars, up 1.59%; US federal debt passed 40 trillion dollars. The insolvency notices comprised 14 administrations, 4 liquidations and 82 winding-up petitions. Consultancy-adjacent names appear but are all micro-firms with no AI angle: VLEONET IT CONSULTANCY SERVICES LIMITED in liquidation, CLAUS OUTSOURCING ADVISORS AND MANAGEMENT LTD and GOLDENPEAKS ADVISERS LIMITED among the petitions. The macro picture matters mainly for the attribution leg: a consultancy contraction produced by 5%-plus long yields, 93-dollar oil and near-3% inflation would not read as AI-caused to a careful analyst, and confounding of this kind cuts against YES.

On the YES side, the window did refresh one tracker. The Outsource Accelerator report "AI-linked layoffs hit 205,000 workers in 2026", published 12 August and modified 19 August 2026, cites the ResumePulse August 2026 tracker: AI or automation named as a primary or contributing driver in job losses affecting 205,000 US workers, already matching the full-year 2025 total in under eight months; the share of organisations citing AI in layoff announcements more than doubled since January 2026; May and June set the tracker's highest monthly AI-cited totals. It also cites Challenger, Gray and Christmas finding AI the leading stated reason for corporate job cuts in March and April 2026, the first time a technology factor topped its monthly rationale rankings, with AI-cited BPO-adjacent cuts approaching 49,000 through mid-year. Crucially, the composition works against the consulting thesis: the cuts are concentrated in customer service, data operations, entry-level software and finance back offices. Challenger's July report, separately, shows technology at 149,023 cuts through July, up 67% year on year and 31% of all cuts, with Services at 23,942 and a headline that hiring plans are up 25% year on year, summarised by Challenger as AI shifting the labour market but not dismantling it. And the Gartner survey of 110 CHROs released 27 July 2026 remains genuinely two-sided: 22% report at least one leader has stopped entry-level hiring because of AI, but only 20% of organisations report significant or transformational value from AI despite 95% having implemented it in some form.

What did not move the estimate: no listed consultancy news at all in the window. CRA International's most recent items remain the 6 August Q2 FY2026 record-revenue release with raised guidance and the same-day 400 million dollar credit facility increase and extension. FTI Consulting published two insight pieces on 18 August, on geopolitical risk in payments and supply chains and on Salesforce configuration in investigations, neither financial. Accenture's most recent reported quarter shows Q3 FY2026 new bookings of 19.32 billion dollars, down 2% in dollars and 3% in local currency, which is a mild YES-side signal but predates this window by two months. Nothing surfaced on NERA, Cornerstone Research, Compass Lexecon, Analysis Group or Brattle. I could not verify any 21 August dated item bearing on the question, and I could not fetch the CPA round-up for 21 August because the URL was outside the allowed provenance set; I note that gap rather than guessing at its contents.

So: a thin window, one strong self-verified disconfirming datapoint on the arithmetic, continued AI-attribution momentum that keeps missing consulting specifically, and a macro backdrop that would confound any contraction that did occur. Minus one point.

question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?

Find Out Now, fieldwork 19 August GB: Conservatives 18 (-2), Labour 23 (+1), Liberal Democrats 11 (nc), Greens 14 (nc), Reform 23 (-1) - also a dead heat, and a two-point relative improvement for Labour against Find Out Now's own 12 August reading of Reform 24, Labour 22. So the direction of travel is not uniform: three of the four newest polls either held Labour's position or improved it against the same pollster's previous wave, and only YouGov moved sharply against. But the level matters more than the direction. Averaging the Labour-versus-Reform margin across the four newest polls gives +2, -2, 0, 0, or zero. The evidence base that supported the 53-54 readings earlier this month averaged materially better: Opinium 12-14 August +2, JL Partners 8-11 August +3, Ipsos 30 July-4 August +3, Trajectory 4-12 August +6, BMG 28-30 July +5. Labour's polled lead has roughly halved to nothing over about two weeks. Third, the aggregators disagree with each other in an instructive way. PollCheck's seven-poll moving average, refetched today and stamped 20 August 2026, reads Labour 25.9, Reform 24.3, Conservatives 19.4, Liberal Democrats 10.7, Greens 10.7 - a 1.6-point Labour lead, actually wider than the 1.0-point lead in its 16 August reading of Labour 25.7, Reform 24.7, Conservatives 20.3. That widening is a rolling-window artefact: weak Labour polls from late July are dropping out faster than the new soft ones are coming in. BritPolls' live poll-of-polls ticker, by contrast, now reads Reform 24.8, Labour 24.6, Conservatives 19.6, Greens 11.2, Liberal Democrats 11.0 - Reform ahead by two tenths, flipped from Labour +1.4 (Reform 23.8, Labour 25.2) in the version cached on 19 August. BritPolls is the weaker source - its body copy still describes Starmer as prime minister and dates its chart to June 2026 - so I weight PollCheck and Pack's raw table more heavily. Taken together the honest read is that the aggregate Labour lead is somewhere between zero and 1.6 points and is no longer growing. Fourth, the seat models. Electoral Calculus has still not refreshed: its prediction page remains stamped 28 July 2026 with Labour 244, Conservatives 132, Reform 127, Liberal Democrats 70, SNP 44, on Labour 23.9 and Reform 23.4, P(Labour largest) 58 per cent, P(Reform largest) 25 per cent, P(Conservative largest) 16 per cent, and a 90 per cent seat interval for Labour of 88-357 against 53-289 for Reform. Its commentary of 30 July still describes a 'definite Burnham bounce'. PollCheck's seat tracker, refetched today, now projects Labour 263, Reform 145, Conservatives 90, Liberal Democrats 74 - Labour largest by 118 seats but down from the Labour 275, Reform 133, Conservatives 101 in the prior. The page still carries a 'data through 29 July 2026' label even though its underlying seven-poll average is stamped 20 August, so I treat the movement as indicative rather than authoritative. Either way, every seat model that has seen post-Burnham fieldwork still has Labour clearly largest, and that first-past-the-post efficiency argument is the load-bearing plank of the YES case. Fifth, the markets barely moved. Ladbrokes still has Labour as favourite for most seats at an implied 38 per cent against Reform at under 31 per cent on OLBG's reading, essentially unchanged from the roughly 40 per cent normalised figure in the prior and still well below Electoral Calculus's today-conditional 58 per cent. Polymarket's 'UK election called by' event did shift, and against the YES case: December 31 2026 now trades at 10 cents, down from 15, and June 30 2027 at 30 cents, down from 32. A later election means more time for the honeymoon to decay and less weight on the currently Labour-favourable seat arithmetic. Sixth, the qualitative ledger is close to a wash and if anything mildly pro-Labour. Reform's organisational attrition continued through the window: Mark Pack's tracker of Reform councillors lost since the May 2026 elections was last modified on 19 August 2026 at 19:52 UTC and now runs to 33 entries from the May 2026 cohort plus 28 from earlier cohorts, with August additions including Matthew Elder in Hillingdon, Alex Barr in South Tyneside, David Rowan suspended in Kirklees, Carol Ney in Plymouth, Helen Butler in Leicestershire and Ian Catchpole in County Durham. One entry is directly diagnostic of the welfare gamble: Cornwall parish councillor John Bell resigned from both his council and from Reform 'over its plans to cut welfare benefits'. Farage's own position also carries a live tail risk - his 14 August Clacton win on 62 per cent of the vote and a 36 per cent majority automatically resumed the parliamentary standards commissioner's inquiry into the 5 million pound gift from Christopher Harborne, a gift separately reported to the National Crime Agency under the suspicious activity report scheme, and a finding against him could trigger a recall petition. Reporting suggests his advisers had incorrectly assumed the inquiry would not restart. Seventh, leader ratings remain the strongest single pillar of the YES case and did not deteriorate. Survation on 18 August has Burnham net +14 against Farage -18 and Badenoch +6; More in Common 14-17 August has Burnham +16 and Farage -20; YouGov's August favourability piece has 46 per cent favourable towards Burnham, up twelve points since before he entered Number 10, for a net +13, the highest its tracker has recorded for a prime minister since May 2020, with favourable views held by 76 per cent of 2024 Labour voters, 68 per cent of Liberal Democrats, 53 per cent of Greens, 31 per cent of Conservatives and 15 per cent of 2024 Reform voters. Eighth, the calendar. Burnham's first budget is confirmed for October 2026, following the removal of the 5 per cent VAT on domestic electricity from 1 October 2026 (worth roughly 45 pounds on an average annual bill, running to March 2027) and a 2 pound single bus fare cap in England outside London from 1 January 2027. The giveaways are front-loaded; the fiscal reckoning is eight weeks away and is the canonical honeymoon-killer. Weighing all this: the fresh fieldwork is the first hard evidence that the Burnham bounce has plateaued and begun to erode at the margin, which is what the mid-term-succession reference class says should happen. The counterweights - three of four polls holding or improving against their own previous wave, PollCheck's average still showing Labour ahead, every post-Burnham seat model still showing Labour largest by 100-plus seats, continuing Reform attrition - are real and stop this being a larger move. A two-point cut to 49 is the proportionate response, leaving the estimate slightly below the coin flip and roughly midway between the bookmakers' 38 and Electoral Calculus's 58.

question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2035?
key_change:
HOLD: 85 to 85. The 19-21 August 2026 window produced an unusually rich news flow for a quiet late-August week, but nothing in it moves a question with an eight-and-a-half year horizon and a rhetorical resolution bar. The most valuable thing I did today was not find news but find a market I had not previously priced. Kalshi runs a series, KXAGICO-COMP, titled 'When will any company achieve AGI?' with the subtitle 'Corporate announcement'. Its rules_primary text, pulled from the Kalshi trade API today, reads: 'If any company (public or private) officially announces that it has achieved Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) after market issuance and before [date], then the market resolves to Yes.' That is an almost exact match for the first limb of this question's resolution criteria, and far closer than the Metaculus, Manifold or Goodheart constructs I have been leaning on. The daily candlesticks as of today show: 'Before Jan 1, 2028' with a bid of 0.40 and an ask of 0.47, last trade 0.41 on 18 August on 200 contracts of volume, open interest 3,875; 'Before Jan 1, 2030' bid 0.67 ask 0.74, last trade 0.67 on 15 August, open interest 2,265; and 'Before Jan 1, 2031' bid 0.73 ask 0.80, last trade 0.80 on 16 August, open interest 3,805. There were zero trades on 19, 20 or 21 August in any of the three, and the bid-ask spreads are 6 to 7 points wide, so this is thin and stale rather than a live consensus. But taking mid prices of roughly 70.5 percent by 2030 and 76.5 percent by 2031, the implied conditional hazard of an AGI announcement in calendar 2030 is about 20 to 24 percent of the surviving mass. Rolling that forward with a slowly decaying hazard through 2032, 2033 and 2034 lands at roughly 85 to 88 percent by 1 January 2035. That is an independent corroboration of my standing central estimate from a contract whose wording nearly matches the question, and it is the reason I am tightening the lower bound of the interval from 73 to 74 rather than changing the central figure. Kalshi has no tranche beyond 2031, so the extrapolation is mine, not the market's, and I have not treated it as more than confirmatory.

The aggregator I have tracked daily is flat. The Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard, fetched today at agi.goodheartlabs.com, reads 'Our combined forecast estimates AGI will arrive in 2031, as of August 21, 2026' with an 80 percent confidence band of 2027 to 2043. That is character-for-character the same median and the same interval as the 18, 19 and 20 August readings. Because the dashboard blends the Metaculus weakly-general question (3479), the Metaculus strict general-AI question (5121), the Metaculus long adversarial Turing test question (11861), the Manifold 'AGI When? [High Quality Turing Test]' distribution and the Kalshi Turing-test contract, a flat print is a five-source null rather than one stale feed. The Metaculus API is now behind authentication and returned 'Permission Error: The API is only available to authenticated users' on both the /api/posts/5121/ and legacy /api2/ endpoints, so I again cannot verify the strict general-AI median directly and am relying on secondary reporting (AIToolsReview, veracalloway) that it remains January 2033 across roughly 1,800 forecasters with about 25 percent by 2029. Treat those as approximately rather than exactly current.

I did pull the Manifold distribution live. The high-quality-Turing-test AGI market (1,076 unique bettors) now puts 0.01 percent on 2024-2025, 0.02 on 2025-2026, 1.71 on 2026-2027, 4.51 on 2027-2028, 8.14 on 2028-2029, 15.59 on 2029-2030, 10.27 on 2030-2031, 7.78 on 2031-2032, 7.25 on 2032-2033, 6.57 on 2033-2034 and 5.93 on 2034-2035. Cumulative mass before 2035 is therefore about 62 to 68 percent depending on how the final bucket is read. Summing the reported bucket-level probability changes, that cumulative figure moved plus 0.7 points over the past week and plus 6.8 points over the past month, with the month's move concentrated in the 2029-2030 bucket (plus 4.96 points) and the 2030-2031 bucket (plus 2.18 points), offset by decay in the 2040s tail. Twenty-four hour volume was 50 mana. So Manifold has drifted modestly earlier over a month, essentially nothing over the window, and on negligible turnover. Polymarket's 'OpenAI announces it has achieved AGI before 2027?' is quoted at 8.5 cents (bid 8, ask 9), last trade 9 cents, one-week price change minus 0.5 points, 24-hour volume of 11 dollars. That is a fractional drift down from the 9 to 11 cent range I recorded previously, on volume too small to interpret. I found no other open Polymarket AGI or Turing-test market in the top 800 by volume.

On forecaster opinion, the one genuinely new dated item is the AI Futures Project's 'Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update: Uplift and Revenue', published 16 August 2026 and picked up in Zvi Mowshowitz's roundup on 20 August. Per that summary, the AGI medians are now 2028 for Daniel Kokotajlo and 2032 for Eli Lifland, with ASI following about a year later, and the authors say their timelines 'haven't changed much (they got slightly shorter)' while their modelling and evidence base have 'noticeably improved', so they feel somewhat more confident. Both medians sit comfortably inside the 2035 horizon, and the Q1 2026 update had already moved Kokotajlo's Automated Coder median from late 2029 to mid 2028. This is a mild positive, but it is the same two forecasters I already count among the fast tail and it is worth well under a point.

Cutting the other way, the single strongest substantive item in the window is the Princeton-led study covered by MIT Technology Review on 18 August under the headline 'AI's recursive self-improvement might not come so quickly after all', with follow-on coverage at R&D World and normaltech on 19-20 August. Peter Kirgis and Sayash Kapoor and colleagues (arXiv 2607.27191) built a 'shadow evaluation' in which agents must answer the research question of an unpublished NeurIPS 2026 submission, so the answer cannot be memorised. Agents running Claude Opus 4.8 on OpenClaw were given six days, 3,000 dollars of Anthropic API credit, a GPU budget, their own virtual machines and open web access. The original human authors graded the resulting papers and rejected both. Kapoor's finding is precise and, for this question, more informative than another benchmark number: the agents could do all the research engineering, reviewed the literature and ran hundreds of experiments, but 'were unambiguously bad at carrying out the research itself' - committing to unpromising approaches too fast, rejecting their own good hypotheses on thin data, unable to backtrack or fundamentally rethink, and unable to incorporate reviewer feedback except by narrowing claims. Notably they did not reward-hack. Anthropic cofounder Jack Clark, writing in Import AI, called this lack of creativity 'a bearish signal on short recursive self-improvement timelines'. Related: Sev Field's interviews with 25 researchers, circulating on 19-20 August, found 20 of 25 naming automated AI R&D as one of the most severe risks but only 6 of 25 expecting winner-take-all dynamics, and only 4 of 20 expecting AI-research-capable models to be publicly released at all. That last figure is the mildly awkward one for this question, since resolution requires a public announcement rather than a public release; but a lab that keeps a model internal can still announce what it has, as OpenAI and Anthropic have both effectively done with Astra and Model 2.

I weight the Kirgis-Kapoor result as a real but small negative, worth perhaps half a point, and I resist a larger move for three reasons. First, Clark's own framing is about short timelines; a two-paper study showing agents cannot yet win at NeurIPS says little about 2032. Second, the study's stated limitations are severe - two papers, graders who knew the work was AI-generated, and large researcher discretion. Third, the authors are rerunning it on Anthropic's Mythos, which is more capable than the Opus 4.8 they tested and is now restricted to approved organisations under Trump administration requirements, so the headline result is already a lower bound on the current frontier.

The rest of the window is context rather than signal. Axios reported on 19 August that Stripe told investors it treats 1 January 2026 as 'the beginning of the singularity' and has run the business on that basis for eight months, alongside confirming an OpenRouter acquisition reported at 7.5 to 8 billion dollars. Zvi's reaction - that Stripe is doing to 'singularity' what Zuckerberg did to 'superintelligence' - is exactly the double-edged dynamic at the heart of this question: term inflation makes a grandiose corporate AGI claim more likely, and simultaneously erodes the currency of the term. Bloomberg reported on 20 August that Anthropic and OpenAI are clashing over a Massachusetts Senate economic development bill requiring independent catastrophic-risk reviews of frontier models at least every 120 days, with results published but no power to halt development; Anthropic's state affairs lead called it 'the clearest and strongest AI safety legislation in the country' while OpenAI warned it could delay cyber-defensive model rollouts. Against that, the 1 August deadline under Executive Order 14409 for a classified NSA/CISA/NIST benchmarking process, a Treasury-led voluntary disclosure framework and an OPM cyber workforce plan lapsed with no public deliverables, which is evidence that federal braking capacity is weaker than the June executive order implied. On money, Bloomberg and TechCrunch reported on 17-18 August that Anthropic's annualised revenue run rate passed 65 billion dollars at the end of July, up from 47 billion in May, with a confidential IPO filing and valuation talk above 2 trillion dollars; and the Nvidia-OpenAI Ohio backstop settled at 105 billion dollars for 4.25 GW firm plus a 3.75 GW option, which Fortune framed on 18 August as 145 billion dollars below earlier reporting. Zvi's 20 August roundup also notes agentic use has reached 64 percent of all OpenAI tokens, up from almost none a year ago, METR raising about 71 million dollars, OpenAI advertising a role in recursive-self-improvement safety, and data centre moratoriums spreading at local level. Netting a slightly bearish RSI study against slightly shorter AI Futures medians, a directly matched Kalshi contract implying the mid-to-high 80s, a flat five-source aggregator and two markets moving by less than a point on trivial volume, this is a textbook hold.

question: Will China initiate a military blockade or invasion of Taiwan before 1 January 2030?
key_change:
HOLD: 7 to 7. The 19-21 August 2026 window was, on the military side, one of the quietest of the month, and the material that did land was overwhelmingly about Taiwanese fiscal politics rather than coercion. I am holding the central estimate and widening the upper bound of the interval by one point, from 10 to 11, for reasons set out at the end.

Start with the biggest dated item. On 20 August 2026 Taiwan's Cabinet approved the 2027 central government budget proposal, allocating NT$1.1225 trillion (US$35.16 billion) to defence, or 3.01 percent of projected GDP. Focus Taiwan timestamped the story at 16:04 on 20 August; the Taipei Times front page of Friday 21 August carries it as its lead, sourced to CNA with additional reporting from Hollie Younger and Reuters, and the Japan Times, Washington Post/AP, Washington Times, SCMP and Janes all ran versions on 20 August. The composition matters: NT$691.9 billion in the Ministry of National Defense budget, NT$218.2 billion in special budgets, NT$60.7 billion in non-profit special funds, plus NT$103.8 billion in military pensions and NT$47.9 billion for the Coast Guard Administration, on a NATO-style definition that President Lai has explicitly adopted. The headline is an 18 percent increase and the first time the figure has passed NT$1 trillion, with Lai targeting 5 percent of GDP by 2030. Two caveats a careless reader would miss. First, as a share of GDP the number falls, from 3.32 percent this year to 3.01 percent next year, because the overall budget rises 29.4 percent to NT$3.9266 trillion on the back of an AI-driven revenue surge and a NT$235.7 billion universal cash handout. Second, the budget still has to survive the opposition-controlled Legislative Yuan, which passed the 2026 budget only on 14 August after what CNA called a record 266-day delay (I note this corrects the 350-day figure carried in my prior write-up). So the defence build-out is real but not yet banked, and 21 August produced no Chinese response to it that I could find in Chinese Foreign Ministry, Taiwan Affairs Office or Global Times output.

The second dated item cuts the same way. On 19 August CNA reported that the first two of 66 F-16V Block 70 aircraft, tail numbers 6727 and 6728, departed the United States on 17 August Eastern time and are en route to Taiwan with air-to-air refuelling and a maintenance stop. The Peace Phoenix Soaring programme cost NT$247.2 billion between 2020 and 2026 and had slipped badly because of the production-line relocation and supply-chain disruption; Lockheed Martin has been running two shifts up to 20 hours a day. Delivery beginning is a genuine, if incremental, hardening of the target.

Third, on 20 August the Mainland Affairs Council released a poll conducted for it by National Chengchi University's Election Study Center between 13 and 17 August, n=1,086, margin of error plus or minus 2.97 points. Some 70.5 percent of respondents regard the Chinese coast guard patrols east of Taiwan as an act of ill will against 7.5 percent who see goodwill; 81.2 percent oppose one country, two systems; 83.6 percent favour maintaining the status quo; 83.9 percent say Taiwan's future should be decided by its 23 million people; 68.9 percent explicitly reject unification with the CCP. MAC notes the trend is stable. This is double-edged. It shows Beijing's maritime-legal accretion is generating hostility rather than acquiescence, which is an argument that the gray-zone track is failing and could eventually be abandoned for something harder; but it also shows that a blockade would face a population with no appetite for capitulation, which is the main reason blockades of this kind rarely deliver political results and are therefore rarely attempted. Also on 20 August the Central Election Commission fixed the nine-in-one local elections for 28 November 2026, with 11,051 offices and roughly 19.65 million eligible voters, pinning the date of the political failure point I have been tracking.

On the military tempo, the window is reassuring rather than alarming, and it revises my reading of the 19 August spike. Taiwan's MND, via its Political Warfare Bureau, logged 20 PLA aircraft sorties, 7 PLAN ships and 6 official ships in the 0600 18 August to 0600 19 August period, with 15 of the 20 entering the northern, central, southwestern and eastern ADIZ. I flagged that four-fold jump as noise on 19 August. It now has an explanation: MND issued a separate press release at 1310 on 18 August stating that from 0855 that morning it had detected 18 sorties of J-10, J-11, J-16 and KJ-500 aircraft, 13 of which penetrated the median line or its extension, coordinating with PLAN vessels under the pretext of a so-called joint combat readiness patrol. Per the GlobalSecurity archive of MND releases, that was the third such JCRP announcement in August alone, after 4 and 15 August. JCRPs are unnamed, short, recurring and have never converted into anything; a JCRP-driven one-day sortie count of 20 sits well inside a 2024-25 baseline that regularly exceeded 30. Nothing in the window resembles a warning indicator: no named exercise, no NOTAM or closure area, no mobilisation, no requisitioning of civilian roll-on/roll-off ferries, no reserve call-up. Taiwan's own Friday front pages, per CNA's 21 August headline roundup at 1019, are the 2027 budget (United Daily News, Liberty Times, Taipei Times), record July export orders of US$97.9 billion (Economic Daily News, Commercial Times) and a KMT unity event (China Times). When Taipei's press treats the strait as unremarkable, that is evidence.

Beijing's output in the window was rhetorical and united-front in character. On 19 August Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian welcomed Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's statement that Taiwan is part of China and repeated that China must and will be reunified, and Global Times ran a companion piece claiming the DPP was rattled; also on 19 August a mainland spokesperson in People's Daily criticised the DPP for obstructing cross-strait exchanges. That is legitimacy work, not military signalling.

The one genuinely upward item consummates rather than extends the story I logged on 19 August. USNI News reported on 20 August that USS George Washington (CVN-73), with USS Robert Smalls (CG-62) and USS Shoup (DDG-86), arrived in the CENTCOM area of responsibility on 19 August after transiting the Arabian Sea, to relieve USS Abraham Lincoln, which has been deployed 272 days and gone 252 without a port call. USS Theodore Roosevelt is in San Diego after RIMPAC 2026, and no replacement carrier has been announced for the western Pacific. So the gap is now a fact, not a projection. I want to flag a trap I nearly fell into: a Newsweek piece headlined 'Oldest US Aircraft Carrier Fills Pacific Power Gap With China' surfaces in searches for this, but it is dated 24 March 2025 and concerns the Nimitz; it does not apply, and I am not treating the gap as filled. Even so, I weight this modestly. A carrier gap in Asia also occurred in 2024 without incident, an invasion requires months of observable preparation that has not begun, and the September summit calendar argues against action.

That calendar is intact. The White House and Secretary Rubio continue to confirm Xi's state visit to Washington on 24 September 2026, with Rubio framing the aim as another positive visit, notwithstanding Trump's July claims that China compromised 220 million voter files, which he himself downplayed within five days and which declassified intelligence undercut per Washington Post reporting of 30 July. Meanwhile the US$14 billion Taiwan arms package that Congress pre-approved in January 2026, reportedly including PAC-3 MSE and NASAMS, was still in administrative review as of 7 August, with Representative McCaul expecting notification soon and analysts expecting it only after the summit. Both capitals are managing to the same date.

Markets, pulled live from the Polymarket Gamma API at 08:27-08:31 UTC on 21 August: invasion by end-2026 sits at 3.8 percent Yes on US$39.88 million volume and US$584.8k liquidity; invasion by 30 September 2026 at 0.85 percent Yes on US$2.00 million; any China-Taiwan military clash before 2027 at 7.55 percent on US$3.23 million. The September market has softened from roughly 98.8 percent No on 12 August to 99.15 percent No. Manifold's ACX 2026 market on China attacking or blockading Taiwan during 2026 is 8.9 percent, and its 'attempt to invade by end of 2027' market 12.1 percent on 180k mana.

Why widen the upper bound. Two things I found today argue my right tail has been narrowing too fast. First, MetaculusBot mirrors on Manifold for the long-running 'full-scale blockade against Taiwan before the following years' series show roughly 41 percent for 2030 and 57 percent for 2035, versus 3.0 percent for the resolved 2025 sub-question. Those mirrors are thin (410 and 345 mana), probably stale, and the live Metaculus aggregate would not render for me, so I treat them as weak evidence. But they are a reminder that a blockade-inclusive question over 3.4 years is a materially different animal from an invasion-only one. Second, Badu and Mastro's East Asia Forum piece of 5 July 2026, which I read in full, argues that US munitions depletion from the Iran campaign, with more than half of the pre-war inventory of four key munitions expended and full Tomahawk replenishment possibly as late as 2030, plus Admiral Paparo's April 2026 testimony on shortfalls in amphibious ships, destroyers and attack submarines, may make the late 2020s look more favourable to Beijing than the present. That places a genuine window inside the back half of this question's horizon. Their countervailing point is stronger still on the assault limb: Xi's purges have removed more than 100 officers since 2022, including 41 of the 47 officers holding three-star rank in or after 2022, leaving the Central Military Commission with two active members after the January 2026 ousters of Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli and six further removals in late June, with the Joint Staff Department hit hardest; the exercise record shows the strain, with Joint Sword organised in three to four days in 2024 against 19 days for Strait Thunder in April 2025. Their conclusion is that reconstituting command and control pushes the invasion timeline back further than US distraction pulls it forward, and that Beijing will prefer coercive maritime pressure and blockade rehearsals. That is a reallocation within my distribution rather than a change in its mass: less weight on assault, more on the blockade limb and on 2028-29 rather than 2026-27. Combined with the June 2026 precedent of Chinese coast guard vessels questioning commercial ships east of Taiwan and Taipei's July instruction that vessels refuse boarding demands, it justifies stopping the compression of the interval. Central estimate unchanged at 7; interval 4 to 11.

question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
key_change: HOLD: 1 to 1, 80% interval unchanged at [0, 1]. Two days after the July print, the evidence arriving on 20 and 21 August 2026 has all pushed in the same direction as the print itself, and the practical floor for an integer forecast is where this question now sits. The structural point flagged in yesterday's reasoning is now verified against primary sources rather than inferred. The ONS release page for 'Consumer price inflation, UK: December 2026' carries a stated release date of 20 January 2027 at 7:00am and is marked 'not yet published', which puts the December reference month unambiguously outside the window. The ONS release pages confirm September 2026 data on 21 October 2026 and October 2026 data on 18 November 2026, and the August 2026 reference month is scheduled for 16 September 2026. November 2026 publishes in mid-December. So exactly four reference months remain publishable before 1 January 2027: August, September, October and November. Four attempts, no more. The arithmetic of those four attempts is now nailed down with the ONS's own index numbers rather than approximations. Table 1 of the July 2026 bulletin gives the CPI index (UK, 2015=100) as 139.0 for July 2025, 139.3 for August 2025, 139.3 for September 2025, 139.8 for October 2025, 139.5 for November 2025, and 142.9 for July 2026. A published annual rate 'below 2.0%' requires a printed 1.9% or lower, which needs a true ratio under roughly 1.0195. Working that through: August 2026 needs an index below about 142.0, September below about 142.0, October below about 142.5, and November below about 142.2. From 142.9 in July, that means the UK price level must fall by about 0.63% in a single month to catch August, by 0.63% cumulatively to catch September, by 0.26% cumulatively over three months to catch October, or by 0.47% cumulatively over four months to catch November. October is the softest target because October 2025 was itself a strong month (index up 0.4% month on month), but it is also the month in which the Ofgem cap resets upward. Every one of these paths requires an outright fall in the price level over a stretch that is seasonally positive, and the Bank of England's own central path implies the index rising to roughly 143.9 by November, about 1.2% above the level that would be needed. Nothing published in the last 48 hours narrows that gap; several things widen it. First, energy. Ofgem's assessment window for the October to December 2026 cap closed on 18 August 2026 and the confirmed level is due by 26 August. Cornwall Insight's August update, the most recent, forecasts a 4% rise to GBP 1,729 under Ofgem's revised typical-consumption definition, up from GBP 1,663 today, with the equivalent figure on the old definition GBP 1,941 against GBP 1,862. That is an upward revision in substance relative to the GBP 1,699.59 figure carried in yesterday's reasoning, and the wider analyst range being quoted ahead of the announcement is GBP 1,701 to GBP 1,747, all of it above the current level. Critically, the zero-rating of VAT on domestic electricity from 1 October 2026 is already netted into that number, so the single largest disinflationary policy event inside the window is not enough to stop the cap rising. On my own arithmetic, a 4% cap rise against an electricity-and-gas CPI weight of roughly four per cent adds on the order of 0.15 percentage points to the index in October alone, which is more than half the 0.26% fall that the October route to YES would require, and it moves the index in the wrong direction. Cornwall Insight's 19 August commentary also points to a further rise on 1 January 2027, which is outside the window for resolution but tells you where the wholesale curve sits. Second, the energy inputs themselves have hardened since the 19 August assessment. Brent traded around USD 92.69 on 20 to 21 August, up more than 4% on the week and up from roughly USD 87 in mid-August, on a US-Iran impasse and an unresolved confrontation over the Strait of Hormuz; President Trump said oil continues to flow but offered only that he would be open to resuming talks 'at some point'. UK gas has moved with it: NBP spot was around USD 19.80 and TTF spot around USD 20.55 in mid-August, both up close to 10%, with the NBP Winter-26 contract settling at 149.20 pence per therm on 11 August. Lower LNG inflows and subdued storage injections are pulling the same way. Third, the official and consensus forecast distribution has if anything tightened around a rising path. HM Treasury published 'Forecasts for the UK economy: August 2026' on 19 August 2026; the July edition of the same comparison had the independent average for Q4 2026 CPI at 3.4%, revised down from 3.7% in June, so even the direction of revision leaves the average some 1.5 percentage points above the threshold. The Bank of England's July 2026 Monetary Policy Report has CPI peaking at around 3.2% in 2026 Q4 with risks tilted to the upside, and an escalation scenario reaching as high as 4.5% by mid-2027. Deutsche Bank has 3.3% to 3.5% in Q4. No publicly identifiable institutional forecast has any month between August and November 2026 below 2.0%, and commentary continues to frame all forecasts as showing inflation above target for the whole of 2026. The Bank also projects annual food price inflation near 3.5% in December, a re-acceleration from the 1.3% recorded in July, which removes the one CPI division currently running well below target as a source of further disinflation. Fourth, the policy signal. A Reuters poll conducted 13 to 18 August found nearly 90% of economists expect Bank Rate held at 3.75% through the end of the year, and no economist expects a change on 17 September; markets on 16 August put roughly a one-in-four chance on a September hike and are pricing one quarter-point increase before year-end. KPMG's Yael Selfin expects a hold for the rest of the year, on the view that the Bank looks through energy-driven rises provided underlying pressures stay contained. A rate path with a hike priced and no cut is flatly inconsistent with sub-2% prints inside four months. Fifth, today's own data. ONS retail sales for July, released 21 August, fell 0.5% on the month, the first decline since April, with non-food volumes down 1.3% and clothing down 2.7%. That is genuine demand weakness and it is the strongest single item on the YES side of today's ledger. But it is partially offset by GfK consumer confidence for August, also published 21 August, at minus 14, a two-year high, up from minus 17 in July and well ahead of the minus 18 consensus. The two cancel to roughly nothing for the four-month price-level question. The upside channels that remain are unchanged and small. Grocery inflation at 2.1% in the four weeks to 9 August and CPI food at 1.3%, the lowest since September 2021, leave food a mild drag, but the Bank expects that to reverse. The labour market is loosening, with unemployment at 4.9% against 4.7% a year earlier, vacancies at 707,000 in May to July and regular pay growth at 3.5%, but 3.5% pay growth is consistent with services inflation near 3.4%, not with a sub-2% headline in 2026. The Autumn Budget is now confirmed for 28 October 2026, Chancellor John Healey's first, and this is the one place a large discretionary shock could still originate. But the timing is now clearly against it: a measure announced on 28 October would have to take effect within days to touch the November reference month, the last one that publishes in time. The government's own announced package points the other way on timing, with the GBP 2 bus fare cap in England starting January 2027, outside the window. That materially weakens the Budget as a route to YES relative to how it was weighted yesterday. Netting it all out, today's information is mildly negative for YES and does not justify a numerical move. The true probability is plausibly a few tenths of one per cent; 1 is the smallest positive integer available and correctly represents the residual mass sitting on a catastrophic energy-price collapse, an unannounced and very large fiscal intervention with an immediate effective date, or an ONS methodology or data incident. Holding at 1 with the interval at [0, 1].

The question does not require the figure to still stand above $1.5B on 31 December; it requires the gross to have exceeded $1.5B by that date, and a cumulative gross is monotonically non-decreasing under normal accounting. So the only paths to NO are (a) a catastrophic downward restatement of about $546M, or 26.7 percent of the published worldwide total, sustained through year end and reflected on both sources, or (b) a resolution-mechanics failure in which neither source is consultable or an adjudicator applies some perverse reading. Neither is live. On (a), major-studio worldwide cumes are compiled from Comscore domestic actuals and studio-reported international actuals; downward revisions do happen, but they run from hundreds of thousands to low single-digit millions and typically arise when a weekend estimate is trued up to actuals or a territory is reclassified. A half-billion-dollar haircut has no precedent for any wide release, still less for one whose milestones have been independently confirmed by three or four trade outlets. The redundancy in the resolution clause reinforces this: the question resolves YES on either source, so an error confined to one aggregator cannot flip it. That both sources agree to the dollar on all three lines today is itself weak positive evidence that the underlying feed is clean rather than one site carrying a stale or mis-keyed number.

On (b), nothing moved adversely. The Numbers resolved on the first attempt; Box Office Mojo resolved on the first attempt and, unlike two days ago, rendered its summary block without difficulty. The forecast therefore stays at 100 with an 80% CI of [100, 100]. To be explicit about what that number means: 100 here is a rounding of a probability above 99.9%, not a claim of logical certainty. The skill's guidance against extreme probabilities absent extreme evidence is satisfied on its own terms, because the evidence is not a prediction but an observation - the outcome has already occurred, is published on both named resolution sources with a 36 percent margin over the threshold, and is cross-confirmed by independent trade reporting. Holding a meaningfully lower number would be a calibration failure in the opposite direction: paying a scoring penalty to hedge against an event class with zero observed instances. The honest residual is a few tenths of a percentage point covering resolver mechanics, wholesale re-audit scenarios and unmodelled pathways, and that residual is below the resolution of the integer scale the tracker uses. question: Will OpenAI and Anthropic have a combined ARR exceeding $70B by 31 December 2026?
key_change:
HOLD: 99 to 99. The 19-21 August window produced one genuinely new dated data point on the competitive split between the two companies and nothing at all that moves the combined run-rate arithmetic toward the $70bn bar. I ran a dozen distinct searches across Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, Reuters, The Information, CNBC, Axios, TechCrunch, Forbes and Fortune coverage plus company disclosures, and the standing verified figures are unchanged from yesterday. Dated items follow.

First, the anchor figures. Anthropic: revenue run rate above $65bn as at end-July 2026, reported by Bloomberg on 17 August (bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-17/anthropic-revenue-run-rate-surpasses-65-billion-ahead-of-ipo) and corroborated the same day by CNBC (cnbc.com/2026/08/17/anthropic-says-annualized-revenue-climbed-to-65-billion-in-july.html), Axios and TechCrunch. That is up from $47bn in May and roughly $9bn at end-2025. Anthropic's preliminary Q2 revenue was above $11.5bn (CNBC, 15 August), refined to $11.6bn with a $559m operating profit in the WSJ's 18 August piece, against $4.73bn in Q1 and $787m a year earlier. Second, OpenAI: annualised revenue run rate above $40bn, reported by Bloomberg on 13 August (bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-13/openai-s-revenue-run-rate-tops-40-billion-ahead-of-ipo) and repeated in Bloomberg's 14 August newsletter under the headline 'OpenAI Revenue Run Rate Tops $40 Billion, Doubling From 2025'. Supporting detail I confirmed today that I had not fully pinned down before: CFO Sarah Friar met investors on Friday 14 August and told them enterprise revenue now exceeds consumer revenue for the first time, that the enterprise line grew 20% in July alone, that business customer count grew 32% in July, and that the overall run rate was up 35% quarter to date with enterprise run rate up 50% quarter to date. OpenAI's Q2 recognised revenue was $6.7bn, up 18% sequentially from $5.7bn, with operating loss widening to $12.3bn from $9.3bn (WSJ, 18 August, corroborated by SiliconANGLE, Investing.com, Yahoo Finance and Outlook Business).

The arithmetic against the bar. On the exit run-rate reading that the word ARR in the resolution language most naturally points at, $65bn plus $40bn equals roughly $105bn against a $70bn threshold. That is a cushion of about $35bn, or 50% of the bar. For NO, the pair would have to shed a third of their combined run rate in the four months and ten days to 31 December, while both are inside live IPO processes, while enterprise adoption is still widening, and while every published monthly observation for either company in 2026 has been an increase. On the harsher reading, trailing-quarter recognised revenue annualised, Q2 gives ($6.7bn + $11.6bn) times four, or $73.2bn, which still clears $70bn with about 4.5% headroom on data already six weeks stale. The question resolves on Q4, not Q2, and Q3 is running above Q2 for both firms on every reported indicator, so that headroom is widening rather than narrowing.

The one new item worth logging is TechCrunch, Julie Bort, published 20 August 2026 at 15:36 PDT, 'OpenAI is gaining on Anthropic with business users, new data indicates', which I fetched in full. It reports Ramp corporate-card data covering more than 70,000 US businesses. Anthropic took the lead in Ramp share in May at 41% to OpenAI's 39%; as of July Anthropic has nearly 44% to OpenAI's nearly 40%. Ramp economist Ara Kharazian says OpenAI is growing faster than Anthropic among this segment in Q3 to date, attributing it to GPT-5.6 Sol adoption among developers, and says Fable 5 'disappointed both in adoption and real-world application given price + data retention requirements'. Ramp declined to give dollar figures and the sample skews to tech. Crucially for this question, the same dataset shows the pie growing: the share of Ramp customers paying for AI at all passed 50% in March and reached nearly 56% by July. That is a share-rotation story between the two named companies, which is exactly the kind of news that leaves a sum unchanged, layered on top of a market-expansion story, which pushes the sum up. It is mildly net positive for the combined figure and I have logged it as such rather than as a change of view.

I also went looking specifically for disconfirming evidence in this window and found four things. One, TickerTrends (via Smartkarma and its own blog) publishes third-party ARR tracking that puts Anthropic at $74.1bn and OpenAI at $41.3bn in July, both above the company-sourced Bloomberg numbers, but argues Anthropic's month-on-month percentage growth has cooled from roughly 55% in the spring to mid-single digits by July. Deceleration in the growth rate is not contraction in the level, and mid-single-digit monthly growth from $65bn compounds to well over $80bn by December for Anthropic alone. Two, the gross-versus-net accounting dispute is now explicit and, importantly, quantified: OpenAI's own briefing to reporters puts the inflation from Anthropic's gross treatment of cloud-reseller end-customer spend at roughly $8bn, not at the punitive halving I stress-tested yesterday. Applying an $8bn haircut gives $57bn plus $40bn, or $97bn, still 39% above the bar. Three, the AI equity complex is under real pressure. CNBC on 18 August carried ECB economists warning that 'a correction of current stock market valuations is likely', and market wraps that day describe the S&P 500 falling for a third straight session as AI names sank. That is a valuation event, not a revenue event, and the transmission channel to booked enterprise contracts inside four months is weak. Four, the June 2026 precedent that the US government can pull a frontier model: I re-read Anthropic's own statement dated 12 June 2026 confirming that Commerce issued an export-control directive that forced Anthropic to disable Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all users. That is the single best-evidenced tail risk in this question, because it is a demonstrated capability of the state rather than a hypothetical. It is also instructive on magnitude: Anthropic's run rate went from $47bn in May to above $65bn at end-July straight through that episode.

No public S-1 exists for either company as of 21 August; Anthropic's confidential draft went in on 1 June and OpenAI's on 8 June, with Anthropic targeting an October Nasdaq listing at a reported $2trn-plus valuation (Fortune and Forbes, 13 August) and OpenAI reportedly pushing to 2027. The FT's reported investor expectation that Anthropic finishes 2026 between $100bn and $120bn implies Anthropic clears the $70bn bar on its own. Nothing in the last 48 hours contradicts any of that. Residual probability continues to sit with resolver mechanics, a simultaneous restatement of both companies, and genuine catastrophic tails, which together I keep at about 1%. Holding at 99, interval 98 to 99.

question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
key_change:
HOLD: 32 to 32. The 19-21 August 2026 window delivered a dense run of UK data, but almost all of it is cyclical, and none of it moves the structural arithmetic that governs this question. Today's items sit either side of that and roughly cancel.

The headline new release is ONS Public sector finances, UK: July 2026, published this morning, 21 August 2026. Public sector net borrowing was 1.8 billion pounds in July, 0.7 billion pounds (68.7 per cent) higher than July 2025, against a consensus of roughly zero and an OBR March 2026 profile that implied a 0.5 billion pound surplus. Borrowing in the financial year to July stands at 56.7 billion pounds - 6 billion pounds lower than at the same point last year, helped by stronger receipts, but more than 2 billion pounds above the OBR path. Public sector net debt is 2.985 trillion pounds, 94.1 per cent of GDP. A record July for income tax receipts was not enough to offset spending and debt interest. Provenance note: I could not fetch the ONS July 2026 bulletin page directly (blocked by provenance restrictions), and the ONS 'latest' public sector finances page exceeded the fetch size limit, so these figures come from wire copy and trade press summaries of this morning's ONS release, including BM Magazine and the PA report carried by LBC, the North Wales Pioneer and the Stratford Herald.

Why this is worth only a fraction of a percentage point on a 2030s question: it pins down, rather than reveals, the shape of the 28 October 2026 Budget. Chancellor John Healey has confirmed that date and said his first fiscal statement will be 'built on fiscal discipline' and 'will meet our fiscal rules'. Independent estimates of the gap he must close cluster around 24 billion pounds by the end of the decade, and this would be Labour's third consecutive tax-raising Budget after the 41.5 billion pound package in 2024 and 26 billion pounds in November 2025. The 2030s channel runs through a higher structural tax burden on capital and labour, and through debt interest crowding out public capital spending. That channel is exactly what the OBR's Fiscal risks and sustainability report of 7 July 2026 describes: the projections start from the March 2026 medium-term forecast position in 2030-31, where a primary surplus of 1.5 per cent of GDP is planned, and show demographic and other pressures pushing a primary deficit back open during the 2030s. A 2 billion pound in-year overshoot does not change that trajectory; it makes the tax-raising Budget marginally more certain.

On rates, the 30-year gilt closed just over 5.61 per cent on 19 August 2026, reported as the highest level since 1998, on shifting expectations for Bank of England cuts. That is consistent with, and slightly below, the 5.7 per cent noted for 18 August in yesterday's write-up, so it confirms an elevated long-run real rate environment rather than signalling fresh deterioration. Elevated term premia remain a real 2030s headwind through the cost of capital and through the fiscal envelope for public investment, but the level is already in the forecast.

Two cyclical prints pull in opposite directions and net to roughly nothing. ONS Retail Sales, Great Britain: July 2026, also published 21 August 2026, showed volumes down 0.5 per cent on the month - the first fall since April - partly reversing a downwardly revised 0.7 per cent June rise, with sales excluding automotive fuel down 0.9 per cent and the annual rate slowing to 1.6 per cent from 3.8 per cent in June. Against that, GfK/NIQ consumer confidence for August 2026, released overnight on 20-21 August, rose to minus 14 from minus 17, a two-year high, beating a Reuters poll expectation of minus 18; the major-purchase sub-index reached its highest since December 2021, and economic expectations hit a two-year high, with commentary attributing the improvement partly to the new Burnham administration and easing energy prices. Confidence indices have close to zero predictive content for decade-ahead potential output, and a single month of retail volumes has less. The British Chambers of Commerce also published 'Businesses Continue to Feel the Inflationary Heat' on 19 August 2026, consistent with the 2.9 per cent July CPI print, and 'Economic Priorities for Government: Devolution' on 18 August - advocacy, not evidence.

I re-checked the structural anchors and none has moved. The OBR's March 2026 Economic and fiscal outlook still assumes trend productivity growth picking up to 1.0 per cent in the medium term, with labour supply growth falling to about 0.5 per cent by 2030, GDP growth of 1.1 per cent in 2026 and an average of 1.6 per cent over the remainder of the forecast. The IMF Executive Board concluded the 2026 Article IV consultation on 16 July 2026, putting 2026 growth at 1.0 per cent and describing the economy as having grown at its potential rate of 1.4 per cent in 2025, with growth stabilising around potential in the medium term. The Bank of England's framing, set out by Andrew Bailey in his May 2026 Cutlers' Feast speech, puts post-financial-crisis potential supply growth at about 1.3 per cent a year - 0.4 percentage points productivity plus 0.8 percentage points labour supply - against 2.8 per cent in 1990-2006. NIESR's trend estimate is 1.25 per cent. That cluster of 1.0 to 1.4 per cent is the single most important fact in this forecast, and the composition matters: the Bank's 1.3 per cent leans on 0.8 percentage points of labour supply that ONS demographics will not reproduce in the 2030s, when natural change turns negative and the working-age population grows at roughly 0.34 per cent a year.

On the AI channel, the evidence in this window remains suggestive rather than decisive. Bank of England analysis reported on 6 August 2026 found software and IT consulting firms increased their contribution to annual productivity growth tenfold versus the pre-Covid decade, to 0.1 percentage point in 2023-2025, with information-service providers flipping from drag to driver. A tenfold increase to 0.1 percentage point is an order of magnitude short of what is needed to close a 0.5 percentage point trend gap. Thomas Aubrey's decomposition for the Bennett School of Public Policy (8 June 2026) is a useful corrective: it shows the RTI-based gains concentrated in Information and Communication, Professional and Scientific and Financial Services, but attributes part of the Information and Communication contribution to a telecoms deflator that has fallen 21 per cent since 2019, and notes that imputed rent adds about 0.5 percentage points to measured whole-economy productivity growth over the period. Some of the apparent improvement is deflator methodology and accounting construct, not diffusion. EY's UK Economic Outlook of 3 August 2026 reinforces the narrowness: ICT plus professional, scientific and technical services accounted for 70 per cent of UK GDP growth between 2020 and 2026, while construction output per hour is broadly unchanged since 1997, and EY downgraded 2026 business investment to minus 0.7 per cent from zero.

Policy news in and around the window is mildly positive but small in magnitude: fiscal devolution announced on 31 July 2026, giving metro mayors a retained share of income tax and business rates from spring 2027 with detail deferred to the Budget; the British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme, due to come into force in 2027, cutting electricity costs by up to 25 per cent for more than 7,000 electricity-intensive firms; and a 300 million pound National Wealth Fund-backed package announced in August 2026 for two data centres in the North Lanarkshire AI Growth Zone, contracted to CoreWeave on a 15-year lease. Each is plausible and each is an order of magnitude too small on its own to shift a decade trend by half a percentage point.

Net: a marginally worse fiscal print and a confirmed 27-year high in long gilt yields on one side; a two-year high in consumer confidence and continued AI-infrastructure commitment on the other. Nothing structural. Hold at 32 with the interval unchanged at 20-46.

question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2030?
key_change:
Move: 30 to 31. The tape over 21-22 August 2026 is genuinely mixed rather than empty, and for the first time in several days the balance tilts marginally upward. The single most striking item is a capability result rather than a market print, and I want to be clear at the outset that I am giving it modest rather than heavy weight, because it is self-reported, run on a public evaluation set, and is a harness result rather than a model result.

On 21 August NVIDIA published a claim that its AVO system - Agentic Variation Operators - reached a 100.00 RHAE score on ARC-AGI-3, completing all 183 levels across all 25 public environments with 12 per cent fewer environment actions than VISTA, the previous top performer. The context is what makes this arresting. ARC-AGI-3 launched in March 2026 with every frontier model scoring under 1 per cent, humans at 100 per cent, and it was explicitly designed by Francois Chollet's ARC Prize Foundation to resist the usual benchmark-inflation routes: an agent is dropped into an environment with no instructions, no stated rules and no stated goal. Claude Opus 5 standalone was at roughly 30 per cent in early August. Wrapped in AVO's memory, supervision and tooling layers it goes to 100. That is the fastest saturation trajectory I have seen on a benchmark that was marketed as the hard case for general agentic reasoning.

I discount it for four specific reasons, all documented rather than inferred. First, it is not a figure on the ARC Prize leaderboard: verified numbers there come from runs the Foundation administers itself, and AVO's result was generated and reported by NVIDIA's own team using its own reimplementation of the task interface. Second, NVIDIA is explicit that these are "not results on the semi-private or fully private competition sets", which exist precisely because public environments leak and become familiar over time. ARC Prize's own testing policy confirms that only ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 semi-private results are run and verified by the Foundation; everything else is self-scored on public data. Third, NVIDIA itself says the comparison against Opus 5's 30 per cent baseline "should not be interpreted as a controlled ablation" - it is a system score, not a model score. Fourth, and most importantly for this question, Chollet's long-standing framing is that ARC is necessary but not sufficient for AGI, so even a verified private-set saturation would not on its own generate the declaration this question requires. Net, I score it around +2pp: real evidence that the scaffolding layer is unlocking long-horizon behaviour that models cannot produce alone, which is the mechanism most likely to shift elite researcher opinion, but not evidence of a declaration.

The announcement-shaped markets did not confirm it, which is why the move is one point rather than three. I pulled the Kalshi trade API this morning.
