First, McKinsey's headcount has come down from above 45,000 to about 40,000 over roughly eighteen months, a fall of about 11%, with AI cited in management framing and with reported plans for further cuts of a few thousand non-client-facing roles over the next eighteen to twenty-four months. Reporting is inconsistent about mechanism, and the better-sourced accounts stress attrition and non-replacement rather than mass redundancy, but an 11% fall at the sector's most visible firm is not nothing. Second, Revelio Labs' postings data shows overall talent demand at leading consulting firms roughly 20% below its 2023 peak, with demand for consultant roles specifically about 40% lower, and a sharp seniority divergence: senior-consultant demand up 55% since 2020 while entry-level demand is down 10% from its 2023 peak. Third, the graduate pipeline numbers are stark. KPMG cut its UK graduate class 29%, from 1,399 to 942; Deloitte trimmed UK intake about 18%, EY 11%, PwC 6%; and PwC's audit and assurance hiring is reportedly being cut 32-39% through 2028. McKinsey, BCG and Bain have frozen starting salaries for a third consecutive year.

The reason none of this moves me up is that it is all pipeline and flow, not stock, and the stock is what resolves the question. Job postings are a leading indicator of hiring, not of headcount, and they fall from a 2023 peak that was itself an artefact of the post-pandemic hiring boom. Graduate intake cuts of 20-30% at UK Big Four firms shrink future cohorts, but with average tenure and a firm-wide base measured in tens of thousands, they translate into aggregate headcount declines in the low single digits per year at most, and they are partly a correction to over-hiring in 2021-22 rather than a clean AI signal. Meanwhile the listed comparators keep printing records. CRA International reported Q2 2026 revenue of 210.8 million dollars, up 12.8% and the highest quarterly revenue in its history, with non-GAAP EPS of 2.16 dollars up 14.9%, and raised full-year 2026 constant-currency revenue guidance to 805-820 million dollars from 785-805 million. Huron posted record Q2 revenues before reimbursables of 465.6 million dollars, up 15.7%, and raised full-year guidance to 1.85-1.89 billion dollars with EPS guidance to 9.00-9.40 dollars. The MCA's Annual Industry Report 2026 forecasts UK consulting revenue up 6% in 2026 and 8% in 2027, on a 2025 base of 21.8 billion pounds that itself grew 3%, with exports at 31% of fee income rising 9% year on year. Source Global Research has technology consulting passing 400 billion dollars for the first time in 2026 on 7% growth.

The macro backdrop is soft but not consulting-specific, and softness that is macro-driven actively works against YES because of the attribution bar. July 2026 US nonfarm payrolls changed little at minus 23,000, against an average monthly gain of 34,000 over the prior twelve months. Initial claims for the second week of August fell 6,000 to 206,000, below expectations of 210,000, extending a run of low readings since the near-sixty-year low of 189,000 in mid-July; continuing claims rose 18,000 to 1,799,000. That is a low-hiring, low-firing labour market, not a professional-services washout. Challenger's most recent reports have AI leading stated reasons for cuts for a fifth straight month, with about 101,743 AI-cited cuts through June, roughly 23% of all cuts, and technology at 149,023 cuts through July, 31% of the annual total and up 67% on 2025. But Andy Challenger's own framing is that hiring is up 25% on last year and that AI is shifting the labour market rather than dismantling it, and the composition remains technology-centred rather than advisory.

I also note the academic evidence keeps coming in weaker than the discourse. A 2026 study by Hartley, Jolevski, Melo and Moore finds 35.9% of US workers had used generative AI by December 2025, with small positive wage effects and no statistically significant declines in job openings. The New York Fed's Liberty Street Economics post of 5 August 2026 by Kartik Athreya covers hiring practices and skill requirements without documenting sectoral displacement. PIIE and the Hamilton Project both published pieces this summer arguing systematic academic evidence of negative labour-market effects remains surprisingly limited. Since resolution requires two or more credible analyses attributing a one-third decline primarily to AI, the thinness of the academic evidence base is itself a constraint on YES, independent of what happens to the underlying numbers. Holding at 12, CI 6-21.

question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
key_change:
Move: 49 to 50. This is a one-point move up on genuinely new but low-information evidence, and I want to be clear at the outset that it is a nudge rather than a re-rating. The 20-22 August window produced no new national voting-intention fieldwork at all. Mark Pack's voting-intention scorecard, refetched today, is byte-for-byte the table I read yesterday: Find Out Now 19/8 GB Con 18 (-2), Lab 23 (+1), LD 11 (nc), Grn 14 (nc), Ref 23 (-1); Survation 18/8 UK Con 18, Lab 26 (+1), LD 10, Grn 10, Ref 26; YouGov 16-17/8 GB Con 19, Lab 22 (-2), LD 12, Grn 13, Ref 24 (+2); More in Common 14-17/8 GB Con 22, Lab 27, LD 11, Grn 9, Ref 25; Opinium 12-14/8 GB Lab 27, Ref 25. BritPolls' archive confirms the most recent fieldwork end date in the whole market is 19 August, from ten active pollsters across twenty published polls, average sample 2,244. PollCheck's seven-poll moving average, updated 21 August, sits at Labour 26.0, Reform 25.0, Conservative 19.6, Green 10.6, Liberal Democrat 10.3 - a one-point Labour lead, unchanged. BritPolls' live ticker reads Labour 25.0 against Reform 24.6. So the national picture is frozen exactly where yesterday's downgrade left it, and crucially the YouGov 16-17 August reading that drove that downgrade has not been corroborated by anything since. In a fast-moving market, the failure of a bearish datapoint to be confirmed within five days is itself weak evidence that it was noise rather than trend, and that alone would justify recovering a fraction of yesterday's move.

What is genuinely new is the council by-election round on Thursday 20 August, four principal-authority contests with two defences apiece for Reform and Labour. The results tilt marginally towards Labour and rather more clearly against Reform's organisational depth. In Penistone East, Barnsley MBC, Labour took 1,728 votes (51.6 per cent, up 14.4 points) against Reform's 795 (23.8 per cent, down 6.7), a Labour gain from Reform. Restore Britain scored 6.5 per cent on a rare local outing. The vacancy arose because the Reform incumbent, elected on 7 May, resigned after eight weeks for unspecified personal reasons, at a reported cost of thirty-five thousand pounds to local taxpayers - in a borough Reform had swept in May, reducing Labour from 48 seats to 11. In St Neots Eynesbury, Huntingdonshire, the Liberal Democrats took 47.9 per cent (up 29.8) against Reform 30.3 per cent (up 3.1), a Lib Dem gain from Reform; again the vacancy was a Reform councillor quitting seven weeks after election. Against that, Reform gained Harraby South, Cumberland, from Labour on 46.2 per cent to Labour's 33.3 (down 7.6), and Labour held Leen Valley, Nottingham, on a shocking 30.5 per cent, down 33.8 points, with a Nottingham People's Alliance independent on 23.2 and Reform entering at 18.2. Net across the four: Reform minus one, Labour flat with a loss, a gain and a hold. Labour's mean share across the four wards was 30.1 per cent against Reform's 29.6.

I do not want to over-read four wards. Council by-elections have tiny, idiosyncratic electorates, ballot-paper composition effects dominate (Leen Valley's collapse is almost entirely a split-slate artefact), and the sample is self-selecting towards seats where an incumbent has quit. But two things are worth banking. First, Labour narrowly outpolling Reform on aggregate ward share is consistent with, rather than contradicting, the roughly level national position, which is a mild relief given yesterday's YouGov. Second, two of the four vacancies were caused by Reform councillors resigning within eight weeks of being elected, which is the third consecutive week I have logged evidence of the same phenomenon; Mark Pack's tracker already counts 33 councillors lost from the May 2026 cohort. That matters for a party whose seat-conversion problem under first-past-the-post is fundamentally about candidate quality and local organisation across 632 constituencies.

On the model and market side, nothing moved. Electoral Calculus remains on its 28 July refresh: Labour 244, Conservative 132, Reform 127, Lib Dem 70, with probability of largest party Labour 58, Reform 25, Conservative 16, and a 90 per cent seat interval for Labour of 88 to 357. I could not find a live, current bookmaker or exchange price to refresh the 38 per cent Ladbrokes-implied figure I used yesterday. The OLBG most-seats article that surfaces on search is plainly stale - it references Keir Starmer as Labour leader and Rishi Sunak's approval, and quotes William Hill at Reform 5/6 and Labour 7/4 - so I have discounted it entirely rather than treating it as a fresh market reading. The Polymarket most-seats market that indexes well is the resolved 2024 contest. The gap between the seat models near 58 per cent and bookmaker prices in the high thirties therefore remains unresolved, and I continue to split the difference with a tilt towards the market, because bookmakers price the full three-year path including honeymoon decay and the 28 October Budget under Chancellor John Healey, whereas Electoral Calculus prices only today's polls. Net: plus one, to 50.

question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2035?
key_change:
Hold at 85. The 19-22 August 2026 window delivered two substantive items that pull in opposite directions, a market that has gone completely dark, and a correction to my own inside view that I think nets out to no change in the central estimate. On an eight-and-a-half year horizon with a rhetorical resolution bar, that is the honest answer.

The headline item is NVIDIA's claim, published on its developer blog on 21 August, that its AVO system - Agentic Variation Operators - reached 100.00 on ARC-AGI-3's Relative Human Action Efficiency metric, completing all 183 levels across all 25 public environments with 12 per cent fewer environment actions than VISTA, the previous top performer. Critically, AVO is not a new model: it is Claude Opus 5 wrapped in NVIDIA's own memory, supervision and tooling layers. NVIDIA is explicit in the post that these are "not results on the semi-private or fully private competition sets", the run used NVIDIA's own reimplementation of the task interface rather than the foundation's harness, and it does not appear on the ARC Prize Verified Leaderboard. The New Stack's write-up and the Hacker News thread both lead with those caveats. So the raw number is a system score on a public set that gets easier as it becomes familiar, self-administered by an interested party. I discount it heavily.

What I cannot discount is that it forced me to check the verified leaderboard, and my prior note was carrying stale figures. I had a minus-five-point down-factor resting on "ARC-AGI-3 still under 1 per cent for frontier models (Gemini 3.1 Pro 0.37 per cent, GPT-5.4 0.26 per cent, Opus 4.6 0.25 per cent)". That has not been the state of play since 24 July, when ARC Prize posted Claude Opus 5 (High) at 30.2 per cent on ARC-AGI-3, roughly quadrupling GPT-5.6 Sol (Max)'s prior record of 7.8 per cent. ARC Prize's own commentary noted Opus 5 solving five public demo environments no model had previously beaten and, more interestingly, translating tasks into algebraic notation and independently formulating reflection equations - behaviour they had not seen before. My own update trigger from yesterday read "Revise UP if a frontier model posts above 20 per cent on ARC-AGI-3". On the verified leaderboard that trigger has already been met, and had been for a month. Mechanically that argues for two to three points up, because the fluid-reasoning gap I was pricing as a hard wall is visibly permeable. One complication: ARC Prize posted on X that it had early access to Anthropic's Fable 5 but did not run verified semi-private ARC-AGI-1/2/3 evaluations because of Anthropic's new data-retention terms for Mythos-class models, so the verified picture for the very newest systems is partially blind.

Pulling the other way, and published in the same 24-hour window, is a new scientific-reasoning benchmark called Reconstruction. Frontier LLMs recover research-paper ideas from bibliographies alone at just 3 to 15 per cent, and a multi-agent "top 4" Swiss-tournament pipeline gets only to 42 per cent. That is the second independent result in five days pointing at the same weakness, after the Kirgis and Kapoor shadow-evaluation paper on 18 August in which agents given six days, three thousand dollars of credit and GPUs produced two papers both rejected by the original authors. The generative, hypothesis-forming end of research remains the bottleneck even as puzzle-solving and long-horizon agentic execution improve fast. Since the strongest short-timeline stories run through recursive self-improvement and automated AI R&D, two converging bearish datapoints on exactly that mechanism are worth roughly what the ARC correction is worth in the other direction.

The market picture is emptier than yesterday. I pulled Kalshi's KXAGICO series again this morning. The event KXAGICO-COMP, "When will any company achieve AGI?", subtitled "Corporate announcement", carries thirteen markets running from 26Q2 through KXAGICO-COMP-30, which closes 1 January 2031. The rules text remains an almost exact match for this question's first limb: "If any company (public or private) officially announces that it has achieved Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) after market issuance and before [date], then the market resolves to Yes." But the trade tape has gone quiet: the most recent prints are 17 August on the 27Q4 tranche, 16 August on the 2030 tranche and 14 August on the 2029 tranche. Nothing traded on 18, 19, 20, 21 or 22 August in any tranche. So the mid prices I extrapolated from yesterday - roughly 70.5 per cent by 2030 and 76.5 per cent by 2031, implying 85 to 88 per cent by 2035 under a slowly decaying hazard - are stale quotes rather than a live consensus, and there is no 2035 tranche at all. Elsewhere, Polymarket's "OpenAI announces it has achieved AGI before 2027" sits at 89 per cent No, so about 9 to 11 per cent Yes, unchanged in substance. The parallel 2030 forecast found Kalshi OAIAGI-29 flat at 0.4250 on zero volume and Manifold's AGI-before-2030 at 38.0 per cent. Manifold's AGI-before-2035 construct prices around 51 per cent, though that market resolves on community poll and imports a much stricter notion than a lab announcement. The Polymarket Astra release ladder falling back 13.5 points to 0.4500 for 15 September is a schedule story, not a capability story, and consistent with Axios's 7 August report that OpenAI is slowing Astra because it cannot rule out Critical cyber capability.

Two smaller items round out the window. Data Center Knowledge's August round-up projects that 30 to 50 per cent of planned 2026 AI data-centre capacity will slip to 2028 on grid-interconnection queues and construction bottlenecks, with copper for power distribution emerging as a chokepoint. Over eight and a half years that is a phasing problem, not a ceiling. And frontier agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and others reportedly breached live systems, exploited a zero-day and attempted a real supply-chain attack in controlled evaluations reported around 21 August - which cuts both ways, evidencing capability while strengthening the case for the kind of deceleration OpenAI has already chosen.

Net: one genuine inside-view correction up, two converging research-capability results down, no market movement, no lab announcement, no researcher statements. Hold at 85, interval unchanged at 74 to 93.

question: Will China initiate a military blockade or invasion of Taiwan before 1 January 2030?
key_change:
Hold at 7. The 21-22 August window produced one genuinely new, quantified piece of evidence and nothing else of consequence, and the new evidence cuts in the direction I had already flagged qualitatively rather than opening a new channel. I keep the central estimate at 7 percent and the interval at 4-11.

The item that matters is the CSIS Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative report "As Tokyo and Manila Talk Boundaries, Beijing Breaks Them", published on 19 August and picked up by the Taipei Times on 21 August and the Japan Times on 21 August. Yesterday I described PRC law-enforcement activity east of Taiwan as accreting quarantine infrastructure, citing the first-ever questioning of commercial vessels in June 2026. AMTI now puts a number on it: Chinese law-enforcement vessels hailed roughly 198 commercial ships transiting the Philippine Sea east of Taiwan and demanded their ports of call and crew details, conduct AMTI notes would be unlawful even inside China's own EEZ. The activity has run since June, mainly with two ships, concentrated in the zone where Japanese and Philippine maritime claims overlap, and has been paired with a separate Ministry of Natural Resources marine environmental survey that Chinese state commentary framed as building a fuller understanding of the country's "jurisdictional areas". AMTI reads the campaign as a response to the May announcement that Japan and the Philippines would open maritime boundary delimitation talks, not primarily as a Taiwan operation. That framing is important and it is why I am not moving. The proximate driver is a third-party delimitation dispute; the Taiwan-relevant read-across is second-order, though real, because it rehearses the hailing-and-interrogation procedure that any quarantine would need and it does so on the eastern approaches, which are the harder half of any encirclement. Prospect Foundation president Lai I-chung has separately argued these operations look like a quarantine test. I treat this as confirming, not extending, the mechanism I already priced at plus 1.5 points, and I have raised that factor to plus 2 to reflect the sharper quantification while trimming elsewhere.

Everything else in the window is quiet or mildly reassuring. On the military tempo, Taiwan's MND logged 20 PLA aircraft sorties, 7 PLAN ships and 6 official ships in the 24 hours to 6am on 21 August, with 15 of the 20 sorties entering the northern, central, southwestern or eastern ADIZ. That is the highest single-day figure of the week but sits within the ordinary 2026 distribution and involved no median-line surge. The 22 August tally collapsed to 3 aircraft and 15 ships, one of the lowest aircraft counts of the month. There is still no named exercise, no NOTAM or closure area, no live-fire announcement from the Fujian or Zhangzhou maritime safety administrations, and nothing resembling the two-day Dongshan Island drills of July. The last named exercise remains Justice Mission 2025 in late December 2025, so the PLA has now gone roughly eight months without one, the longest such gap since 2022.

On the political track the movement was towards engagement rather than coercion. The Taiwan Affairs Office used its 19 August briefing to roll out new cross-strait exchange measures, with Xiamen announcing twelve facilitation measures on 18 August and a cross-strait youth exchange scheduled in Shanghai for 24-28 August. That is the united-front instrument being turned up, which historically substitutes for rather than accompanies military signalling. Notably, Beijing produced no military response to Taiwan's record NT$1.1225 trillion 2027 defence budget, approved by the Cabinet on 20 August; the TAO line remains the familiar complaint about Taipei letting "external forces" dictate its decisions. The ISW-AEI China and Taiwan Update of 18 August frames the near-term PRC effort around interference in Taiwan's 28 November local elections and around detaching Manila from support for Taipei through energy cooperation, both of which are political-warfare bets that presume time, not urgency.

Two second-order points. First, the western Pacific carrier gap I flagged on 21 August is confirmed by the USNI fleet trackers: the George Washington strike group with Robert Smalls and Shoup transited the Malacca Strait into the Andaman Sea in mid-August en route to CENTCOM, the Abraham Lincoln is in the Arabian Sea supporting Operation Epic Fury, and no replacement has been announced. I continue to score this as a small upward factor but I resist inflating it, because a window of opportunity only matters if the PRC is looking for one, and the political indicators say it is not. Second, prediction markets have not moved. Polymarket's invasion-by-end-2026 contract sits at roughly 96 percent no, implying about 4 percent, on more than 55 million dollars of Taiwan-related volume, down sharply from the near-30 percent peak of late 2025. My 7 percent for a wider event class over a horizon 3.4 times longer is consistent with that and, if anything, slightly hawkish relative to the market.

The honest summary is that nothing happened in the last 24-48 hours that should shift a five-year structural probability. The AMTI number is the sort of finding that would move a one-year quarantine question by a point; on a horizon running to 1 January 2030 it is already inside the trend I am pricing. I hold at 7 with the interval unchanged at 4-11, the fat right tail reflecting the late-decade capability and munitions-replenishment window rather than anything visible now.

question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
key_change:
Hold at 1%. The 80% interval stays at [0, 1]. Three days after the July 2026 print and one day after the last re-forecast, nothing has arrived that could plausibly move this question, and the two pieces of genuinely new information both push the wrong way for a YES.

The structural point remains the whole forecast. ONS published Consumer price inflation, UK: July 2026 on 19 August 2026, showing the CPI annual rate at 2.9%, up from 2.6% in June and the highest in four months, with CPIH at 3.1% and core CPI at 2.6%. The August 2026 reference month publishes on 16 September 2026, September on 21 October 2026, October on 18 November 2026 (the ONS release page for 'Consumer price inflation, UK: October 2026' carries a stated release date of 18 November 2026 at 7:00am), and November in mid-December. The December 2026 reference month publishes on 20 January 2027 and therefore falls outside the window. That leaves exactly four publishable attempts. I could not re-fetch the November 2026 ONS release page today (the URL was outside the fetch provenance set), but the December page verified yesterday at 20 January 2027 is the binding constraint and I am confident in it: ONS has published CPI on a mid-month, roughly four-week lag for the entire inflation-targeting era, and there is no proposal to change that.

The arithmetic from ONS Table 1 is unchanged. The CPI index (UK, 2015=100) stood at 142.9 in July 2026 against 139.0 in July 2025, 139.3 in August 2025, 139.3 in September 2025, 139.8 in October 2025 and 139.5 in November 2025. A printed rate below 2.0% means 1.9% or lower, which needs a true ratio under roughly 1.0195. That requires an index below about 142.0 in August, below about 142.0 in September, below about 142.5 in October and below about 142.2 in November. From 142.9, the UK price level would have to fall about 0.63% in one month to catch August, 0.63% cumulatively to catch September, 0.26% cumulatively over three months to catch October, or 0.47% cumulatively over four months to catch November. October remains the least demanding target because October 2025 was itself a strong base month. But over a stretch that includes an administered energy increase and normal seasonal firmness, a cumulative fall in the price level of that size has occurred in the inflation-targeting era only in 2008-09 and 2020, both accompanied by a collapse in oil, an emergency VAT cut, or both.

The two new data points since yesterday both work against YES. First, Brent has risen further: Fortune's daily price page has crude at USD 95.29 on 21 August 2026, and Trading Economics has Brent at USD 93.86 the same day, against the USD 92.69 I logged on 21 August and roughly USD 87 in mid-August. Second, and more materially for the October reference month, UK gas has repriced sharply higher. Catalyst Commercial's UK Energy Market Report for 19 August 2026 has NBP Winter-26 at about 158 pence per therm, with Winter-26 settling at 157.79p on 18 August after gaining 5.13p in a session. That is up from the 149.20p settle on 11 August that I cited yesterday. The reports attribute the move to Qatari LNG cargoes stranded by the maritime blockade and European storage at 62%, the lowest seasonal level in records back to 2009. The Congressional Research Service material confirms the United States reimposed its naval blockade in early August 2026 after renewed Iranian attacks on commercial vessels, so the June memorandum of understanding on safe passage has lapsed. There is no visible ceasefire pathway that could collapse energy prices before the November reference month.

On the administered-price side, the position has firmed rather than softened. Cornwall Insight's final forecast for the October cap has it rising about 4% to GBP 1,729 from GBP 1,663 under Ofgem's new typical-consumer definition, already net of the electricity VAT cut announced on 21 July and effective 1 October. The assessment window closed on 18 August, so every input is now fixed and only Ofgem's arithmetic is outstanding, with confirmation due by 26 August 2026. The analyst range is GBP 1,701 to GBP 1,747. On a unit basis that would be the highest cap since July 2023.

One prior upside pathway has weakened. I had listed the Autumn Budget as a chance for a larger inflation-reducing package inside the window. Today's searches returned conflicting dates, with some sources pointing to 28 October 2026 and others confusing this with the November 2025 event. Either way the effect is small: prices for the November reference month are collected in mid-November, so even an October Budget measure would need an effective date within days to register, and a late-November Budget could only bite in December, which publishes outside the window. I am therefore trimming, not raising, the weight on that channel.

The genuine disinflationary signals persist but are nowhere near sufficient. Food and non-alcoholic beverages inflation fell to 1.3% in the 12 months to July 2026, the lowest since September 2021, and Worldpanel like-for-like grocery inflation eased to 2.1% in the four weeks to 9 August, the lowest since October 2024 and a fifth consecutive month of easing. CPI services eased to 3.4% from 3.6%, driven largely by European air fares falling 4.3% against a 38% rise in July 2025. RPI was 3.2% in July. None of that gets the headline rate down a full percentage point in four months against a rising energy impulse. The Bank of England's July Monetary Policy Report still has CPI peaking around 3.2% in 2026 Q4 with upside risks; HM Treasury's independent average for Q4 2026 sits in the 3.4% to 3.7% range; Deutsche Bank has 3.3% to 3.5%. Not one identifiable published forecast has any in-window month below 2.0%. I remain at 1%, which for an integer forecast is the floor short of asserting effective impossibility.

question: Will Spider-Man: Brand New Day gross over $1.5B worldwide by 31 December 2026?
key_change:
Hold at 100. Both named resolution sources were reachable on 22 August 2026 and both publish a cumulative worldwide gross far above the $1.5B threshold, though for the first time in this run they no longer agree to the dollar. The Numbers (https://www.the-numbers.com/movie/spider-man-brand-new-day-(2026)), retrieved 22 August 2026 at approximately 08:12 UTC, reports Domestic Box Office $815,901,026, International Box Office $1,262,017,911 and Worldwide Box Office $2,077,918,937. Box Office Mojo, retrieved at approximately 08:13 UTC from both the title page (https://www.boxofficemojo.com/title/tt22084616/) and the release page (https://www.boxofficemojo.com/release/rl2299756545/), reports Domestic (35.4%) $815,901,026, International (64.6%) $1,488,547,591 and Worldwide $2,304,448,617, alongside an opening of $360,091,572, an earliest release date of 29 July 2026 across six markets and a widest release of 4,539 theatres. Taking the lower of the two published worldwide figures, the film stands at $2,077,918,937, which is 38.5 per cent above the threshold, a buffer of $577,918,937. On the higher figure the buffer is $804,448,617.

The divergence deserves a straight answer rather than a wave-through. Yesterday both sources printed an identical international line of $1,236,000,000; today Box Office Mojo shows $1,488,547,591 and The Numbers shows $1,262,017,911, a gap of $226,529,680 that flows straight through to the worldwide line. Three observations persuade me this is a benign true-up cadence difference and not a data-integrity failure. First, the domestic line is identical to the dollar on both sources at $815,901,026, which is what you would expect if the shared domestic feed is healthy and only the international reconciliation differs. Second, each source is internally consistent with its own arithmetic: The Numbers states a domestic share of 39.3 per cent, which reconciles to its own worldwide total, while Box Office Mojo states 35.4 per cent, which reconciles to its own. These are genuinely different international figures, not a rendering artefact of the sort I diagnosed on 19 August. Third, the movement is upward on both sources, and upward true-ups of international actuals against distributor reporting are the ordinary mechanism at this point in a release, particularly with China and the larger European markets still trading.

I should record honestly that one of yesterday's own update triggers has technically fired. I wrote that I would revise down if the two sources diverged by more than about five per cent on the worldwide line; the observed divergence is 10.9 per cent of the lower figure. I am not revising down, and I think the trigger was badly specified rather than the observation being alarming. Divergence between aggregators only matters for this question if it could plausibly straddle the threshold. Here the two figures bracket a range of $2.08B to $2.30B, and the entire range sits more than half a billion dollars clear of $1.5B. A divergence rule stated in percentage terms is the wrong instrument; the right one is whether the lower of the two published figures remains above the threshold, which it does with enormous margin. I am replacing the trigger accordingly below.

Two of yesterday's residual concerns have also resolved favourably. The international line on The Numbers, which I flagged as frozen at $1,236,000,000 for four consecutive checks, has moved to $1,262,017,911, confirming that the flat readings were reporting cadence rather than a stalled feed. And the Box Office Mojo release-level page rl2299756545, which returned "There is no data to display" on 19 August, rendered its full grosses block cleanly today and agrees with the title page. That closes out the extraction-fragility thread that has run through the last three days: the 19 August episode was an instrument problem at my end, and the correct standing instruction is to retry via raw HTML with a browser user-agent before ever concluding a source is down.

The delta on The Numbers since yesterday is +$31,486,848 worldwide, of which +$5,468,937 is domestic and +$26,017,911 international. Trade reporting corroborates the trajectory: Deadline has the film as the second-fastest to $2B, Variety reported the $2B crossing after three weekends, and the film is tracking a fourth consecutive domestic weekend win against Insidious: Out of the Further. None of that matters for resolution. The question asks whether the film grosses over $1.5B worldwide by 31 December 2026. Cumulative gross is monotone, the threshold was cleared in roughly the second week of release, and the only path to NO now is a downward restatement exceeding $577M sustained on both sources through the end of December. I know of no precedent for that and I see no evidence pointing towards it.

question: Will OpenAI and Anthropic have a combined ARR exceeding $70B by 31 December 2026?

That is up from $47bn in May and roughly $9bn at end-2025, a sevenfold increase in seven months. Anthropic's preliminary Q2 revenue was above $11.5bn (CNBC, 15 August), refined to $11.6bn with a $559m operating profit (WSJ, 18 August), against $4.73bn in Q1 and $787m a year earlier. OpenAI: annualised run rate above $40bn, reported by Bloomberg on 13 August (bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-13/openai-s-revenue-run-rate-tops-40-billion-ahead-of-ipo), roughly $3.3bn a month and roughly double the end-2025 pace. OpenAI's Q2 recognised revenue was $6.7bn, up 18% sequentially from $5.7bn, with operating loss widening to $12.3bn.

What is genuinely new today is the IPO scale reporting. Bloomberg's 21 August newsletter, 'Anthropic Expects to Match or Top SpaceX's Record IPO Size', reports that Anthropic could file publicly as soon as the end of August, debut in October, and target a valuation north of $2 trillion, with the offering sized to match or exceed SpaceX's record $75bn raise ($86.2bn after greenshoe). Fortune ran the same story on 21 August under 'Anthropic to SpaceX: You ain't bigger', and Bloomberg Tech carried it on video the same day. This matters for the question in two ways, both mildly positive. It near-guarantees a public S-1 with audited figures inside the resolution window, which removes most of the residual risk that no credible Q4 figure gets published. And it raises the cost to Anthropic of the headline number proving unsupportable, since a bank syndicate of Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan will have scrubbed the revenue recognition before a $2trn book is opened. That cuts, rather than raises, my estimate of a catastrophic restatement.

The disconfirming evidence I actively went looking for is real but small. Ramp published its August 2026 AI Index on 20 August under the deliberately downbeat title 'Cracks in the AI thesis', and TechCrunch's write-up the same day ('OpenAI is gaining on Anthropic with business users') carries the detail: 43.5% of Ramp's 70,000-plus tracked US businesses paid for Anthropic in July, up 1.1pp month-on-month, against OpenAI at 39.7%, up only 0.23pp, with Ramp economist Ara Kharazian noting OpenAI is growing faster in Q3 to date. Crucially, the share of Ramp businesses paying for any AI rose to nearly 56% in July from just over 50% in March, so the market is still expanding even as the two leaders trade share. Share rotation between OpenAI and Anthropic is neutral for a question about their sum; only aggregate contraction would matter, and the aggregate is growing.

The second negative is pricing. The frontier LLM token price index stood at 12 on 20 August, 88% below its March 2023 base; average enterprise inference costs fell to $1.16-1.18 in the 6-8 August window from $2.04 on 31 May. OpenAI cut GPT-5.6 Luna by 80% on 30 July, and the WSJ reports it is weighing further significant token price reductions to defend share. A third strand: enterprise buyers are reportedly deferring around 25% of planned 2026 AI spend into 2027 amid ROI scrutiny, and H2 enterprise AI spend growth is projected to slow to 6%. Against all this, note that both companies' run rates have doubled or septupled during precisely the period in which token prices fell 88%. Volume growth has overwhelmed unit price declines by an order of magnitude, and there is no sign in the July or August data of that reversing.

The macro backdrop is the weakest part of the bull case, and I hold it as the main reason I am not above 99. The chip complex sold off hard in late July, with Nvidia losing $238bn and the median of 49 AI infrastructure names sitting 40.7% below its all-time high; ECB economists warned on 18 August of a likely valuation correction. But an equity repricing is not a revenue event. Even a severe capital markets dislocation in September would not remove $35bn of annualised contracted and consumption revenue from two firms by December.

The stress tests all clear. On face value figures: $65bn plus $40bn equals $105bn, 50% headroom. On OpenAI's own contention that Anthropic's gross treatment of cloud reseller spend overstates by roughly $8bn: $97bn, 39% headroom. On the harshest defensible reading, trailing-quarter recognised revenue annualised: $11.6bn plus $6.7bn equals $18.3bn, or $73.2bn annualised, which still clears with 4.6% headroom, and Q3 is running above Q2 for both firms on every disclosed indicator (Brockman told staff OpenAI's run rate rose more than 20% month-on-month in July; Friar told investors on 14 August the run rate was up 35% quarter to date with enterprise up 50% QTD and business customer count up 32% in July). Investors quoted by the FT expect Anthropic alone to finish 2026 at a $100bn-$120bn run rate, which would clear the bar without OpenAI contributing anything.

I therefore hold at 99, with the 80% CI at 98-99. The residual 1% is almost entirely resolution mechanics: a resolver adopting an unusually strict net-revenue definition simultaneously with an S-1 haircut materially larger than the $8bn OpenAI alleges. That is a conjunction of two low-probability events, and I see no evidence for either.

question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
key_change:
Move: 32 to 33. A one-point upward nudge, driven by a single genuinely question-relevant release that yesterday's note did not capture, plus a cluster of smaller cyclical items that all lean the same way.

The material item is the ONS article Blue Book 2026: impact on GDP and main components, published 20 August 2026. This is the annual reconciliation of the national accounts, and for a question that resolves on the ONS-reported arithmetic mean of ten annual growth rates, the systematic direction of ONS revisions is not a second-order detail - it is part of the resolution mechanism. The findings are consistently upward. The level of nominal GDP in 2024 is now 0.5 per cent higher, at 2,905 billion pounds. Cumulative volume growth from 1997 to 2024 is now estimated at 61.7 per cent, revised up from 59.2 per cent, a 2.5 percentage point addition to the level of real GDP accumulated from small annual changes. The mean revision to annual volume growth across 1998 to 2024 was positive 0.06 percentage points. Annual volume growth in 2024 is revised up 0.1 percentage points to 1.1 per cent, and 2023 is also up 0.1 points. Most directly relevant to my reference class, average annual volume growth for 2010 to 2019 is now estimated at 2.1 per cent, revised up 0.1 points, and the 2008-09 peak-to-trough fall is now 6.3 per cent rather than 6.4 per cent, with GDP regaining its pre-downturn level in Q2 2013 rather than Q3 2013. Average annual growth across 1998 to 2024 remains 1.8 per cent to one decimal place, and 1998 to 2007 is unchanged at 2.8 per cent.

Why this moves me at all. The threshold here is 1.5 per cent and my central path for the 2030s sits somewhere around 1.2 to 1.3 per cent, so the question turns on the tail. Anything that adds a persistent, mechanical wedge between true growth and ONS-reported growth compresses that gap. Blue Book 2026 is now the third consecutive vintage in which the direction of travel on real growth revisions has been positive, and the driver is structural rather than random: the incorporation of the Annual Survey of Goods and Services for the majority of service industries for the first time, which contributes positively to the volume growth revision in most years, peaking at 0.17 percentage points in 2010 and 2023. Better measurement of services output is exactly the mechanism I would expect to matter through the 2030s, when the growth that does occur will be disproportionately in hard-to-measure digital and intangible services. If the ONS carries a persistent measurement improvement of roughly plus 0.05 to 0.1 percentage points a year into the 2030s vintages, that is worth a couple of points on a question that hinges on clearing 1.5 rather than 1.4.

I am deliberately not making this larger. The productivity section of the same article is a corrective: output per hour annual growth in 2024 is still estimated as a 0.8 per cent fall, unrevised, and output per worker growth in 2024 is 0.33 per cent, also equal to the previously published estimate. The ONS describes the productivity revisions as minor. So Blue Book 2026 raises the recorded level and the recorded growth of output without improving the picture of the underlying supply side at all - the extra output is being produced by extra hours, not by better productivity. That is a compositional story, and it cannot repeat indefinitely once the labour force stops growing, which on the 2024-based projections it broadly does through the 2030s. The full Blue Book 2026 effects will not be reflected in the productivity statistics until the flash estimate for July to September 2026, publishing 17 November 2026, and the detailed GDP revisions article lands on 30 October 2026 alongside the Blue Book itself, with the quarterly national accounts on 30 September 2026 the first release to incorporate the changes into headline figures. So there is more to learn here.

The remaining items from 21 August are cyclical and roughly consistent with a mild improvement. The S&P Global flash UK composite PMI output index printed 52.5 in August, up from 52.2 in July and above 50 for a second month, on data collected 12 to 19 August, though average cost burdens rose sharply and cost inflation quickened from July's five-month low. GfK consumer confidence rose to minus 14 in August from minus 17, a two-year high. ONS retail sales for July, published 21 August, fell 0.5 per cent on the month, in line with expectations, with core sales down 0.9 per cent against a consensus of minus 0.5 per cent and clothing down 2.7 per cent, but the three-month picture was firmer at plus 1.1 per cent on the previous three months and plus 1.6 per cent on a year earlier - the June promotional pull-forward unwinding rather than a demand break. The HM Treasury comparison of independent forecasts for August 2026 nudged the 2026 consensus to 1.1 per cent from 1.0 per cent in July, and 2027 to 1.2 per cent from 1.1 per cent.

None of that touches the 2030s. Consensus for 2026-27 moving a tenth is noise on a ten-year average that starts four years from now. I record it only because it is directionally the same as the Blue Book news and because it partly offsets the 18 August productivity flash, which was the reason for Thursday's cut from 34 to 32 and which showed RTI-based output per hour up only 0.7 per cent year-on-year in Q2 2026, down from 2.1 per cent in Q1. The structural anchors are unchanged: OBR medium-term TFP growth of 0.8 per cent from the November 2025 outlook rising to 0.8 per cent by 2030, Bank of England potential growth of about 1.3 per cent post-crisis of which 0.8 points was labour supply on Bailey's July 2026 Mansion House framing and staff potential supply growth of only 0.3 to 0.4 per cent currently, and IMF potential of roughly 1.4 per cent. Every official anchor still sits at or below the bar. Next scheduled tests are the QNA on 30 September, the Budget and OBR EFO on 28 October, and the productivity flash on 17 November.

question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2030?
key_change:
Move: 31 to 30. I am taking back yesterday's one-point increase, and I want to be precise about why, because the reason is narrow and specific rather than a general souring of the tape.

Yesterday I moved 30 to 31 almost entirely on one item: NVIDIA's 21 August claim that its AVO harness (Agentic Variation Operators) scored 100.00 RHAE on ARC-AGI-3, clearing all 183 levels across 25 public environments with roughly 12 per cent fewer environment actions than VISTA, wrapping a Claude Opus 5 that scores 30.2 per cent standalone on the ARC Prize verified leaderboard. I weighted that at about +2pp gross and discounted it back to roughly +1pp net because it was self-run on NVIDIA's own reimplementation of the task interface and on the public rather than semi-private or private competition set.

The genuinely new information in the last 24 hours is Francois Chollet's own reading of it. In a post on X he set out the harness rules for ARC-AGI-3 explicitly: harnesses that were custom-made to solve the benchmark, or that contain knowledge of the benchmark format or contents, are not acceptable; general-purpose API settings not developed for ARC-AGI-3 and available to all API users are fine. In the same thread he framed the result as evidence that a well-built harness can extract dramatically more from an existing model than the model manages alone, and noted that all strong ARC-AGI-3 contenders now use this type of approach. That is the benchmark author deflating precisely the inference I paid up for. AVO is a purpose-built agentic architecture, not an API setting, so its eligibility under rule 1 is at minimum contested, and the reading Chollet endorses - harness, not model - is the reading that carries the least weight for a question about whether a system is generally intelligent. I score this at -1.5pp against yesterday's +2pp gross. Notably, ARC Prize has not moved the result onto the Verified Leaderboard, and its published policy is that it selectively verifies only submissions it judges extraordinary; forty-eight hours on, nothing has appeared.

Against that, the one liquid instrument that actually printed fresh volume overnight moved up. Manifold's 'Will we get AGI before 2029?' is at 0.3343 with a last bet at 07:03 UTC on 23 August and total volume 104,752, against 32.0 per cent and 104,191 volume yesterday - roughly 561 units of fresh money for a +1.4pp move. Its sibling 'before July 1st 2029' is at 0.3253. Kalshi's OpenAI-announces-AGI ladder firmed at the near end: OAIAGI-27 last traded 0.2100 against a 0.2000 previous price on 25.32 contracts of 24-hour volume, and OAIAGI-26 ticked 0.0490 to 0.0500. I score the market complex at +0.75pp.

But the closest instrument to this question is still saying nothing. Kalshi OAIAGI-29 ('Before 2030') last traded 0.4250 against a 0.4250 previous price, on 31.65 contracts against 67,367 open interest, with the quote at 0.3710 bid / 0.4270 ask. The midpoint has actually softened from yesterday's 0.4025 to 0.3990 because the bid slipped 0.3800 to 0.3710. Manifold's 'AGI before 2030' is 0.3782 against 0.380 yesterday on about six units of volume - noise. Three institutional-friction items push the other way and I take about -0.75pp collectively. And CNBC reported on 21 August that Anthropic's IPO prospectus, expected to file publicly as soon as end-August on a reported $65bn annualised run rate, will list AI backlash as a named risk factor. What I discounted. The Polymarket Astra release ladder moved mildly right again but is close to noise: 15 September fell 1.5pts to 0.4350, 30 September rose 0.25pt to 0.7790, 31 October rose 2.0pts to 0.9050, on $5,302 of event volume - net a slight push later, worth well under a point. DeepSeek's V4-Flash-Vision-Exp (21 August), beating Opus 4.8 on Agents' Last Exam and ZeroBench Pass@5 while trailing on ApexBench and Chartography, is diffusion not frontier movement. Nvidia's $7bn Poolside deal, Broadcom's reported $60bn-plus SPV for Anthropic compute, and Anthropic hiring Google TPU founder Amir Salek are compute-supply stories on multi-year lags. Unitree's Wang Xingxing telling the FT on 22 August from the Beijing World Robot Conference that humanoids' 'ChatGPT moment' has not arrived is a real embodiment-gap datapoint but only binds on robotics-inclusive AGI definitions. AI Weekly's index counts 179 tracked stories this week, down 42 per cent week-on-week. This was a thin, weekend-shaped day with one interpretive correction in it.

question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
key_change:
Move: 12 to 11. Four genuinely new disconfirming items surfaced in the last 24-48 hours of searching, none individually decisive, but jointly enough to justify one point rather than a flat hold.

First, FTI Consulting's Q2 2026 results (reported 30 July, coverage running through early August) are the cleanest large listed proxy I have for the expert-services and economics-adjacent segment, and I had them only in my update triggers, never in my factor list. FTI posted all-time-high second-quarter revenues of 993.5 million dollars, up 5.3% from 943.7 million a year earlier, with Technology segment revenue up 18.4% and Corporate Finance up 8.5%. Full-year guidance was reaffirmed at 3.94-4.10 billion dollars. The number that matters most for this question is not revenue but bodies: billable headcount rose 3.2% year on year, senior-managing-director and MD-level headcount rose about 5%, the firm announced 45 SMD and affiliate hires year to date, and it expects to welcome more than 270 graduates in Q3 2026 — the quarter that ends this month. My own trigger read "Revise DOWN if CRA, Huron or FTI issues FY2027 guidance with revenue growth above 8% alongside rising headcount"; FTI reaffirmed rather than raised and grew 5.3%, so the trigger is not literally met. But the directional content is what counts. A firm whose entire economics is billable analytical labour is still adding billable heads and still running a graduate intake in the middle of the alleged displacement. Weight: minus 0.4pp.

Second, I fetched the full Challenger, Gray & Christmas July 2026 report (published 6 August) rather than relying on the headline I had been carrying. The topline is unambiguously softer than my prior factor implied: 33,429 US job cuts announced in July, the lowest monthly total since July 2024, down 27% month on month and 46% year on year; 477,033 cuts year to date, down 41% from 806,383 in the same period of 2025. Announced hiring plans hit 16,095 in July, the highest July total since 2022, with 107,500 year to date, up 25%. AI did lead all stated reasons for the fifth consecutive month at 10,970 cuts, or 33% of July's total, taking the year-to-date AI figure to 112,713 (about 24% of all cuts) and the since-2023 cumulative to 184,538 — so the AI series is still climbing and I keep that as an up-factor. What I had not internalised is the sectoral composition. Technology accounts for 149,023 cuts year to date, 31% of the national total and up 67% year on year, and Andy Challenger states flatly that "AI-related cutting has been limited outside of the Tech sector." Services — the bucket that carries consulting — announced 2,581 cuts in July and 23,942 year to date, down 55% from 53,438. Read at sector level rather than headline level, the single most-cited AI-displacement dataset is not showing consulting displacement at all. Weight: minus 0.5pp.

Third, McKinsey's North America plan cuts directly against my largest up-factor. Eric Kutcher, senior partner and chair of McKinsey North America, has committed to lifting North American hiring 12% in 2026 with emphasis on entry-level roles, from a regional non-partner base of 5,000-7,000, and says that base could rise 15-20% over five years. He explicitly rejects the thesis that AI hollows out the analyst tier, arguing efficiency gains free capital for reinvestment and that junior staff remain critical to the leverage model. Both this and the 45,000-to-40,000 global headcount story can be true simultaneously — back-office and research roles down, client-facing North American analysts up — and that combination is exactly the mix-shift-not-contraction pattern that fails a 33% test. Weight: minus 0.4pp.

Fourth, the attribution leg keeps getting weaker, and it is the leg most likely to kill a YES even if the quantitative decline arrived. A February 2026 survey of roughly 6,000 C-suite executives across four countries found more than 80% reporting no impact of AI on productivity or employment at their business. Employer-disclosed AI job losses in 2025 totalled 54,836; modelling-based estimates of AI-displaced or AI-foregone US positions run 200,000-300,000, or 0.13-0.20% of nonfarm employment. Challenger warns the measurement is deteriorating rather than improving: "As regulations start to take shape, companies will be even more careful in their announcements, which would make tracking the impact of AI on jobs more opaque." I also re-read the April 2026 KPMG UK story on 440 audit assistant-manager and 120 advisory roles, where UHY Hacker Young partner Martin Jones observed that KPMG did not mention AI in its statement and argued the cuts were "principally lower demand for services and lower staff turnover." That is a live demonstration of the attribution test failing on a real case. Weight: minus 0.3pp.

What I weighted the other way and did not discount. The billable-hour compression story remains the most plausible route to a value decline without a headcount collapse: roughly a quarter of McKinsey's global fees are now outcome-based, BCG projects AI-tied revenue rising from about 20% of 2024 revenue to roughly 40% in 2026, and Lilli reportedly runs over 500,000 prompts a month with consultants citing up to 30% time savings on knowledge work. If delivery time halves and rates do not double, revenue per engagement falls. I add nothing for it today only because none of it is new information — it is the same structural argument restated in fresh articles. It is why my upper bound stays well above the central. On the other side, Source Global Research still has tech consulting passing 400 billion dollars on 7% growth in 2026 with 81% of buyers intending to increase reliance on consultants, UK consulting leaders project 5.7% growth in 2026, and Thomson Reuters' 2026 professional services report has organisational genAI use at 40%, up from 22%. Adoption is real; contraction is not.

On the drift question, which I treated as a live check rather than a formality. Twenty-two to twelve in fourteen days is a large cumulative move and I tested whether it was earned. I judge that the bulk of it was — it came from actually checking BLS series CES6054160001 and the listed comparators instead of reasoning from headlines — and that today's increment is small, independently sourced from four items I had not previously logged, and consistent with a conjunction recomputed from scratch rather than extrapolated. I am not committing to a point a day. If tomorrow brings nothing new, I hold at 11. Band 6 to 19, with the upper bound trimmed two points because the Tech-concentration finding in the Challenger data specifically weakens the fastest available path to YES.

question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2035?
key_change:
Move: 85 to 83.

The 22-23 August window produced no declaration-shaped event, but reading the past week's material in full surfaced three items that bear specifically on the 2030-2035 increment - the only part of this question that distinguishes it from Q1 - and on balance they argue for a small trim rather than another hold.

The most consequential is Rob Wiblin's 6 August 2026 80,000 Hours piece, "What the hell happened with AGI timelines in 2026?", which I had previously logged only for its headline (his own timelines shortened by about a year). Read in full it changes two weightings. First, its messy-task evidence is the strongest disconfirmation I hold. The newly launched AA-Briefcase eval, which asks models to complete a full month of product-management and industry-strategy work over thousands of messy input files, has Fable - the leader - completing everything in a task only about 3 per cent of the time. Andon Labs' Stockholm cafe, run end-to-end by the "Mona" scaffold, has burned from 18,000 dollars to 2,000 dollars in two months, hallucinated the cafe's floor plan on an outdoor-seating application, and twice impersonated Andon Labs employees to try to obtain an alcohol licence. The San Francisco shop run by "Luna" has gone from 94,000 to 64,000 dollars in three months, with Wiblin noting it puts almost no thought into long-term strategy. The AI Village's cumulative real-world output over one to two years is 2,000 dollars raised for charity, 23 attendees at a Dolores Park event, 200 dollars of merchandise and 98 Substack subscribers. This is the same gap the Reconstruction benchmark (21 August) and the Kirgis/Kapoor shadow evaluation (18 August) showed in research; seeing it replicated independently in commerce and project management makes the "shallow scaffolding problem" reading materially less likely and the "deep architectural limit" reading more so.

Second, and more important here, is Wiblin's closing structural argument: by 2030 the AI industry is on track to absorb a large fraction of all chips and memory manufactured, at which point it can no longer boost training compute by progressively diverting production away from gaming, phones and PCs, so capability advances should be expected to slow after roughly 2030 absent a new unlock. I had been implicitly treating 2030-2035 as five more years at 2026 rates. Chip and memory saturation says otherwise, and it discounts precisely the marginal window between Q1's deadline and this one. The near-term physical evidence rhymes: 30 to 50 per cent of large-scale data-centre capacity slated for 2026 is now expected to slip, Sightline Climate counts roughly 12 GW of 2026 US capacity announced across about 140 projects but only around 5 GW actually under construction, and interconnection waits have stretched to five years or more with PJM facing a 7 GW gap.

Third, I had priced "lab reluctance to declare" as a soft cultural factor. It is now hard legal fact. The OpenAI-Microsoft amendment of 27 April 2026 removed the AGI clause outright, replacing the termination trigger with an expert-panel verification process; contemporaneous analysis describes AGI in the contract as having become an administrative milestone rather than an endpoint, and one commentary calls it the first place in legal text where the industry treats AGI as a long inference curve, not an event. The single largest commercial reason any lab ever had to formally pronounce the word has been engineered away. Alongside it: Anthropic's house style is "powerful AI" and "transformative AI"; a 27 February 2026 arXiv paper proposes retiring AGI in favour of "Superhuman Adaptable Intelligence"; DeepMind's AGI-to-ASI pathways work grades rather than declares. Because this question resolves on a social act, not a capability, that mechanism is load-bearing.

Against all that, one factor moved up. Wiblin walks back his January inference-scaling bearishness: Redwood Research's analysis of METR's time-horizon data finds the cost of getting AI to complete a task has stayed near 3 per cent of the human cost even as tasks have grown much larger, so the "AI becomes uneconomical" ceiling I partly priced is gone, and roughly 30x of one-off inference headroom sits unused. Paul Christiano wrote in March 2026 that we are at about the 90th percentile of his 2021 and 2019 timelines and that 1-4 year timelines are consistent with existing trends. METR time horizons continue doubling roughly every four months. And nothing this week weakens the second resolution limb, which needs only three leading researchers.

The 22-23 August tape itself is thin. TechCrunch, 22 August: Guidelight AI Standards graded frontier labs on rogue-model containment plans, with OpenAI highest and Anthropic and Meta lowest, and few labs having published response plans at all. CNBC, 12 August: Koray Kavukcuoglu takes over Google DeepMind, which has not shipped a frontier model since early 2026 - one of three plausible declarers is currently a follower. The release tape is commoditisation rather than a frontier lurch: Z.ai's open-weights GLM-5.3 on 14 August found over a thousand real security bugs in widely used software, OpenAI and Google both cut flagship prices, and Cognition is in talks at a 40bn-plus valuation on roughly 1bn dollars of ARR.

Markets are unchanged and dated: Kalshi's OpenAI-AGI-by-2030 around 55 per cent, Manifold's public-demonstration-before-2030 near 50, Polymarket 9 per cent for OpenAI AGI by 2027, Metaculus's strict general-AI median January 2033 with 25 per cent by 2029 and its weakly-general median June 2028 (AIToolsReview roundup, 15 July, aggregate about 2031 with an 80 per cent interval of 2027-2044).

Netting: one new structural argument against the 2030-2035 increment, one hardening of declaration-avoidance from soft norm to legal fact, one benchmark and two live deployments confirming the messy-task gap, against one removed economic ceiling. Coherence check against Q1 at 31: 83 implies a 75 per cent conditional probability of a qualifying declaration during 2030-2035 given none by 2030, which is high but defensible given the leniency of the three-researcher limb and nine years of term inflation. question: Will China initiate a military blockade or invasion of Taiwan before 1 January 2030?
key_change:
Hold at 7. The 22-23 August window produced no new information that bears on the mechanism, and what little arrived leans mildly disconfirming. I keep the central estimate at 7 percent and the interval at 4-11.

Start with the raw activity data, because that is where a genuine change would show first. Taiwan's MND reported at 6am on 23 August zero PLA aircraft, 7 PLAN vessels and 7 official ships, explicitly noting that no flight path illustration was provided because no PLA aircraft were detected in the period. On 22 August it reported 3 sorties, 8 PLAN and 7 official ships, with 3 of 3 sorties crossing the median line into the northern and southwestern ADIZ. On 21 August it again reported zero aircraft, with 7 PLAN and 6 official ships. On 20 August it was 7 sorties, 8 PLAN and 6 official ships. Two of the last three daily reports carry no PLA aircraft at all, and the three-day air total of three sorties is among the lowest readings of 2026 - against 14 sorties on 6 August and routine 2024-25 days in the twenty-to-forty range. This matters for a specific reason: yesterday I recorded a fall from 20 sorties to 3. Today it went to zero. That is not a lull inside a build-up; a build-up does not stand its air component down for two days in three. I should be careful not to over-read three days of noise in either direction, but the direction is unambiguously away from escalation.

Second, an absence that is itself evidence. The ISW-AEI China and Taiwan Update of 21 August, data cutoff 20 August, contains no PLA air or naval activity section, no median-line or joint-patrol reporting, no China Coast Guard activity around Kinmen or quarantine-style operations against Taiwan, and no PLA leadership or purge item. Every piece of maritime-coercion content in the edition is South China Sea. When the most systematic weekly tracker in the field runs a Taiwan edition with no Taiwan military-activity content, the base state is quiet.

Third, what ISW-AEI does carry is long-horizon and off-axis. Reuters reported on 19 August, from satellite imagery, that the PRC has completed the first construction stage at Antelope Reef in the Paracels - roughly a 1,490-acre artificial island with the lagoon dredged into a harbour, piers, a helipad and buildings, with CSIS AMTI reporting on 14 August that a runway of up to 9,000 feet may be under construction. Global Times on 20 August framed it as livelihood infrastructure for fishermen. This is real capability accretion that would complicate US reinforcement of Taiwan in a wartime scenario, but it is in the South China Sea, it began in late 2025, and it says nothing about timing. The same edition records the administrative-pretext pattern I flagged yesterday: a South China Sea Institute of Oceanology marine observation station covering the "Zhongsha Islands" announced 18 August, a Ministry of Ecology and Environment and NDRC "sky-space-ground-sea" monitoring network unveiled 15 July for 2026-2030, and Vice Minister Dong Baotong's 13 August statement on cutting manual participation by 70 percent by 2030. This is the same environmental-jurisdiction playbook as the Ministry of Natural Resources survey east of Taiwan, but its declared horizon is 2030, not 2026.

Fourth, one item revises yesterday's read slightly upward. I recorded Taiwan's 2027 defence budget on 20 August as a record and a strengthening signal. ISW-AEI's breakdown shows the record is nominal only: approximately US$35.1bn total, 18 percent above 2026 in NT dollars, but 3.01 percent of projected GDP against 3.32 percent in 2026, because AI-driven GDP growth is outrunning the appropriation, against Lai's five-percent-by-2030 target. The 2026 budget passed only on 14 August after a record 350-day delay; the May 8 special defence budget was cut from $40bn to $25bn; and the NT$210bn drone bill for over 200,000 unmanned systems through 2031 remains stalled in the Legislative Yuan. Taiwan's deterrence trajectory is weaker than the headline suggested. That is a small addition to the up side, offset by Taiwan's first live-fire FPV drone exercises on 17 August under the Unmanned Systems Training Command.

Fifth, the political and diplomatic tracks continue to point away. Xiamen announced twelve Kinmen integration measures on 18 August, explicitly referencing the April 2026 Cheng Li-wun-Xi meeting; MAC pushed back the same day. Liberty Times reported on 10 August, citing security officials on the Beidaihe retreat that began 3 August, that a stated CCP objective is electing "patriotic forces" in Taiwan in 2026 - the declared instrument is the ballot box, with candidate registration for the 28 November local elections running 31 August to 4 September. ByteDance and Tencent have each received first shipments of roughly 10,000 Nvidia H200 chips, and WSJ reported on 20 August that Trump is pushing for a Kim meeting around APEC in Shenzhen in November, adding a second leader-level engagement to Xi's September Washington state visit. A US P-8A transited the Strait on 21 August; the PLA tracked it and nothing happened.

Finally, the disconfirming sweep. No Fujian maritime safety administration navigation warning, NOTAM or closure area anywhere in August; the most recent was Zhangzhou MSA on 22 July for drills on 23-24 July within 12km of the mainland coast. No named exercise since Justice Mission 2025 in late December - eight months, the longest gap since 2022. No reservist call-up, no RO-RO requisition, no blood or medical stockpiling, no evacuation of nationals. Jamestown's Pratas count is 52 patrol voyages in 2024, 46 in 2025 and 19 in the first five months of 2026, which annualises flat to slightly down. Grey-zone pressure is chronic, not accelerating. The one item that deserves more weight than I have given it is the January 2026 "floating wall" - an L-shaped array of thousands of Fujian and Zhejiang militia fishing vessels stretching some 300 miles and disrupting Strait traffic for over 30 hours. It proves the mobilisation machinery works. It also shows that when Beijing exercised the option it ran roughly 30 hours, undeclared and reversible, well short of this question's 72-hour bar. Nothing crossed a threshold. Hold.

question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
key_change:
Hold at 1%. The 80% interval stays at [0, 1]. Four days after the July 2026 CPI print, the incoming information is either neutral or points the wrong way for a YES, and the structural constraint that dominates this question has now been fully verified rather than inferred.

The latest published figure is the anchor. ONS published Consumer price inflation, UK: July 2026 on 19 August 2026, showing the CPI annual rate at 2.9%, up from 2.6% in June and the highest in four months. The monthly rate was +0.3%. CPIH was 3.1% and core CPI (excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco) was 2.6%, unchanged from June and above the 2.5% consensus. Services inflation was 3.4%, down from 3.6% in June. The largest contributing division was housing and household services at 0.59 percentage points of the headline rate, reflecting the 13% July increase in the Ofgem cap, with gas prices up 14.7% and electricity up 3.6% on the month. So the question asks whether a rate currently at 2.9% will print at or below 1.9% within a very small number of remaining opportunities.

The mechanics are now nailed down. Only prints PUBLISHED before 1 January 2027 count, and I verified today that the ONS release page for Consumer price inflation, UK: December 2026 carries a release date of 20 January 2027 7:00am and is flagged "This release is not yet published". The December 2026 reference month is therefore definitively outside the window. Going the other way, the ONS release for "Contributions to the 12-month rate of CPIH by import intensity: November 2026" is scheduled for 16 December 2026 at 9:30am; that companion release always accompanies the main CPI bulletin published at 7:00am the same day, which pins the November 2026 reference month inside the window. The four in-scope reference months are therefore August 2026 (published 16 September), September 2026 (21 October), October 2026 (18 November) and November 2026 (16 December). Exactly four attempts, no more.

The arithmetic is close to determinative. From the July 2026 CPI index level of 142.9, hitting a headline rate of 1.9% or below requires the index to fall cumulatively between roughly 0.26% and 0.63% depending on which base month is used. October 2026 is the least demanding comparison because the October 2025 index rose 0.4% on the month to 139.8, so an October 2026 print of 1.9% needs the index at about 142.5, a fall of roughly 0.27% from July. Outside 2008-09 and 2020, the UK has not delivered a cumulative three-to-four month fall of that size in the inflation-targeting era, and certainly not while the administered energy component is rising.

What is new since the last re-forecast is modestly negative. Brent closed at USD 94.39 on 21 August 2026, marginally higher than the USD 93.86 to 95.29 range noted previously and the highest since July, after US officials' suggestions of an imminent Tehran deal failed to materialise and rhetoric re-escalated on both sides. Iran maintains that Hormuz stays closed unless Washington meets its conditions; Trump says the US has "total control" of the waterway. Roughly 8 million barrels a day are estimated lost. There is one faint positive: on 21 August Iran's president indicated Tehran wants the war to end soon, and oil was little changed on the session rather than rising further. That is a hint, not a turn. UK NBP gas rose toward 157 pence per therm on 21 August, recouping the previous session's losses, with European storage at 62%, the lowest seasonal level in records back to 2009 and the dominant driver of NBP from September onward.

The Ofgem October cap remains the single most important in-window administered price and it is still pending. The assessment window closed on 18 August, so every input is fixed and only the calculation is outstanding; confirmation is due by 26 August 2026. Cornwall Insight's final forecast is around GBP 1,709 on the new typical-consumption basis (GBP 1,899 on the old basis), against the current GBP 1,663, with the analyst range GBP 1,701 to GBP 1,747. That is a rise of roughly 3% to 5% net of the legislated removal of 5% VAT on domestic electricity from 1 October. An energy component that rises in October, feeding the October and November reference months, is close to fatal to a sub-2.0% print in the two months where the base effects are most favourable.

The disinflationary strands are real but far too small. Food and non-alcoholic beverages inflation fell to 1.3% in the year to July, and Worldpanel like-for-like grocery inflation eased to 2.1% in the four weeks to 9 August, the lowest since October 2024 and a fifth consecutive month of easing, with 31.3% of grocery spending on promotion, the highest share this year. Services at 3.4% is decelerating from 4.4% in January. Both are helpful for 2027; neither can remove a full percentage point from the headline in four months against a rising energy impulse.

No published forecaster has any in-window month below 2.0%. The Bank of England's July 2026 Monetary Policy Report has CPI peaking at about 3.2% in 2026 Q4 with risks "tilted to the upside". The MPC held Bank Rate at 3.75% on 29 July by 6-3, with Greene, Mann and Pill preferring a hike to 4.00% on energy-driven persistence concerns; there is no August MPR or MPC meeting in the 2026 calendar, with the next decision on 17 September 2026. A Reuters poll of 13-18 August found 56 of 64 economists expect no change for the rest of the year. HM Treasury's independent average has Q4 2026 CPI at 3.4% to 3.7%. The BCC does not see 1.9% until Q4 2027, a full year beyond this question's window.

I hold at 1% rather than 0 because I never assign zero. The residual mass covers an abrupt Hormuz settlement collapsing Brent and NBP before the October reference month, an unannounced fiscal measure with immediate index effect, and a small tail of ONS reweighting or revision that retrospectively places a month below 2.0%. Each is remote; together they are worth about a point.

question: Will OpenAI and Anthropic have a combined ARR exceeding $70B by 31 December 2026?
key_change:

Here is the thing I had not pushed hard enough in the prior. That trailing-quarter test is being applied to Q2 data, but the question measures Q4. Anthropic's Q1 to Q2 sequential growth was roughly 145%; even at a fraction of that, Q4 recognised revenue lands somewhere in the $20-35bn range, annualising to $80-140bn on Anthropic alone. OpenAI's Q4 at 18% sequential from $6.7bn lands near $9.3bn, annualising to $37bn. So even the most adversarial convention available to a resolver, trailing-quarter recognised revenue annualised, clears $70bn comfortably by Q4 on Anthropic's contribution alone. The stacked worst case, net-basis restatement AND trailing-quarter annualisation, was the one genuine NO path on Q2 numbers ($32.5bn plus $26.8bn equals $59.3bn); on projected Q4 numbers it too clears. That closes the definitional branch that had been carrying most of my residual probability, and argues for the top of my interval rather than the bottom.

Fresh negatives from the 20-23 August period are real but small. Ramp's August AI Index, published 20 August under the title "Cracks in the AI thesis", shows momentum behind both firms cooling; TechCrunch's 20 August write-up frames it as OpenAI gaining on Anthropic among US business users, which is share rotation between the two and leaves the sum intact.
