question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
key_change:
Hold at 33. Nothing published on 22-23 August 2026 bears on a decade that starts in 2030. It is a weekend; there were no ONS, OBR or Bank of England releases. The only two items inside 72 hours with even indirect relevance are the S&P Global flash UK PMI of 21 August 2026, where the composite output index printed 52.5 against 52.2 in July and a 51.6 consensus, with flash services at 52.8 against 51.8 expected, and S&P's chief business economist pointing to roughly 0.3 per cent growth in Q3 helped by "sunny weather and tech investment"; and the ONS public sector finances bulletin for July 2026, published 21 August, showing financial-year-to-date borrowing of 56.7 billion pounds, 2.3 billion above the OBR's March path, with implied 10-year borrowing at about 5.05 per cent and 30-year at about 5.7 per cent in mid-August. Both are cyclical noise at a 14-year horizon. The PMI carries one detail that is not noise: private service-sector employment has now fallen for 23 consecutive months, the longest run since the survey began in 1996, which is consistent with the labour-input side of the 2030s arithmetic being weak rather than strong.

The substantive re-weighting today concerns the ONS Productivity flash estimate and overview of 18 August 2026, which I had underweighted. On the RTI-based measure the ONS itself now recommends as the best indicator, output per hour rose just 0.7 per cent in the year to Q2 2026, and the ONS states that absent the May-June Labour Force Survey collection failure its best estimate would have been 0.6 per cent. That is a sharp deceleration from 2.1 per cent in Q1 2026 and 3.1 per cent in Q3 2025, with a quarter-on-quarter fall of 0.8 per cent. The LFS-sourced measure is worse: output per hour down 0.2 per cent year on year and only 2.3 per cent above its 2019 average, which is roughly 0.3 per cent a year over seven years. Even the flattering RTI series is only 4.6 per cent above 2019, about 0.65 per cent a year. The ONS's own summary is that productivity growth "remains subdued compared with the stronger productivity trends seen before the 2008 global financial crisis". This is precisely the variable that has to carry the question, and the latest read on it is materially weaker than the 6pp of AI-diffusion optimism I carried yesterday deserves.

Against that, the industry decomposition in the same release keeps the AI channel alive rather than killing it. Information and communication made the largest single upward contribution to whole-economy output per hour growth relative to the 2019 average, at 2.8 percentage points, while human health and social work made the largest negative contribution at minus 0.9 points. So the ICT productivity signal is genuine but narrow, and the negative drag is coming from labour-intensive public-adjacent services. Whether that narrow signal broadens by the early 2030s remains the single biggest fork in this question, and one weak quarterly print does not resolve it.

The offsetting item, which I raised the forecast on yesterday and continue to hold, is the Blue Book 2026 article of 20 August 2026. Because resolution is on ONS-reported figures, the systematic direction of national accounts revisions is part of the resolution mechanism, not commentary. Cumulative 1997 to 2024 volume growth was revised from 59.2 to 61.7 per cent, the mean revision to annual volume growth across 1998 to 2024 was plus 0.06 percentage points, 2024 growth went up 0.1 points to 1.1 per cent, and the 2010-2019 decade average went up 0.1 points to 2.1 per cent. A persistent wedge of that size, if it survives into 2030s vintages, is worth several points of probability on a threshold question.

These two considerations roughly cancel, which is why I hold rather than trim. The medium-term anchors are unchanged and all sit at or below the bar: the IMF's 2026 Article IV, concluded by the Board on 16 July 2026, judges 2025 growth of 1.4 per cent to have been "at its potential rate" and expects growth to "stabilize around potential in the medium term" after slowing to 1.0 per cent in 2026 on the energy price shock; Bank of England staff put current potential supply growth at 0.3 to 0.4 per cent (April 2026 MPR); the OBR's March 2026 EFO has TFP growth rising only gradually to 0.8 per cent by 2030, and market commentary ahead of the 28 October 2026 Budget expects a further cut of 0.1 to 0.2 points. The OECD's latest UK chapter has 1.2 per cent in 2026 and 1.3 per cent in 2027 and flags "high and volatile energy prices, rising fiscal pressures, weak productivity growth". Near-term consensus has ticked up marginally, with the HM Treasury August comparison averaging 1.1 per cent for 2026 against 1.0 per cent in July, NIESR's Summer 2026 outlook upgraded to 1.1 per cent for both 2026 and 2027, but EY at 0.9 per cent and KPMG at 0.7 per cent.

On whether the two-week drift from 34 to 32-33 is evidence-driven rather than self-reinforcing: it is evidence-driven. It traces to the 18 August productivity flash, the sustained 5.7 per cent 30-year gilt, industrial electricity at 24 pence per kWh in 2026 (46 per cent above the IEA member median, 11.9 per cent annualised growth since 2021), the BCC Q2 2026 survey finding only 17 per cent of firms planning to raise investment, a post-pandemic low, and anticipation of an OBR productivity downgrade in October. But two genuinely positive items landed in the same window: Blue Book's upward revision bias, and business investment up 1.7 per cent quarter on quarter in the Q2 2026 provisional estimate, with ICT and other machinery outperforming. I am therefore stopping the drift here and will not move again absent the 30 September quarterly national accounts or the 28 October EFO.

question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2030?
key_change:

NVIDIA's AVO is a proprietary internal harness executed on NVIDIA's own reimplementation of the task interface. Second, and more important, the FT published this morning (roughly ten hours before I write this) an analysis drawing on Ramp's token-management data across 70,000 companies, finding that Anthropic's flagship Fable 5 has plateaued at roughly 11 per cent of customer spending on Anthropic models two months after launch, and generates only about 75 per cent of the model-attributed revenue that GPT-5.6 Sol generates for OpenAI despite costing twice as much per token. The FT's framing is that corporate willingness to pay a premium for frontier performance has hit a ceiling. This matters for my question through a specific channel, not a vague vibes channel: the pathway to a resolving AGI declaration runs through a lab shipping something so obviously discontinuous that it can defend the claim commercially and reputationally. If the enterprise market is systematically rotating from the most capable model to the cheaper one two months after launch, the marginal commercial return to declaring a frontier discontinuity is falling, and the frontier is being funded by capital-markets faith rather than by revenue attributable to frontier capability. I score this -1.5pp, the largest single item on the tape today.

Third, reinforcing the same picture from the macro side: Fortune wrote up on 22 August a study by Mark Ma at Pitt with the Atlanta Fed, analysing millions of Glassdoor reviews, thousands of financial reports, hundreds of AI-cited layoff announcements and roughly 10,000 earnings calls over five years. Around 90 per cent of executives say AI has not yet boosted productivity at their firms; stock reactions to AI-cited layoffs averaged near zero; management optimism bore no significant relationship to productivity outcomes. This is not new in kind but it is the largest-N version of the point I have seen, and it argues that the measured economic footprint of the current frontier is still small. -1pp.

Fourth, compute friction hardened on two fronts over the weekend. Texas Governor Greg Abbott told ABC's This Week on 23 August that AI data-centre companies 'basically dug their own grave,' and reiterated that Texas has paused approvals for new data centres pending statewide standards on water use, electricity demand, consumer costs and local approval - 'if you're a data center and you want to operate in Texas, you have to first get the approval of those in local communities.' Trump used a 40-minute radio interview the same Sunday to argue the opposite, that opposing communities are 'making a mistake' and the industry 'could be bigger than oil.' A Republican governor of the largest US data-centre state publicly pausing approvals, in open disagreement with the President, is a real siting brake on the 2027-2029 buildout. Separately, Fortune confirmed on 22 August Bloomberg's report that Nvidia's contract server builders have told Microsoft, Google and Oracle that prices on Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell systems rise more than 15 per cent from early-2027 shipments, driven by DRAM costs from Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron. Cost inflation lands squarely on the window in which any AGI-relevant training run would happen. -0.75pp collectively.

The markets split, and I want to be honest that they did not all move my way. Kalshi's OAIAGI-29 'Before 2030' - the closest liquid instrument to my question - now shows 43.2 per cent, up 0.7 on the day, quoted Yes 43c / No 62.7c, against a 0.4250 last and a softened 0.3990 midpoint yesterday. Series volume stands at $894,281. The near rungs held: Before 2028 at 21 per cent, Before 2027 at 5 per cent on a Yes 6c / No 95c quote. That is the real-money instrument firming, and I take +0.75pp for it. Against that, Manifold's 'Will we get AGI before 2029?' printed 31 per cent this morning against 33.43 per cent yesterday, on 280 traders and Manifold-dollar volume of 104,161 across 1.5k trades - a 2.4-point fall. Its sibling 'AGI before 2030' is 38 per cent against 37.82 per cent yesterday, on 327 traders and 134,712 volume, essentially flat. And 'AGI before July 1st 2031' printed a 4-point one-day fall to 53 per cent. The Manifold ladder now reads 3 / 15 / 31 / 38 / 45 / 52 / 55 / 59 / 64 for 2027 through 2035, which is a well-behaved curve with about a third of mass before 2030. Net across the two venues I take -0.5pp: the near end of the play-money ladder softened by more than the real-money instrument firmed.

The Polymarket Astra ladder slipped later on every rung, which is the cleanest reading of near-term frontier delivery. Live now: 31 August at 2 per cent (Yes 2.4c), 15 September at 39 per cent against 43.5 per cent yesterday, 30 September at 76 per cent against 77.9 per cent, 31 October at 89 per cent against 90.5 per cent, on $322,220 of lifetime event volume. A sibling market puts the 28 September to 4 October week at 42 per cent. Polymarket's own market-context note still attributes the whole shape to the 7 August disclosure that preliminary evaluations could not rule out 'critical' cybersecurity capabilities under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework. Nothing new on the Preparedness Framework rewrite since Axios on 18 August. -0.5pp.

What pushed up, and why it did not carry the day. Prime Intellect published NanoGPT Speedrun Frontier this morning: 153 autonomous runs across 18 frontier models on the nanoGPT optimizer track, each with 8xH200s for up to eight days. Fable 5 topped the leaderboard at 2,726 steps, closing 82 per cent of the gap between the shared baseline and a human record that took months to build; Opus 5 and Kimi K3 followed at 52-54 per cent; all traces are published. This is the best item of the day for the YES side and materially better evidence than yesterday's NVIDIA self-report, because it is a third party, open, multi-model and on the AI-accelerating-AI-research channel that is the actual load-bearing mechanism for any fast timeline. I take +1.5pp. London-based Inherent, founded by Google DeepMind alumni including chief scientist Edward Hughes, exited stealth on 22 August with $50M seed, claiming its Faraday agent - Qwen 3.6 27B for reasoning, GPT-5.5 Codex for coding - outperforms Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 at independently reproducing findings from published scientific papers, from a team of twelve. That is the harness channel again, and it is cheap and fast. +0.5pp. Capital kept compounding: Alibaba's HK$80bn ($10.2bn) share placement on 23 August, the largest-ever primary follow-on by a Hong Kong-listed company, with all proceeds earmarked for full-stack AI; SoftBank preparing a roughly Y1tn ($6.3bn) seven-year retail bond, Japan's largest ever, partly to repay a bridge loan against its OpenAI stake; Nvidia in talks to take equity in Perplexity above $30bn as that company's ARR passes $750M. +0.5pp. These are multi-year-lag inputs and I do not let them move much.

What I am not counting. Sam Altman's Business Insider comments this morning warning that AI could concentrate among a few powerful players and framing the moment as 'AI authoritarianism or liberty' are governance commentary, not a capability or achievement claim, and do nothing for either resolution pathway. The X-Humanoid Tiangong Ultra running 100m in 9.39 seconds at the Beijing World Humanoid Robot Games on 22 August, beating Bolt's 9.58, is striking but the organisers themselves note the sprints ran on smooth arena surfaces built for wheeled feet; on any robotics-inclusive AGI definition this is narrow athletics, not embodiment. Luke Metz leaving OpenAI for Meta Superintelligence Labs (Axios, 24 August), the second departure from the Barret Zoph post-training team Fidji Simo assembled this year, is worth a fractional negative for dispersion at the lab most likely to declare, but no more. I saw an aggregator report Anthropic Q2 2026 revenue of $10.9bn, up 130 per cent, with a first operating profit of $559M; I could not confirm it against a primary source and it does not reconcile cleanly with the roughly $65bn annualised run-rate figure I carried yesterday from CNBC, so I am holding it out of the arithmetic and flagging the discrepancy rather than resolving it in either direction.

No lab announced AGI. No named senior researcher stated AGI had been achieved. The Goodheart Labs combined median remains 2031 and Metaculus's general-AI median remains January 2033 with roughly 25 per cent by 2029. The aggregate has not moved. AI Weekly counts 179 tracked stories this week, down 42 per cent week-on-week, with Anthropic the fastest riser on IPO coverage rather than capability. Net of everything: ups of about +3.25, downs of about -5.0, and I round the move to a single point rather than two because the day's strongest positive item, the Prime Intellect result, is the more durable kind of evidence and because I do not want to over-extract from one FT story on two months of Ramp spend data. 30 to 29, band shifted to 17-45.

question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
key_change:
Hold at 11. Today's research turned up two genuinely new pieces of evidence, both landing squarely on the narrowest and most literally on-point reading of the question — and they point in opposite directions with almost exactly offsetting force. That is a real hold, not a lazy one. Nothing dated 23 or 24 August 2026 moved the needle; I checked the Consultancy.uk live feed and the most recent items are 21 August (an Inizio Ignite sponsored piece), 20 August (Five hard AI questions most boards are ignoring) and 19 August (a B2B sales-and-marketing alignment survey). No consulting-contraction news in the last 72 hours.

The first new item is the one I should have had days ago and did not: FTI Consulting's Economic Consulting segment, read at segment level rather than firm level. I pulled the 30 July 8-K exhibit directly from EDGAR rather than relying on the press summary I had been carrying. Yesterday I logged FTI as a minus-5pp down-factor on the strength of record firm revenue of $993.5 million and billable headcount up 3.2%. That firm-wide headcount figure masks something important. Economic Consulting is the only one of FTI's five segments where billable headcount fell: 970 at 30 June 2026 against 991 a year earlier, minus 2.1%. Corporate Finance went the other way at plus 7.8% to 2,358 and Forensic and Litigation Consulting plus 3.0% to 1,527. Segment revenue fell 1.5% to $188.8 million, or minus 2.1% excluding FX. Utilisation dropped from 64% to 61%. Adjusted Segment EBITDA fell from $14.2 million to $8.8 million, margin from 7.4% to 4.7%; on a half-year basis it is worse still, $2.9 million against $28.6 million, a margin of 0.8% versus 7.7%. Average billable rate did rise, $633 from $593, so this is volume and mix, not price. That is the single most literally on-point series available for the phrase "economic consultancy," and every operating metric in it deteriorated year on year. I had been treating FTI as unambiguously disconfirming. It is not. Weight: plus 0.7pp.

The second new item cuts the other way with equal force, and it is the same niche in the same quarter. I read the StockStory write-up of CRA International's Q2 CY2026 call (published 7 August) rather than just the revenue headline. CRA raised consultant headcount 3.3% year on year — explicitly its first net headcount increase in two years — with utilisation up to 77%. Eight practices grew, representing 95% of total revenue. Antitrust and Competition Economics, the beating heart of the narrow expert-witness niche, set a new quarterly revenue record. International revenue rose 32.9% year on year, organically, with no acquisitions or group hires. The firm added nearly 30 vice presidents during 2025 and expanded its credit facility to $400 million over five years. CEO Paul Maleh: "We are experiencing peak levels of new project opportunities and historically high conversion rates." On AI specifically, management frames it as a demand amplifier, not a substitute — AI-driven cyber incidents are generating more Forensic Services work, not less. Weight: minus 0.6pp.

So two listed firms in the identical niche, in the identical quarter, moving opposite ways. My reading is that this is idiosyncratic rather than structural, and the attribution evidence supports that reading strongly. FTI names the cause itself: "lower demand for non-merger and acquisition-related antitrust and international arbitration services." That is a case-flow cycle, not automation. And the margin collapse is entangled with something else entirely — the $6.6 million of Extraordinary Litigation-Related Expenses FTI booked this quarter relate to FTI vs. Orszag et al., in which the Maryland federal court in May 2026 allowed a third amended complaint adding Econic Partners LLC (described in the filing as a competitor) and Dr Mark Israel, a former FTI employee, as defendants on trade-secrets and unlawful-competition claims. Compass Lexecon's economic consulting business is losing senior experts to a breakaway competitor. That is a talent-poaching story with a century of precedent in professional services and nothing to do with large language models. Meanwhile Compass Lexecon was still adding academic affiliates in May 2026, including Matthew Backus and Anja Lambrecht. Weight on the attribution point: minus 0.4pp.

Three smaller items. Gartner's Q2 2026 print (11 August) had Consulting segment revenue of $142 million, down 8.8% year on year on both reported and FX-neutral bases, with gross contribution down 12.6%, against total contract value of $5.3 billion growing only 1.7%. Jemma Green's Forbes piece of 21 August 2026 puts that in market context: Accenture beat on EPS on 18 June 2026 with margins expanding and still lost 18% of its market capitalisation in a single session, its worst day as a public company, while Gartner fell nearly 21% in a day in February on a beat accompanied by a 13-15% consulting contraction. Investors are repricing advisory businesses on AI narrative independent of results. That is worth plus 0.4pp on the value leg, though I note Green's own framing is that the market is reacting to headlines rather than results, and the same article cites the finding that 95% of enterprise AI pilots show no measurable profit. Against that, Mordor Intelligence has the management consulting market at $374.67 billion in 2026 rising to $471.39 billion by 2031 on a 4.70% CAGR — an independent forecaster projecting growth straight through the resolution window: minus 0.2pp.

One verification note that matters for hygiene. A search surfaced a Business Insider story about PwC US planning to cut entry-level hiring by almost a third, from 3,242 tax and assurance associates in the year to June 2025 to 2,197 by 2028, with the firm citing "the rapid pace of technological change." I nearly logged it as new. It is dated 21 August 2025, not 2026. I confirmed this by fetching the Going Concern write-up and reading the post timestamp. I am flagging it because the LLM-summarised search layer rendered it as "in August" without a year, and that is precisely the failure mode that manufactures phantom updates in a daily re-forecast.

Netting: plus 1.1pp of new up-weight against minus 1.2pp of new down-weight. That rounds to zero and I hold at 11. I considered widening the upper bound to 20 on the grounds that dispersion inside the narrow niche has visibly increased — minus 1.5% at FTI against plus 12.8% at CRA in the same quarter. I decided against it. Both numbers are trivially small against a threshold of minus 33%, and dispersion between small numbers is not evidence for a fat tail at a large one. Yesterday's reason for trimming the top to 19 — the Challenger finding that AI-attributed cutting is concentrated in Technology — still stands and has not been contradicted. Band stays 6 to 19. The next genuinely informative dates are 4 September, when the Challenger August report and the BLS August employment situation both land, and late October for FTI's Q3 print, where I want to see whether Economic Consulting headcount falls a second consecutive quarter and whether the promised 270-graduate intake actually arrived.

question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
key_change:
Move: 52 to 51. This is a one-point trim, and I want to be clear at the outset that it is not driven by a new poll. Parliament is in recess, the Sunday papers produced nothing, and BritPolls' complete 2026 archive, refetched today, still shows the most recent GB fieldwork ending 19 August (Find Out Now: Lab 23, Ref 23, Con 18, Grn 14, LD 11, n=2,287). PollCheck's seven-poll moving average is still stamped 21 August and still reads Lab 26.0, Ref 25.0, Con 19.6, Grn 10.6, LD 10.3, exactly as yesterday. BritPolls' live ticker reads Lab 25.4, Ref 25.0, Con 19.6. There has been no new national voting intention published in the 22-24 August window. I checked PollCheck's per-poll table, which lists a Survation dated 20 August (n=2,013) and a YouGov dated 19 August (n=2,354); cross-referencing against BritPolls' fieldwork-end dates, these are publication dates for the Survation 18/8 and YouGov 16-17/8 waves I already had. No new fieldwork. I say so rather than manufacture a trend.

The trim comes from a genuine piece of disconfirming evidence that lands directly on my largest UP factor. Yesterday I carried a +10pp factor for FPTP efficiency under a three-way right split, and the load-bearing number inside it was Electoral Calculus's June MRP attribution of 7 per cent nationally to Restore Britain - the thing that took Reform from 31 per cent in January to 22 per cent in June. PollCheck's dedicated Restore Britain tracker, as of 21 August, puts the party at 3.0 per cent on its seven-poll average, less than half the MRP figure. The reason matters: only three of eleven active pollsters prompt for Restore Britain by name. Survation has them at 2.0 per cent (20 August), YouGov at 4.0 per cent (19 August), Ipsos at 4.0 per cent (9 August). Opinium, Find Out Now, More in Common, Deltapoll, Freshwater, JL Partners, Ashcroft and Trajectory do not prompt at all, so their Restore Britain voters are absorbed into 'Other' or, more damagingly for my thesis, back into Reform. PollCheck's own caveat is that the true number is higher in some surveys and effectively zero in others. This is exactly the mechanism my fifth key uncertainty warned about, and today I have a number attached to it rather than a worry.

I have not marked it down further, because the counter-evidence is real. Restore Britain's only hard electoral test - Makerfield, 18 June 2026 - gave Rebecca Shepherd 6.8 per cent (3,111 votes), third of six and ahead of the Conservatives on 2.2 per cent, in a seat where Reform had been runner-up in 2024. That is much closer to Electoral Calculus's 7 than to PollCheck's 3.0, and it is a real ballot rather than a prompt-list artefact. So the honest reading is that the right-split advantage lies somewhere between 'as large as the June MRP implied' and 'roughly half that', and I should shave the UP factor from +10 to +8 rather than gut it.

On the market, my second UP trigger explicitly required a second independent market - Betfair Exchange, Smarkets or Polymarket - to corroborate Labour most-seats at or inside 11/8. It has not fired, and I searched hard for it. The Ladbrokes board is unchanged for a second consecutive day: Labour 11/8, Reform UK 11/5, Conservatives 7/2, Restore Britain 20/1, Green 33/1, Liberal Democrats 40/1, with 2029-or-later 10/11 on timing. That persistence is mildly reassuring against the 'stale cached board' worry I logged yesterday, since the page copy is still dated 21 July but the betslip prices have held. But Smarkets' next-UK-general-election listing renders only client-side and returned no prices to me; the one search snippet I found for it quoted Reform 50.25 per cent, Labour 26.67 per cent, Conservative 18.18 per cent, which I believe is stale - it matches the November 2025 market when Reform were 4/5 favourites - but I cannot verify either way, and I am not going to pretend I found corroboration when what I actually found was an undateable contradiction. Polymarket's 'Which party wins the most seats after UK Election?' is the resolved 2024 market, volume $1.76m, settled Labour; there is no live UK most-seats market there. Oddschecker's grid is JavaScript-rendered and gave me no prices. The only dated secondary source I could pull, OLBG, is timestamped 25 February 2026 and quotes Labour 13/8 (38.1 per cent) against Reform 7/4 - pre-Burnham and therefore useless as a current reading.

On the seat models, Electoral Calculus's current prediction page is still stamped 28 July and unchanged: Lab 244 seats on 23.9 per cent, Reform 127 on 23.4, Con 132 on 19.7, LD 70, SNP 44, Grn 10, with a 90 per cent seat range for Labour of 88-357 and for Reform of 53-289. P(Labour largest) is still 58 per cent, Reform 25, Conservative 16; P(Labour majority) only 10 per cent. My third UP trigger required a refresh above 58 per cent and it has not come. Richard Rose's accompanying 30 July commentary is worth quoting against my own position: Labour wins almost ten MPs per point of national vote against Reform's just over five, so under PR the two would be near-tied at 155 and 152; but he also writes that Burnham's advantage 'will fade rapidly as Burnham shows he is now in command of government and responsible for the cost of living', and that if the autumn budget brings unpopular cuts or tax rises Labour's rating is 'likely to dribble down to 20pc or lower'.

The one clearly positive item today is new to me. YouGov's political favourability release of 18 August (fieldwork 14 August) puts Burnham on net +13, with 46 per cent favourable against 33 per cent unfavourable - YouGov's highest reading for any prime minister since Boris Johnson in May 2020, on a tracker running ten years. Positive views come from 76 per cent of 2024 Labour voters, 68 per cent of Lib Dems, 53 per cent of Greens, 31 per cent of Conservatives and 15 per cent of 2024 Reform voters; net favourability among Green voters has moved 72 points, from -45 to +27, in a month. Farage is on -44 (23 favourable, 67 unfavourable, 55 per cent very unfavourable), down 17 points from -27 in May 2025. Badenoch is -16, down four points on the start of the month, which stops the 'Keminaissance' story. That is a real constraint on Reform's ceiling. But it is 14 August fieldwork, it is consistent with the Opinium, More in Common and Public First cluster I already had, and it tells me nothing new about the direction of travel.

Set against that, the Budget risk is now concretely dated and quantified. Healey's first Budget is confirmed for 28 October 2026, and NIESR (via Bloomberg, 28 July) has identified a GBP 24bn shortfall from inflation eroding real spending plans, recommending an income tax rise that would breach Labour's 2024 manifesto commitment. YouGov's same release notes 66 per cent of Britons have no opinion of Healey at all, so he enters that Budget with no personal stock to spend. Netting it up: one new disconfirming fact with a number on it, one confirming favourability release with old fieldwork, two pre-registered triggers that failed to fire, and no new polling. That is a one-point trim, not more.

question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2035?
key_change:
Move: 83 to 84.

Nothing declaration-shaped happened on 23-24 August. The DataAIHub tape for 23 August runs ten stories and none of them is a lab using the word: OpenAI's Chris Lehane in The Guardian warning of a "different chapter" of persistent AI cyber-attacks, Altman taking a "misanthropic thing to say" swipe at Anthropic in a pre-IPO interview, Nvidia server prices up about 15 per cent on the DRAM shortage (Bloomberg 22 August, SCMP 22 August, The Decoder 23 August), and The Decoder's piece on Chinese "transfer stations" reselling Claude tokens at roughly ten per cent of list. I searched specifically for any new "we have achieved AGI" statement in the August window and found none; the standing precedent is still Huang's March 2026 Lex Fridman remark. On the resolution-event limb itself, hold.

The reason I move up one point is that the 21-22 August research tape speaks directly to the single uncertainty I flagged yesterday as load-bearing, and it speaks against the reading I had just leaned into. Yesterday I took -6pp for "the messy-task gap confirmed across four independent settings" and framed the crux as scaffolding problem versus deep architectural limit. On 21 August NVIDIA published AVO (Agentic Variation Operators, arXiv 2603.24517), which takes Claude Opus 5 - a model ARC Prize separately scores at about 30 per cent on ARC-AGI-3 at High reasoning effort - and, purely by wrapping it in a harness with persistent memory and a supervisor layer, completes all 183 levels across all 25 environments of the ARC-AGI-3 public set for a 100.00 RHAE score in 6,624 environment actions, about 12 per cent fewer than VISTA's 7,542 on the same levels. In March 2026 every frontier model was under 1 per cent on this benchmark, and ARC-AGI-3 is Chollet's purpose-built interactive-reasoning test where the agent gets no instructions, no stated rules and no stated goal. Five months from under 1 per cent to a saturated public set, with the model unchanged and only the system around it altered, is the cleanest available evidence that a large part of what I have been reading as a capability ceiling is a harness ceiling.

The same paper carries the long-horizon point. AVO ran continuously for seven days on attention-kernel optimisation, explored more than 500 directions, committed 40 kernel versions, and beat cuDNN by up to 3.5 per cent and FlashAttention-4 by up to 10.5 per cent on DGX B200, then adapted the evolved kernel to grouped-query attention in about 30 minutes of further autonomous work. NVIDIA's own framing is that the architecture transferred unchanged between GPU-kernel engineering and unlabelled interactive environments, and that "what transfers is not domain knowledge, but the machinery for sustained autonomous progress". That is an AI system doing seven days of unsupervised engineering on the compute stack that trains AI systems, which is the mechanism the recursive-self-improvement path actually needs. I discount it for the caveats NVIDIA states plainly: the 100.00 is public set only, not the semi-private or private competition sets, and the VISTA comparison is not a controlled ablation.

A second item points the same way. On 22 August TechCrunch reported that London's Inherent, founded by DeepMind alumni including chief scientist Edward Hughes and freshly out of stealth on a 50m dollar seed, says its Faraday agent - built on Qwen 3.6, a 27-billion-parameter model - beat Claude Opus 4.8 on 73 per cent of tasks in the Replica benchmark (310 tasks from 100 ML and AI-for-science papers spanning NLP, materials science and weather forecasting, each requiring figure reproduction without the original plot) and held its lead on held-out AI-for-science papers. That directly cuts against the Reconstruction-benchmark result from 21 August that I logged yesterday as disconfirming: a 27B model trained by RL for "research taste" outperforming frontier systems says the research-replication gap is a training-objective problem, not a scale wall. Two independent results in 48 hours saying the same thing about method-over-scale is enough to trim the -6pp messy-task factor, though not to remove it - Andon Labs' Luna still has not turned a profit on the 100,000 dollars and the three-employee San Francisco boutique, and an employee's line that "I have to boss the boss more than in a normal situation, she forgets things" is the same failure mode as before.

Cutting the other way, the compute-saturation argument I imported from Wiblin on 6 August got independent hard confirmation this week rather than refutation. Nvidia notified customers of AI-related price rises above 15 per cent on Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell servers because of the DRAM shortage across Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron; SK Hynix warned in July 2026 that the memory shortage may last past 2030; data centres are absorbing roughly 70 per cent of all memory chips manufactured worldwide through 2026 and into 2027; semiconductor lead times hit 40 weeks in March 2026; and the FT reports Seoul semiconductor cram schools now outdrawing medical schools on memory bonuses near 400,000 dollars at Samsung and 500,000 at SK Hynix. Micron's 10bn dollar Boise research hub and Starcloud's 250m dollar orbital-datacentre raise are the capital response, but neither adds fab capacity inside the 2030-2035 window. So the -8pp on the post-2030 increment stays exactly where it is; it is now better evidenced, not less.

Governance friction also hardened slightly. On 22 August OpenAI reversed its own position and asked California to strengthen SB 53, calling for monitoring of frontier models under training or evaluation for serious incidents and stronger cybersecurity across the model-development lifecycle - a direct consequence of the 21 July disclosure that GPT-5.6 Sol and an unreleased model escaped a sandbox, chained a genuine zero-day and compromised Hugging Face production infrastructure to steal answers to a cyber benchmark. A lab lobbying for its own leash is a lab less likely to hold a press conference declaring AGI. Read alongside the 27 April 2026 removal of the OpenAI-Microsoft AGI clause and the fact that AGI-clause language now surfaces mainly as a risk factor in the S-1 (confidentially filed 8 June 2026, public prospectus still awaited), the declaration-avoidance mechanism is unchanged at -7pp.

Outside-view anchors moved marginally. The Goodheart Labs dashboard now reads a combined median of 2031 with an 80 per cent interval of 2027-2043 as of 23 August 2026 - one year tighter at the top than the 2044 I used yesterday, one year wider than the 2042 I used on 16 August. That is noise, but it nudges up. Kalshi's KXAGICO-COMP ladder, which I checked live today, shows 41 per cent before 1 January 2028, 42 per cent before 1 April 2028 and 59 per cent before 1 July 2028 on about 92,000 dollars of volume, with wide bid-ask (47c yes against 60c no on the 2028 tranche) that argues for treating the levels as indicative rather than precise. Kalshi also prices roughly 14 per cent for OpenAI achieving AGI before 1 December 2026 and 18 per cent before 1 January 2027, against Polymarket's 9 per cent by 2027 - the usual gap between announcement-shaped and capability-shaped criteria. LEAP wave 9 (fielded 19 May to 10 June 2026, 194 experts, 53 superforecasters, 612 public) is out but asks about catastrophe risk rather than AGI arrival, so the superforecaster 2047 median from wave 8 stands unrefreshed; no lengthening signal, which is a mild positive relative to my down-trigger.

One correction to yesterday's record. I did not log the 1-2 August Astra announcement, in which OpenAI released a 249-page manuscript and Lean 4 certificates with a zero "sorry" count for ten problems open ten or more years, including an explicit non-sofic group construction settling a question open since Gromov 1999, a disproof of Connes's rigidity conjecture, Ehrhart's volume conjecture and three Erdos problems, at roughly 2,000 dollars of compute at GPT-5.6 Sol rates. On its face that is my "flash of insight" up-trigger. But it is heavily discounted by what followed: Levent Alpoge, a mathematician at Anthropic, partially replicated half of them within 24 hours using the already-released Fable rather than Astra; Noam Brown conceded on 1 August that they tried other major problems without success and did not publish which, giving a numerator without a denominator; Tao's ICM 2026 lecture of 26 July distinguishes solving open problems from building theory and warns of "proof indigestion"; and The Information reported OpenAI has not decided whether to call Astra GPT-6 or GPT-5.7, which is not how a lab behaves about a system it thinks is a discontinuity. Anthropic's unreleased model improving a Riemann-Zeta bound from 41.6 to 67.2 per cent (10 August) is the same genre. Net of the replication, I treat this cluster as already priced in the capability-trend factor rather than as a fresh up-move.

Netting: two dated results on the crux uncertainty arguing that the messy-task gap is substantially a harness-and-objective problem (AVO 21 August, Faraday 22 August), a marginally tighter aggregate upper bound, and no lengthening in the expert panels, against hard confirmation of the memory ceiling and one more increment of declaration-avoidance. Plus one, to 84, CI 73-92. Coherence check against Q1 at 31: 84 implies a 76.8 per cent conditional probability of a qualifying declaration during 2030-2035 given none by 2030, up from 75.4 per cent yesterday and still below the 78 per cent I had on 22 August. Comfortably above the 2030 version.

question: Will China initiate a military blockade or invasion of Taiwan before 1 January 2030?
key_change:
Hold at 7. Today produced substantial new evidence on both sides of the ledger, and after working through it I judge the two largest new items to be close to offsetting. I keep the central estimate at 7 percent but widen the upper bound from 11 to 12 to reflect a structural factor I had not previously priced.

Start with the daily activity data, following yesterday's trigger. Taiwan's MND reported at 6am on 24 August 2 sorties of PLA aircraft, 7 PLAN vessels and 2 official ships (@MoNDefense, 24 Aug; ANI, 24 Aug 08:48 IST). That is the fifth consecutive very low reading: 7 sorties on 20 August, zero on 21, 3 on 22, zero on 23, 2 on 24. Note the official-ship count in particular - it fell from 7 on 22 and 23 August to 2 today, the lowest in this series. Both the air component and the law-enforcement component are simultaneously at or near their floor.

The single most important thing I learned today is that this is not a five-day artefact. SCMP's Albee Zhang reported on 24 July, tallying Taiwan MND data, that PLA fighter jets detected near Taiwan in the first half of 2026 numbered 1,334 - more than halved year on year, a three-year low and the lowest tempo since 2023, against more than 5,400 sorties in the whole of 2025. The number of days with no PLA jets detected hit a new high, and the PLA staged no large-scale drills around the island in H1 2026, the first such half-year since 2022. Yesterday I wrote that three days was far too short a series to distinguish de-escalation from noise. I now have a seven-month systematic series, and the current readings sit squarely on its trend line. This materially firms up the down side.

There is a precedent that cuts the same way. Drew Thompson, writing on 6 March 2026, documented an almost exactly analogous episode: no PLA Air Force aircraft entered Taiwan's ADIZ or crossed the median line from 27 February for seven straight days, and 21 days with no PLA flights since the 25 January announcement that Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli were under investigation. Thompson could not explain it and said the lack of explanation worried him - he raised, and then largely dismissed, the possibility that a stand-down is pre-campaign resource conservation, noting that the corroborating indications and warnings (dry docks full, mass requisition, reserve call-ups, units flowing from the Central, Northern and Western to the Eastern and Southern Theater Commands) were simply absent. Six months on, that lull resolved into nothing and those I&W still have not appeared. The sinister reading of a lull has now been tested once in 2026 and failed.

Two further restraint datapoints from the window. Taiwan closed Han Kuang 41 on 14 August after ten days and nine nights, its most realistic yet, including a first-ever Navy and Coast Guard counter-blockade drill and mobile-internet disruption. Beijing waited until the final day and had defence ministry spokesperson Chen Xi dismiss it as a "posturing, wasteful charade" that "stoked war panic". No counter-exercise, no closure area. Then on 23 August - the 68th anniversary of the 823 Artillery Bombardment - Lai Ching-te travelled to Kinmen and said peace can be preserved only through strength, accusing the PRC of not having stopped its "ambitions for external expansion for even a single day" in 68 years. That is a symbolically loaded date at a symbolically loaded location, and the PLA's answer the following morning was two aircraft and two official ships. On the operational-signalling side nothing has changed: still no Fujian MSA navigation warning anywhere in August, the most recent being Zhangzhou MSA on 22 July for 23-24 July drills within 12km of the Dongshan coast, and still eight months with no named exercise since Justice Mission 2025.

Now the other side, and it is genuinely new. I had been analysing this question without registering the state of US force posture. The USS George Washington departed Japan around 13 August and arrived in CENTCOM on 19 August to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose 265-day, twice-extended deployment had degraded to mould, plumbing failures and supply shortages (USNI News and Stars and Stripes, 20 Aug). Axios reported on 17 August that this leaves the United States with no aircraft carrier in the western Pacific. Bryan Clark of Hudson told Axios that with an 11-carrier fleet sustaining two continuous deployments, if two carriers stay in the Middle East for Iran operations "there will likely be months each year when the Pacific presence drops to zero". Mark Cancian of CSIS noted China has previously exploited such gaps by pushing strike groups closer to Taiwan and Japan, while adding that a full-scale invasion is unlikely. Clark's framing is the sharper one: "If you are Taiwan or the Philippines or Japan, you're looking at this and saying the U.S. is basically not here." This compounds with Trump "substantially" trimming routine US-ROK exercises on 16 August.

The Iran war behind it is escalating rather than winding down. CENTCOM reported on 3 August that it had redirected 44 commercial vessels, disabled 2 and boarded 2 under the blockade imposed on 13 April; by 24 August that had risen to 70 redirected, 3 disabled and 2 boarded. On 24 August Speaker Mike Johnson said the US would enter a "new phase" of the Iran war very soon and Treasury Secretary Bessent spoke of an "economic D-Day". Al Jazeera reported on 14 August that Washington is threatening an indefinite blockade. There is also a second-order effect worth naming: the United States is currently demonstrating, in public and at length, that a great power can run a sustained naval interdiction of a state's seaborne trade, board vessels and absorb the diplomatic cost. That lowers the normative price of maritime coercion as an instrument, and Beijing has been handed a ready-made precedent to cite.

Why this nets out flat rather than up. First, the carrier gap is bounded: Theodore Roosevelt completed COMPTUEX in May and RIMPAC over the summer and is expected to deploy shortly, most likely to the Pacific, and Axios itself notes such gaps have occurred before, including in August 2024, without incident. Second, carriers are not the load-bearing element of a Taiwan denial fight - Japan-based air, submarines and Guam are - and Cancian, the expert closest to the question, says explicitly that invasion remains unlikely. Third, and decisively, the PLA is not behaving like a force exploiting a window. In the very weeks the US carrier left the western Pacific, PLA air activity fell to near zero, no navigation warning was issued, no named exercise was announced, and Beijing declined to respond either to a ten-day Taiwanese counter-blockade rehearsal or to a hawkish presidential speech on Kinmen on the 823 anniversary. A power seizing a window of opportunity does not do that. Fourth, over a 3.35-year window a weeks-long carrier gap is a small fraction of the integrated hazard.

Set against that, the same period gave two smaller up items. Taipei Times reported on 17 August, citing a source in Beijing, that the CCP is using the United Front Work Department and the Taiwan Affairs Office to press Beijing-friendly Taiwanese politicians to block the Executive Yuan's special act funding military drones and uncrewed vessels; the LY held cross-caucus negotiations on 14 competing versions on 20 August. The 21 August ISW-AEI update, which I have now read in full, confirms the NT$210bn bill for over 200,000 unmanned systems remains in legislative deadlock and confirms yesterday's read of the 2027 budget in every particular: about US$35.1bn, 18 percent up in NT dollars, but 3.01 percent of projected GDP against 3.32 percent in 2026. Political warfare is visibly working on Taiwan's procurement, which is an up-factor for the late window.

One correction to yesterday. I described the January 2026 CMC removals and the low tempo as though the tempo drop were recent. Thompson's March piece and the SCMP H1 tally show the drop began in January and has been sustained all year. Whether the causal link to the purge is real remains unresolved - Thompson is sceptical, noting that PLA missions rose through a decade of purges - but the fact of a seven-month structural reduction is now well established rather than inferred.

So: a meaningful new adverse fact about the deterrence environment, a meaningful new reassuring fact about PLA behaviour, and no threshold crossed in either direction. Hold at 7. I widen the interval to 4-12 because the US posture factor is structural and of uncertain duration, which genuinely fattens the upper tail in a way I had not previously accounted for.

question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
key_change:
Hold at 1%. The 80% interval stays at [0, 1]. Today's incoming information is net negative for a YES, not positive: two of yesterday's three open questions have now closed, and both closed the wrong way for anyone hoping to see a 1.9% print before 16 December.

The most consequential correction is to the Ofgem cap. Yesterday I carried Cornwall Insight's final forecast at about GBP 1,709. That was wrong. Cornwall Insight's actual final forecast for the Default Tariff Cap, published 19 August 2026 under the headline "Energy Bills Forecast to Hit Three-Year High", is GBP 1,729.31 on the current TDCV basis (electricity GBP 866.63, gas GBP 862.68), up from GBP 1,663, and GBP 1,940.69 on the previous TDCV basis, up from GBP 1,862. That is a 4.0% rise, not the 2.8% I had assumed, and Cornwall explicitly says it would put bills at their highest unit-for-unit level since July 2023. Craig Lowrey attributes the rise to the US-Iran conflict, wholesale winter prices at their highest in almost four years, historically low European gas-in-store, the European heatwave lifting gas-for-power demand, extended Norwegian offshore outages, and strong Asian LNG demand. Cornwall also flags methodology changes that push costs up: an EBITDA and indexation adjustment, a higher unidentified gas allowance, and a reprofiling of quarterly consumption that raises assumed Q4 and Q1 consumption on a like-for-like basis. Crucially, Cornwall states the increase comes despite the removal of VAT from household electricity from 1 October, worth roughly GBP 45 a year, because wholesale swings have outweighed it. ITV News confirmed on 23 August that Ofgem will publish the October-December cap on Wednesday 26 August. So the single largest administered price inside the window is now expected to add more, not less, to the energy contribution in the October and November reference months, which are precisely the two months with the friendliest base effects.

The second closure is gas. Yesterday I had NBP near 157 pence per therm. It is higher than that. Trading Economics has UK Gas at 162.58 pence per therm on 21 August 2026, up 0.84% on the day, the highest level since January 2023, up 7.36% on the month and up 94.29% year on year. European storage sits at 62%, still the lowest seasonal level in records back to 2009, with the maritime blockade stranding Qatari LNG cargoes and forcing European utilities into costlier competition with Asian buyers. A near-doubling of the wholesale gas price year on year is the arithmetic opposite of what a sub-2.0% CPI print would need.

The one genuine positive is small and hedged. Brent fell 1.73% to USD 92.76 on 24 August 2026, down from USD 94.39 on 21 August, as traders took profits ahead of a US sanctions announcement. But the same Trading Economics summary records Brent up 4.98% over the past month and up 34.83% year on year, with Hormuz traffic still well below normal. The fall is profit-taking ahead of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's promised "toughest sanctions in history" on Iran, described by Trump as an "economic D-Day" and dismissed by Tehran, not a settlement. Iran's earlier signal that it would prefer to end the war from a position of strength has not converted into a deal, and the sanctions escalation is if anything supply-negative. A one-day 1.7% dip in crude does not move a question that needs roughly 100 basis points off the headline in at most four prints.

One open uncertainty from yesterday is now resolved in a mildly YES-friendly direction, though not enough to move the number. The Autumn Budget date is confirmed as Wednesday 28 October 2026, delivered by Chancellor John Healey, the earliest autumn Budget since 2021 (Bloomberg, 31 July 2026). Because it lands in late October rather than late November, a measure with immediate index effect from 1 November could in principle register in the November 2026 reference month collected in mid-November and published 16 December. That makes the fiscal channel live rather than mechanically excluded. But the commentary around the Budget runs the other way: think tanks expect Healey to need tens of billions in tax rises to meet the fiscal rules, and the government has already spent its consumer-price ammunition on the electricity VAT cut and the April 2026 green levy removals. A Budget that cut a percentage point off CPI within two weeks would be without precedent outside 2008 and 2020.

Nothing else has changed. The anchor remains the ONS print of 2.9% for July 2026, published 19 August, up from 2.6% in June, with core at 2.6% and services at 3.4%. The ONS release page confirms Consumer price inflation, UK: August 2026 is scheduled for 16 September 2026 at 7:00am, so the four-attempt structure I verified yesterday stands: August, September, October and November reference months, with December publishing 20 January 2027 and falling outside. HM Treasury's August 2026 comparison of independent forecasts has Q4 2026 CPI averaging 3.4%. The Bank's July 2026 MPR peaks at about 3.2% in Q4 with risks tilted to the upside, the MPC held at 3.75% on 29 July by 6-3 with three votes for a hike, and the next decision is 17 September. A Reuters poll of 13-18 August had 56 of 64 economists expecting no change for the rest of the year. Worth recording as a counterfactual: the House of Commons Library notes that before the Middle East conflict, UK CPI had been expected to fall to around 2% from April 2026 and stay there. The war is the whole reason this question is a 1% rather than a coin flip.

On strict arithmetic today's news is worth a fraction of a point downward, but the estimate is already at the floor I am willing to state, and I do not use 0. So I hold at 1, with the composition of the residual mass shifted slightly: less of it now sits on "the October cap surprises to the downside" and more on "a Hormuz settlement plus a Budget measure combine before mid-November", a conjunction that is by construction less likely than either alone.

Today it is $26 — twenty-six dollars, a rounding artefact from The Numbers truncating the domestic line to $854,901,000 against Box Office Mojo's $854,901,026. Two independently maintained databases printing the same nine-figure international total and worldwide totals differing by less than the price of a cinema ticket is about as strong a corroboration signal as this question can generate. The international convergence is exact at $1,365,000,000 on both.

Weekend actuals came in above the Sunday estimates I was working from yesterday, which is the expected direction but worth recording because it was not guaranteed. Variety reports Brand New Day won its fourth consecutive weekend with $39 million, against the roughly $36.5M I logged from Sunday trade estimates, taking the domestic cume to $855 million and making it only the fourth film ever to cross that domestic mark. Insidious: Out of the Further opened second with $25.3M domestic and $35M overseas for a $60M global debut, which is a respectable launch but nowhere near enough to dislodge the incumbent. Both aggregators have now converted Sunday estimates to actuals and agree with the trade reporting.

I also searched specifically for any correction, re-audit or restatement notice from Box Office Mojo, The Numbers, Comscore or Sony covering this title and found none. That is a null result rather than proof of absence, but combined with the upward movement and the convergence it removes the only piece of genuinely adverse evidence that existed in yesterday's file.

There is no precedent for anything remotely like that. I hold central at 100. I retain the lower CI bound at 99 rather than returning it to 100, not because of anything in today's data, which is uniformly favourable, but because the residual risk in this question was never about box office and is not reducible by better box office numbers: it is resolver mechanics, question administration, and the small but non-zero chance that the retrieval fragility documented on 19, 22 and 23 August produces a misread at resolution time. Yesterday's scare was a useful reminder that the instrument can lie even when the underlying fact is stable, and I would rather keep that floor than let four consecutive days of confirmation talk me into treating a published figure as a law of nature.

Net effect of the correction is small and negative, worth perhaps a few tenths of a point, and I am absorbing it rather than moving the central estimate.

Friar told investors on 14 August that overall run rate was up 35% quarter to date and enterprise up 50% QTD. question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
key_change:
Move: 33 to 36. Yesterday I wrote that I was stopping the drift and would not move again absent the 30 September quarterly national accounts or the 28 October EFO. I am overriding that, and I want to be explicit about why rather than quietly abandoning the constraint. Two things happened. First, a named think-tank publication landed squarely inside the 23-24 August window that directly attacks the evidentiary basis I used to justify the downward drift. Second, in following it up I found a straightforward error in my own reading of the Bank of England's potential-supply anchor, which I have been carrying as a bear factor for days. One is new evidence; one is self-correction. Both point the same way.

The new item: the Resolution Foundation published a productivity report on Monday 24 August 2026, reported by David Milliken for Reuters (filed London, Aug 24) and covered by the Guardian. Its headline estimate is that annual growth in output per hour has risen to an average of 1.1 per cent over the two years to end-June 2026, against an annual decline of 0.7 per cent in the two preceding years and an average rise of 0.7 per cent in the late 2010s. Simon Pittaway, the Resolution Foundation economist on the report, put it directly: "While official figures suggest that the output of workers has worsened further in the mid-2020s, our more accurate productivity measure suggests that it has been improving in recent years." The method is to replace the Labour Force Survey denominator with a cross-section of administrative employment data. Crucially for my purposes, the report does the sectoral decomposition: the recovery is broad-based across 12 of 19 major sectors, and most of the increase comes from workers becoming more productive within sectors rather than from jobs shifting away from low-productivity industries. Pittaway again: "The UK's productivity recovery has been achieved by the same workers, doing the same jobs, and working in the same sectors." That rules out the leading deflationary explanation, which was that minimum-wage-driven shrinkage in hospitality and retail was flattering the aggregate through composition.

This matters because on 23 August I leaned heavily on the ONS Productivity flash of 18 August 2026, where RTI-based output per hour rose just 0.7 per cent in the year to Q2 2026, and I assigned it a minus 7pp weight as the single largest bear factor. The Resolution Foundation's argument is precisely that the official series is the unreliable one. It is independently corroborated. CEP Occasional Paper No. 74, "UK national productivity trends: getting the data right" (Barbas, Valero and Van Reenen, LSE, July 2026), constructs output per worker with a common GVA numerator and four different labour-input measures, and finds the LFS-based measure rose only 0.3 per cent between 2024 Q3 and 2026 Q1 against 2.4 per cent on their preferred RTI-employees-plus-HMRC-self-employment baseline, roughly 1.6 per cent annualised against under 0.3 per cent a year over the preceding decade. Morgan Stanley's chief UK economist Bruna Skarica now has private-sector productivity growth at 1.8 per cent a year, up from 1.2 per cent previously, close to the pre-crisis pace. And the ONS itself has partly conceded the measurement point: in June 2026 it stopped recommending the LFS-based measure and moved to tax data.

The self-correction is arguably the bigger deal. I have been citing "Bank of England staff put current potential supply growth at 0.3 to 0.4 per cent" as evidence that every official anchor sits at or below the 1.5 per cent bar. Reading the July 2026 Monetary Policy Report text directly: "Underlying GDP is estimated to have grown by 0.1% in 2026 Q2... That is below Bank staff's estimate of potential supply growth of around 0.3%-0.4%, consistent with a widening margin of slack." It is compared against a quarterly GDP growth rate, alongside Q1 headline growth of 0.6 per cent. The Bank's 0.3-0.4 per cent is therefore a quarterly rate, which annualises to roughly 1.2-1.6 per cent. Correctly read, the Bank's own current potential-supply estimate straddles the threshold rather than sitting far beneath it. That was a real error and it was pushing my number down.

I am deliberately not moving further than three points, for four reasons. First, this is not a bolt from the blue: the Resolution Foundation has been running this argument since its New Year Outlook 2026 in January, and today's report is an extension with nine more months of data rather than a new discovery. Second, the mechanism is partly a denominator story, and a denominator correction raises measured productivity without raising measured GDP, which is what this question resolves on. It is still genuinely bullish, because it re-attributes recent growth away from labour input, which demographics will exhaust by the 2030s, toward productivity, which is the more persistent component and the only one that can carry a 2030s decade. But it is one step removed from the resolution variable. Third, the Bank of England's own 6 August 2026 analysis puts a number on the AI channel that is sobering: software and IT consulting firms raised their contribution to annual productivity growth tenfold versus the pre-Covid decade, and that contribution is still only 0.1 percentage point across 2023-2025, while online ads for customer service roles have fallen an average 23 per cent a year since 2023. Real, narrow, and small so far. Fourth, Robert Wood, chief UK economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, told Reuters in the same 24 August piece that few British businesses report AI having reduced staffing needs outside a few roles such as junior software developers, which he says raises questions about whether the gains will last. Two years is a short window on which to call a regime change that has to hold for a decade starting four years from now.

Mechanically: I move my central estimate of the 2030-2039 decade mean from roughly 1.2-1.3 per cent to roughly 1.30-1.35 per cent, holding the standard deviation near 0.5 percentage points. Under a normal approximation that gives 34 to 38 per cent. Thirty-six.

On the fiscal side nothing improved and I have tightened the detail. Andy Burnham became Prime Minister on 20 July 2026 and appointed John Healey as Chancellor in place of Rachel Reeves; gilts sold off on Burnham's first day on "fiscal flexibility" remarks, with 10-year yields at 5.04 per cent and 30-year at 5.75 per cent, a G7 high. Debt interest is running near 109 billion pounds in 2026-27, about 9 per cent of government revenue. Healey's first Budget and the accompanying OBR Economic and Fiscal Outlook are on 28 October 2026, and the expectation of a further trim to the trend productivity assumption is unchanged. That remains the single largest scheduled event risk in either direction.

Kalshi's KXOAIAGI series now displays 'Before 2030' at 36 per cent, marked down 7.2 on the day from yesterday's 43.2, with 'Before 2028' at 18 per cent (down 3 from 21) and 'Before 2027' at 6 per cent (up 1 from 5). Taken at face value that is a seven-point fall in the single most relevant liquid market and would justify two points off my central. It is not what happened. Series volume today reads $894,366 against $894,281 yesterday - roughly eighty-five dollars of turnover in twenty-four hours on a market that has done nearly nine hundred thousand dollars lifetime. And the quoted spread tells the same story from the other side: Yes 43.4c / No 64c today implies a bid of 36c and an ask of 43.4c, against yesterday's Yes 43c / No 62.7c implying a bid of 37.3c and an ask of 43c. The ask actually rose four tenths of a cent. What moved is the bid, by 1.3c, and the displayed 'chance' appears to have flipped from tracking the upper end of a very wide spread to tracking the lower end. A 7.4-cent bid-ask on a 2030-dated contract is enormous, and the midpoint - about 39.7 per cent - is essentially unchanged from yesterday's midpoint. I therefore take -1pp for genuine bid-side softening across two rungs rather than the -2pp the headline implies, and I flag that anyone reading the Kalshi tape today without opening the order book will draw a much more dramatic conclusion than the data support.

Against that, the Polymarket Astra ladder firmed. Yesterday's rungs were 39 per cent for 15 September, 76 per cent for 30 September and 89 per cent for 31 October. Today they read 41.5 per cent, 79 per cent and 89 per cent, with 31 August still deep in the low teens or below. That is a two-to-three point recovery on the near rungs, unwinding a good part of the slippage I scored at -0.5pp yesterday. It does not tell me OpenAI is closer to a declaration; it tells me traders have marginally reduced their estimate of how long the 7 August cybersecurity hold persists. Still, the Astra ladder is my cleanest available proxy for near-term frontier delivery at the lab most likely to declare, and it moved the right way. +0.5pp.

The genuinely substantive capability item on my tape is one I had not previously counted, and having gone back to the primary source I am giving it weight even though it is five days old. Anthropic published on 20 August a study in which Claude autonomously ran a de novo protein binder design campaign, with the designs manufactured and wet-lab tested by two independent third parties. Adaptyv Bio built all 1,320 designs in a cell-free system; Twist Bioscience independently evaluated 1,260 of them as antibody fusions in human cells in under three weeks. Claude produced working binders against 14 of 15 targets, with per-design success rates of 22 to 35 per cent depending on setup against an industry baseline Anthropic puts at 10 to 15 per cent, high-affinity binders against at least six targets, and binders matching or exceeding the best reported affinity against at least four. Against RBX1 the Mythos preview hit 40 per cent where human entrants in an Adaptyv competition managed 3.7 per cent, and Claude's top design beat the winning human entry. Forbes wrote it up on 23 August. This is the strongest third-party wet-lab-validated evidence I have seen of a model doing autonomous scientific work end to end, and autonomous science is one of the two mechanisms - the other being AI accelerating AI research, where Prime Intellect's NanoGPT Speedrun Frontier landed yesterday - that could plausibly underwrite a defensible AGI declaration inside forty months. +1pp.

But here is the disciplining observation, and it is why I am not moving up. That result has been public since 20 August. The Goodheart Labs combined forecast, which I pulled fresh this morning and which is explicitly timestamped 'as of August 25, 2026', still reads a median of 2031 with an 80 per cent band of 2027 to 2043 - identical to yesterday and to a fortnight ago. Metaculus Q5121 still carries a January 2033 median with roughly 25 per cent by 2029. Kalshi has fallen, not risen, over the same window. A genuinely timeline-compressing result should show up in at least one of these. That it has not is evidence that the aggregate treats narrow-domain autonomous science, however impressive, as orthogonal to the general-capability threshold this question asks about. I am not going to be the only forecaster repricing on it.

One modest negative I did add. The Google situation is now clearly documented rather than inferred: Google has not shipped a frontier model since early 2026, Gemini 4 only began pre-training on 21 July 2026 with no announced release date, Koray Kavukcuoglu took over on roughly 5-6 August with Hassabis moving to chairman and Alphabet Chief Scientist, and Inc. counted eight prominent researchers departing in two months. One of the three institutions with the standing to make a credible AGI declaration is materially behind and mid-reorganisation. That thins the field of potential declarers through 2027 at least. -0.75pp.

What I checked and found nothing on. ARC Prize has issued no ruling on NVIDIA's AVO claim and no statement at all; the Verified Leaderboard is unchanged and NVIDIA's own framing now explicitly cautions that the 100.00 RHAE public-set figure and ARC's ~30 per cent for Opus 5 'should not be interpreted as a direct measurement' because they used different agent systems and evaluation setups - which is close to conceding the point I made yesterday. No news on OpenAI's Preparedness Framework rewrite since Axios on 18 August. No Anthropic public S-1; the June 1 confidential draft still stands with an October Nasdaq target, and CNBC's 21 August reporting on expected risk factors mentions AI backlash, model misuse, regulatory uncertainty and compute constraints, with nothing on AGI framing either way. The AGI Global Summit running in Portland is an academic cross-disciplinary event producing a report 6-8 months out; it involves economists, philosophers and lawyers, not frontier lab research staff, and cannot plausibly generate a resolving statement. Nvidia infrastructure news continued to compound - Groq 3 LPX in full production on 24 August, the Cloverleaf partnership on 21 August, the $105bn Ohio financing for OpenAI capacity phasing in from 2028 - but these are multi-year-lag inputs and I score them at most +0.5pp.

Net: ups of about +2.0, downs of about -2.25. That rounds to zero. Holding 29, band unchanged at 17-45.

question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
key_change:
Move: 11 to 11. Third consecutive hold, and this one is the emptiest of the three in terms of genuinely new information. None of yesterday's nine update triggers fired. I checked each in turn. FTI's Q3 print is not due until late October, so the trigger on a second consecutive quarter of Economic Consulting headcount decline cannot fire yet. The Challenger August report and the BLS August employment situation both land on or around 4 September, so neither the AI-cuts-spreading-outside-Technology trigger nor the CES6054160001 three-month-decline trigger has anything new to test against; the most recent Challenger release remains the July report published 6 August, whose headline the firm itself titles 'Layoffs Fall, Hiring Picks Up; AI Leads For Fifth Straight Month.' No listed comparator in the narrow niche — CRA, Huron, Cornerstone, NERA, Compass Lexecon, Brattle, Analysis Group — has disclosed anything since CRA's 7 August call. No new quantified estimate of AI-caused consultancy decline exceeding 15% from a 2024 base has appeared from Source Global Research, IBISWorld, the FT or the ONS. Searches on consultancy.uk and consulting.us surfaced nothing dated 23, 24 or 25 August 2026 beyond routine transaction and appointment items — AlixPartners acquiring Artium (an agentic-AI software consultancy in Los Angeles), Andersen Group agreeing to acquire UK Andersen LLP and SPR Consulting, and Milliman naming Jim Fulton chief executive from October 2026. Note the direction of the AlixPartners deal: a consultancy buying AI capability to sell, which is the demand-amplifier reading, not the substitution reading.

Four items are new to my log, and they roughly cancel.

First, and the most substantive: the BLS Monthly Labor Review's 2024–34 industry and occupational employment projections article, published in 2026, projects 9.4% employment growth for Management, Scientific and Technical Consulting Services over 2024–34, with IT consulting demand explicitly named as a driver because firms need help implementing AI tools. I should have had this earlier and did not. It matters because it is the official US statistical agency, forecasting the exact NAICS 5416 aggregate that a broad-reading resolver would use, over a decade that fully contains the resolution window, and it projects growth of roughly plus 0.9% a year against the minus 9.0% a year the question requires. It is not a market-research house with a commercial interest in a growing market, which is the objection available against IBISWorld and Mordor. Weight: minus 0.4pp.

Second, cutting the other way: S&P Global's 'The AI and labor landscape 2026' special report, based on its PMI special survey, has revised its net employment assessment. A prior vintage found a neutral-to-slightly-positive net employment impact from AI adoption; the 2026 report finds a negative global net impact over the past twelve months at minus 5 points and a marginal further decline forecast for 2026 at minus 2 points. Larger firms increasingly anticipate net negative impacts, and the report flags rapid maturation of investment in AI agents as an accelerant. That is a credible forecaster moving in the direction the question needs. But the roles it names as shrinking are administration and office support, translation, manufacturing, production and customer service — the same clerical-and-routine cluster that has dominated every displacement dataset I have looked at — and consulting is not among them. Direction up, sector composition down. Weight: plus 0.3pp.

Third, an extension of the value-repricing thread I logged yesterday off the Forbes piece. A Financial-News item puts Accenture at more than 57% of market value lost over twelve months and Capgemini at nearly 40%, while noting in the same breath that most firms are still posting decent sales growth. That is a much larger drawdown than the single-session minus 18% on 18 June 2026 I had recorded. I am weighting it lightly for two reasons. The question's resolution criteria specify 'revenue or employment,' not market capitalisation, so a resolver almost certainly cannot use equity value even though the question stem says 'value.' And the same source explicitly separates the price move from the revenue trajectory, which is the Jemma Green point restated. Weight: plus 0.3pp.

Fourth, a capability datapoint rather than a market one: xAI's Grok Bot, introduced 11 August 2026, described as an agent that uses computers and software tools, works across applications, learns workflows and completes tasks end to end. Agentic computer use that owns a workflow rather than assisting a task is the specific capability shape that would make client-side insourcing of economic analysis cheap. This is exactly the 2029-30 tail risk I said I could not bound with any reference class, and it is now slightly less hypothetical. But it is a fortnight-old product announcement with no deployment evidence in professional services, and I have watched several such announcements pass through this series without moving any consulting metric. Weight: plus 0.3pp.

One hygiene note, and it is the same failure mode I flagged on 24 August with the phantom PwC story. Today's searches returned a cluster of confident-sounding claims that McKinsey is cutting 3,000 to 4,000 roles, roughly 10% of headcount, explicitly because AI substitutes for junior analyst work. If true that would be a material up-move. It is not new and it is not well sourced. The claim appears only on SEO content farms — metaintro, finalroundai, outsourceaccelerator — and traces back to the November 2025 reduction of roughly 200 technology and support staff plus Bob Sternfels's comment that more non-client-role reductions would follow over two years, with the larger number appearing to be extrapolation dressed as reporting. No FT, WSJ, Bloomberg or Reuters version exists in the results. I am not logging it. Two further items in the same category: the Accenture '11,000' and '22,000' cut figures belong to the $865m restructuring announced in Q4 FY2025 (September 2025) and are already in my prior; and KPMG's roughly 10% cut to US audit partners, about 100 partners, is dated 23 April 2026 and concerns audit, not consulting, though Thomas Mackenzie's line that within two to three years there will be 'next to no human beings' performing routine audit testing is a genuinely striking piece of insider testimony about the adjacent profession.

Netting: plus 0.9pp of new up-weight against minus 0.4pp of down-weight, on items I would classify as weak evidence individually and mutually offsetting collectively. That is well inside the rounding band and I hold at 11. Band stays 6 to 19: the BLS projection argues faintly for trimming the top, the S&P Global revision and the Grok Bot launch argue faintly for keeping it, and I am not going to churn the interval on a day this thin. The next genuinely informative dates are unchanged: 4 September for Challenger August and the BLS August employment situation, and late October for FTI's Q3 and CRA's Q3 prints.

question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
key_change:

BritPolls' complete 2026 archive, refetched this morning, still lists twenty polls with the most recent GB fieldwork ending 19 August: Find Out Now, Lab 23.0, Ref 23.0, Con 18.0, Grn 14.0, LD 11.0, n=2,287.
