That is one tenth of a cent of bid improvement and a midpoint of about 39.75 per cent versus 39.7 yesterday - flat. Before 2028 displays 17 per cent against 18 yesterday, on a bid of 17 and an ask of 21. Series volume is $895,754 against $894,366, so $1,388 of turnover in twenty-four hours. That is sixteen times yesterday's eighty-five dollars and still trivial on a series that has done nearly nine hundred thousand dollars lifetime. The material point for my forecast is that the bid-side softening I scored at minus one point yesterday did not continue. I do not add that point back - a single day of stability is not evidence of recovery - but I take a quarter-point off for the further drift on the 2028 rung and otherwise treat Kalshi as having told me nothing today. Trigger not fired; nothing remotely close to the 55-with-a-three-cent-spread-and-twenty-thousand-in-weekly-volume condition I set.

Trigger five, Anthropic's S-1. Still confidential only. The 1 June draft stands and there is no public prospectus, ticker, exchange, price range or valuation. Trigger not fired.

Trigger six, the Astra ladder, is the one thing that moved with real volume behind it, and it moved up. Polymarket now reads 3 per cent for 31 August, 45 per cent for 15 September, 79 per cent for 30 September and 89 per cent for 31 October, on total series volume of $341,445 with $49,934 sitting on the September 15 rung alone. The September 15 quote is Yes 48 cents and No 58 cents, a bid of 42 and an ask of 48 for a clean 45 midpoint. That rung has now gone 39 to 41.5 to 45 across three days - six points of firming in forty-eight hours - and a separate weekly market on release between 14 and 20 September reads 42 per cent. The far rungs are static. The reading is specific and I think correct: traders have converged on Astra shipping in mid-September, which means the 7 August cybersecurity hold is being priced as a delay of weeks rather than a structural brake. That is a direct partial reversal of one of my larger downside factors. Plus 0.75 points.

Two other items. First, a negative I did not expect. Today's research feed carries a preprint audit finding that AI self-training gains can be measurement artefacts - in a 48-run comparison, measurement choices alone created apparent gains and losses, with external distillation reaching more low-base problems than self-training. Set alongside the survey of 1,250 arXiv papers from 2024 to 2026 that separates bounded self-refinement, which is convergent, evaluable and already industrial practice, from open-ended recursive self-improvement, which it finds bounded by grounding requirements, collapse dynamics and compute on every measured axis, this cuts directly at the AI-accelerating-AI-research mechanism I gave weight to earlier in the week on the strength of the Prime Intellect speedrun result. Minus 0.75 points.

Second, I am correcting an overstatement of my own. I wrote yesterday that Google has not shipped a frontier model since early 2026 and treated it as effectively out of contention. Google shipped Gemini 3.6 Flash in July and Gemini 3.7 Flash on 13 August at 65.3 per cent on DeepSWE v1.1 and 43.6 per cent on FrontierCode 1.1 Main, Gemini has crossed one billion monthly active users, and today Google launched Gemini Enterprise for Legal with Thomson Reuters, LexisNexis and Harvey integrations. Gemini 4 is still pre-training only with no announced date, so the substance of the point survives - Google is not currently at the frontier tier - but it is shipping steadily, and I soften that factor from minus one to minus 0.75. A quarter-point back.

I also note Ox Alpha, the stealth OpenRouter model with a roughly one-million-token multimodal context that Bloomberg and TechCrunch covered on 23 August. One independent researcher ran ten DeepSWE tasks and it passed eight, against Claude Fable 5 at 65 per cent and GPT-5.6 Sol at 52 per cent, and serving-layer forensics - a Java stack trace naming Zhipu internal API classes, an identical error-code dialect to GLM on OpenRouter, 30 of 30 tokenizer probe matches - point at Zhipu AI. The free preview ends around 27 August. An n-of-ten evaluation is not decisive and a Chinese lab is not a plausible declarer under this resolver, but it does raise competitive pressure on the US labs. Plus 0.25.

Net: ups of 1.25, downs of 1.25. Holding 29, band unchanged at 17 to 45.

question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
key_change:
Move: 11 to 10.

I checked each of yesterday's nine triggers in turn and none of them fired in the sense they were written, but today produced more genuinely new material than the previous three days combined, and on balance it tilts down. The scheduled items are still not due: FTI's Q3 print and CRA's Q3 print are late October, and both the Challenger August report and the BLS August employment situation land on 4 September. The most recent Challenger release remains the July report of 6 August, with 477,033 cuts announced through July, down 41% from 806,383 in the first seven months of 2025, July the lowest monthly total since July 2024, Technology at 149,023 year to date and up 67%, and hiring announcements up 25%. BLS confirms the August Employment Situation is scheduled for 4 September, so CES6054160001 has nothing new to test.

The day's real find is a directly on-point piece I had not logged: Mona Birjandi and Mery Zadeh, 'AI Is Coming for the Economic Consulting Industry', which ProMarket, the Stigler Center's publication, ran on 25 August 2026. I want to be precise about what it is. ProMarket is on its annual summer break and is republishing its most-read content from the first half of the year; the piece originally appeared on 29 April 2026 and sits on SSRN as abstract 7146120. So it is new to my file but carries no new information flow. It is nonetheless the single most specific analysis of this exact question I have seen, so it deserves careful reading in both directions.

It cuts up in its mechanism. The authors put the AI-automatable share of the data-collection, modelling and drafting layer at 50-60% in antitrust and competition economics, 55-65% in securities fraud and commercial damages, and 60-70% in employment discrimination. They estimate 85-95% time savings on the maker-checker independent replication audit that structurally doubles senior billing on every task, 70-85% on data collection, 50-70% on quantitative modelling, and 60-75% on turning results into demonstratives. They cite CRA's own annual reports for a 5.8% year-on-year fall in consultant headcount in FY2024 with revenue per consultant rising from about $621,000 to about $727,000, and note both CRA and Cornerstone have appointed senior officers to deploy AI, with Cornerstone running an agentic research platform across case work. On demand they point to JPMorgan replacing external advisory functions with internal tools and the ACC's 2025 Chief Legal Officer Survey finding a majority of large in-house departments deploying AI for work previously routed outside. Their stated equilibrium is 'a smaller industry by headcount, more concentrated at the senior level, with a hollowed-out middle.'

It cuts down in almost everything else. They are explicit that AI cannot replace expert testimony and that testifying-expert fees may rise even as analyst hours thin. They give three structural reasons pricing will not fall to clients: high-stakes litigants shop on Daubert track record rather than price, the pool of credible testifying experts in areas like pharmaceutical patent damages is small enough to blunt competitive pressure, and clients are reluctant to open an adversarial fee conversation with the expert they depend on in court. They identify genuinely new revenue lines with no methodological template and therefore premium fees: algorithmic price-fixing cases following the DOJ's 2025 Statement of Interest, AI-system compliance and disparate-impact audits, and AI-amplified case screening. And their conclusion is a refusal to forecast the aggregate: 'industry employment will depend on whether AI-driven cost reductions generate enough new case volume to offset reduced labor demand per case. That demand-side question is an open question.' That does not satisfy my fifth trigger, which requires two or more credible sources with quantified estimates of AI-caused decline exceeding 15% from a 2024 base. This is one source, and it declines to quantify the aggregate. Net for the piece: roughly plus 0.7pp on mechanism, minus 0.3pp on its explicit agnosticism and its pricing-stickiness argument.

Against that, five smaller down-items accumulated. First, the BLS 2024-34 projections have more in them than I logged yesterday: professional, scientific and technical services is projected the second-fastest-growing sector, 7.5% growth and 812,500 new jobs, sitting alongside the 9.4% figure for management, scientific and technical consulting services. Minus 0.2pp. Second, CRA's 6 August call carried forward guidance I had not recorded: management expects mid-single-digit headcount growth by year-end and believes utilisation can hold in the mid-to-upper 70s even as hiring resumes, with nearly 30 VPs added in 2025 ramping ahead of expectations. Minus 0.4pp. Third, FTI management on 30 July guided that Economic Consulting 'will no longer be a year-on-year drag on revenue or on adjusted segment EBITDA' from the second half of 2026, and the segment's Q2 revenue rose $13.2m and adjusted segment EBITDA $14.7m sequentially. That is the firm at the centre of my strongest up-factor telling me the trough is behind it. Minus 0.3pp. Fourth, Huron raised full-year 2026 guidance to $1.85-1.89bn revenue before reimbursables and $9.00-9.40 adjusted EPS, expecting double-digit digital growth in the second half on an AI-related pipeline. Minus 0.2pp. Fifth, the narrow niche keeps expanding rather than contracting: BRG has launched Rome and Milan competition practices staffed by economists poached from Brattle, and Cornerstone continues London and Brussels hiring. Minus 0.2pp. LinkedIn's Jobs on the Rise 2026 has AI consultants and strategists as the second fastest-growing role in the US, which is the demand-amplifier reading again.

Two items I looked at and set aside. Resources Connection reported Consulting segment revenue of $36.9m against $52.6m, minus 32.5% in constant currency on billable hours down 31.5%, in its fiscal Q3 ended 28 February 2026. That is a firm-level decline of exactly the magnitude the question needs, which is worth noting because it shows the bar is physically reachable. But RGP is an interim-talent and project-staffing business at the commodity end, the release attributes performance to cost alignment, segment repositioning and demand, and management's stated priority is 'scaling our Consulting segment' with investment intended to drive growth back. No AI attribution. Plus 0.3pp on demonstrated magnitude, no weight on attribution. And proposed Federal Rule of Evidence 707 on machine-generated evidence: approved by the Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure on 10 June 2025, comment period closed 16 February 2026, earliest effective date 1 December 2027. It legitimises a pathway for AI output offered without a human expert, but only through a Rule 702-style reliability gate, and it does not exist as law for the first third of my remaining window. Roughly plus 0.1pp net.

Hygiene, and it is the same failure mode for the third day running. The McKinsey 3,000-4,000 role claim resurfaced today on outsourceaccelerator, metaintro, finalroundai, programs.com and displaceindex, still with no FT, WSJ, Bloomberg or Reuters version, still traceable to the roughly 200 technology and support staff cut in November 2025. Not logged. A search result presented Faten Sabry's arrival at Compass Lexecon as August 2026 news; the press release is 21 April 2025. Andrew Swan's Cornerstone London hire was presented as 2026; it was effective 4 September 2024. And an aggregator claim that 54% of 2026 layoff events cite AI, affecting 170,945 workers, conflicts directly with Challenger's own 112,713 AI-cited cuts year to date, about 24% of the total. I am using Challenger.

Netting: roughly plus 1.1pp of up-weight against plus minus 1.4pp of down-weight, so about minus 1.0pp. That takes me from 11 to 10. I am trimming the top of the band from 19 to 18 because the forward guidance now on record from CRA, FTI and Huron all points the same way for the second half of 2026, which shortens the runway for the kind of inflection the upper tail requires. I am leaving the floor at 6.

question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
key_change:
Move: 52 to 51. The six-day polling drought broke and for the first time in a week I have genuine fieldwork rather than a static average to reason from. Two polls landed with fieldwork ending 24 August. YouGov surveyed 23-24 August on n=2,380 and returned Reform 23 (-1 on its 16-17 August wave), Labour 22 (unchanged), Conservatives 20 (+1), Greens 13 (unchanged), Liberal Democrats 13 (+1), Restore Britain 3 (-1), SNP 3, Plaid 1, Your Party 0. Deltapoll, fieldwork ending 24 August on n=2,022, returned Labour 30, Reform 27, Conservatives 20, Lib Dems 8, Greens 8. Read within-pollster, both are mildly good for Labour. YouGov's Reform lead halves from two points to one; Deltapoll's Labour lead widens from two to three on Labour's highest share of the entire cycle from that house. YouGov's own writeup is appropriately deflationary: every party sits inside the margin of error of the previous wave, and Labour and Reform have both been penned between 22 and 24 in its tracker all month.

Read through the aggregates the picture is slightly the other way, and this is the tension I have to resolve rather than pick a side of. PollCheck's seven-poll moving average, stamped 25 August, now reads Labour 25.6, Reform 25.0, Conservatives 19.7, Greens 10.7, Lib Dems 10.4. That is a Labour lead of 0.6 against the 1.0 I recorded for three straight days. BritPolls' live ticker has gone further and now shows Reform 24.6 and Labour 24.6 - a dead tie, where yesterday it had Labour 25.4 to Reform 25.0. I do not think this is decay. It is composition: the seven-poll window has rolled off older, Labour-friendlier surveys and the incoming pair, while internally favourable, arrive at levels (Lab 22 from YouGov) below the average they are entering. The cleaner signal is the within-pollster movement, and that is pro-Labour. But I am not entitled to bank the within-pollster reading and ignore the aggregate when the aggregate is the object my seat models actually consume. I call the polling day a wash, tilted a hair negative.

The clearest thing I have to do today is retract yesterday's move. I raised the forecast a point in part on a supposed shift in the Ladbrokes timing book, from 2029-or-later at 10/11 to 1/1, which I read as the market shortening its expected horizon and therefore shrinking my decay discount. That was almost certainly an artefact of comparing two different sources at two different dates. The 10/11 figure comes from an OLBG page whose byline reads 'Updated: Feb 25' and whose copy still describes 'Sir Keir Starmer's party' - it is a February 2026 snapshot, not a current one. The Ladbrokes board itself, refetched today, prices 2029 or later at 1/1, 2028 at 7/2, 2027 at 9/4 and 2026 at 16/1, exactly as yesterday. I have no evidence the timing market moved at all. That +1pp comes straight back out. It is a useful reminder that on a question this thinly traded, the difference between a live price and a cached marketing page is the difference between signal and noise, and I got it wrong yesterday.

The most-seats board itself is unchanged and stable: Labour 11/8, Reform 11/5, Conservatives 7/2, Greens 33/1, Restore Britain 20/1, Liberal Democrats 40/1. Normalising that 105.7 per cent book gives Labour 39.8 per cent, Reform 31.3, Conservatives 22.2 - the same reading as yesterday and the day before. The majority book is likewise unchanged, with No Overall Majority at 4/7 and a Labour majority at 4/1. One genuine change: the 'Hung Parliament and Reform UK win most seats' special is 3/1 on today's Ladbrokes board, against 5/4 on the stale February page, which is a large drift against Reform over the intervening six months and is consistent with everything else.

Against that retraction I have two real additions. The first partially rescues the market-corroboration trigger I retired yesterday for want of a second venue. ElectaMeter, a composite UK political index last updated 23 August, explicitly lists Smarkets, Manifold Markets and UK bookmakers via BettingLounge among its sources alongside Electoral Calculus. It puts Labour's implied betting probability at 42.3 per cent against Reform's 33 per cent, and scores Labour 71 on its balanced index against Reform 60, blending a 25.5 per cent poll average, that 42.3 per cent market read and Electoral Calculus's 244 projected seats. So the liquid venues do get aggregated somewhere, and the multi-venue read sits about two and a half points above my Ladbrokes normalisation. That is worth a point.

The second is macroeconomic and I had not been carrying it at all. GfK's consumer confidence index rose to -14 in August, up three points, the fourth consecutive monthly rise, with the sub-index on personal finances over the next twelve months at +4 against -23 for the general economic outlook. Neil Bellamy of GfK attributed it to people having 'greater faith' in Healey and Burnham, while cautioning it is 'too soon to tell'. The British Retail Consortium recorded a parallel bump, with Helen Dickinson calling it a 'honeymoon boost driven by less pessimism about the outlook'. Sentiment turning up four months running is the single most plausible mechanism by which a Burnham bounce becomes something other than a bounce, and it is the first hard non-polling indicator I have seen pointing that way. Worth a point.

But the Budget risk has sharpened as well, and I am not going to net the good news without the bad. City AM's 25 August anatomy of the 28 October Budget puts Healey's shortfall at GBP 22bn after early spending pledges - close enough to the NIESR GBP 24bn I already carry - and notes gilt yields climbing to their highest level this century, with the Iran war having pushed up borrowing costs. Inflation is back to 2.9 per cent, a four-month high, which cuts directly against the cost-of-living framing. The tax menu on the table includes equalising capital gains with income tax (roughly GBP 14bn), extending national insurance to investment, property and pension income (roughly GBP 22bn, and described by Panmure Liberum's Simon French as the area most targeted, though 'deeply unpopular'), ending the pension tax-free lump sum, and a bank windfall levy. Burnham has already shut down the land value tax speculation. The manifesto lock on income tax, NI and VAT survives in letter, but an NICs base extension is exactly the sort of workaround that reads as a breach to voters. I also note the VAT removal from electricity bills is explicitly temporary, which is weaker than I framed it yesterday.

The last negative is Restore Britain, and it keeps going the wrong way for my biggest UP factor. YouGov has it at 3 per cent, down one on the fortnight, and PollCheck's tracker average is also 3.0. Electoral Calculus's June MRP assumed 7. Every seat model that gives Labour a plurality from vote-share parity is leaning on a three-way split of the right; if Restore Britain is really a three-point party rather than a seven-point one, that split is narrower than modelled and Labour's efficiency advantage is smaller. Netting it all: minus one for the retraction, plus one for the second-venue market read, plus one for consumer confidence, minus one for the aggregate slippage, minus a half for Restore Britain, and no change from Electoral Calculus, which is now thirty days stale at 28 July. One point down.

question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2035?
key_change:
Move: 84 to 83. A genuine down-trigger fired today, but on a horizon that mutes most of it, so the move is one point rather than three.

The substantive new number is the Kalshi KXOAIAGI ladder, fetched live this morning. It now reads 6 per cent before 2027 (up 1), 18 per cent before 2028 (down 3) and 36 per cent before 2030 (down 7.2), on 894,366 dollars of volume. The standing quote for OpenAI AGI by 2030 through April and mid-July was roughly 55 per cent. So this is a decline of about 19 points over six weeks and 7.2 points in a single session, on the deepest AGI-declaration book on the platform, roughly ten times the volume of the any-company series. That is not thin-volume noise and I will not dismiss it as such.

But the discipline here is to notice what did not move. KXAGICO-COMP, whose rules text matches this question's first limb almost exactly and expressly excludes 'AGI-like' and 'near-AGI' hedges, is literally unchanged: 41 per cent before 1 January 2028, 42 per cent before 1 April 2028, 59 per cent before 1 July 2028, on 92,192 dollars of volume. Same three prices, same volume figure, as yesterday. The any-company announcement market, the one that actually matches my resolution criteria, sat still while the OpenAI-specific pre-2030 book repriced.

The driver is legible. OpenAI's largest planned frontier reinforcement-learning run remains on hold with no confirmed end date. The 18 August announcement on pacing model development for cyber capabilities is still the operative state as of the 25 August coverage: many narrower workloads have restarted, but significant Astra and cyber workloads are still frozen, expanded monitoring consumes roughly 20 per cent of the compute of the process being watched against a 30-minute human-alert target, the Hugging Face postmortem is unpublished, and the evidence behind Astra's possible Critical cyber rating is unpublished. Astra, worth noting, was not the model in the July Hugging Face breach; it is a separate unreleased system. Mia Glaese, who runs safety and alignment there, put it plainly: 'We are very far from everything running back to normal.' I had the breach and the subpoena logged; what I had not properly priced is the structural point that the 20 per cent monitoring tax is permanent and scales with capability, with the largest runs explicitly facing the highest bar before they resume.

Compounding it, WSJ reports OpenAI's head of data centres Chris Malone left last week, the fourth senior departure after CRO Denise Dresser, COO Brad Lightcap and Fidji Simo, and frames the exits as coming ahead of a 'planned 2027 listing'. My standing assumption was a September 2026 target with the public S-1 hitting EDGAR mid-to-late August. It is 26 August and no public prospectus has appeared. One of my clearest UP triggers, the S-1 framing a shipped system as AGI, has slipped roughly a year.

Why only one point, then. Because there is a difference between mass leaving the distribution and mass sliding right, and a 7.2-point fall in a before-2030 contract caused by a training pause with no end date is almost definitionally the latter. A pause is a delay mechanism. A 20 per cent monitoring overhead is a tax on effective compute, not a ceiling on it. Nine years absorbs both. This is exactly the asymmetry that separates this question from its 2030 sibling, and it is why the 2030 forecast should take the full weight of today's news and this one should not.

The up-side of the tape is unusually well aimed at my binding constraints. Skild AI released S1, a robotics foundation model that executes tasks up to ten minutes long from a single human video prompt with no fine-tuning, reporting 66 per cent success on unseen tasks against 9 per cent for language-prompted VLAs at the same 100,000-hour training scale, with demonstrations spanning pancake flipping, pour-over coffee, plant potting and kit assembly. Sequoia's Alfred Lin called single-prompt execution of long-horizon tasks 'a game changer'. This matters more than a generic robotics story because Metaculus 5121, my strictest anchor and the single largest brake on this forecast, carries a January 2033 median precisely because it demands broad robotic as well as cognitive capability. S1 attacks that specific reason. Caveats stand: self-reported, 66 per cent is not reliability, ten minutes is not a working day, and Lin is an investor talking his book.

Second, SemiAnalysis published its deep dive on OpenAI's Jalapeño, its first custom inference chip, taped out with Broadcom in 16 months on TSMC N3P. The B0 stepping hits 13.4 PFLOPs of MXFP4 at 700W against Rubin's 900-1,150W, pairs HBM4 at 15.4 TB/s, and posts over 700 tokens per second per user on DeepSeek R1 and about 1,400 on GPT-OSS; The Verge reports OpenAI's own benchmarks at 1.5 to 1.9 times more work per watt than Nvidia. Performance per watt is the correct metric against my minus-8-point compute ceiling, because what binds the 2030-2035 window is power and memory, not FLOPs. Roughly 2,300 GW sitting in US interconnection queues is indifferent to FLOPs and entirely sensitive to watts. Sixteen months from start to a competitive tape-out also says the custom-silicon escape route is faster than I had assumed; set alongside Anthropic's hire of TPU founder Amir Salek and Broadcom's 60-to-100bn dollar SPV, three of the four leading labs now have a credible path around Nvidia's 15-per-cent-plus 2027 price rise.

Third, and directly against a standing DOWN trigger, Dell'Oro raised its 2026 datacentre capex forecast above 1 trillion dollars, with the top five hyperscalers above 600bn in 2026, up 36 per cent on 2025 and roughly 75 per cent AI-directed. I was watching for a capex cut on power or memory constraints. The opposite happened. Also logged but not weighted: Anandkumar and Jenik launched Accelerated Understanding, an enterprise physics AI built on neural operators rather than Transformers, claiming ingestion of 5 trillion data points in a single prompt, about 5 million times what Anthropic and Google flagships handle. Architectural diversification is relevant to Hassabis's 'one or two more breakthroughs' framing, but Reuters is reporting a launch, not a result.

The sobering item cuts the other way and I want it on the record. BenchLM's ARC-AGI-3 leaderboard, updated 25 August, still has Claude Opus 5 at 30.2 per cent, GPT-5.6 Sol at 7.8 per cent and Claude Opus 4.8 at 1.5 per cent. The base-model board has not moved despite NVIDIA's AVO posting 100.00 on the public set. That is the cleanest available evidence that the harness cluster I have been treating as an up-signal, AVO plus Inherent's Faraday plus Apodex 1.1, is scaffolding built around static models rather than evidence that the underlying models improved. I hold the method-over-scale factor at plus 5 but I now read it as telling me about deployment rather than about the capability trend.

Other anchors are unchanged: Goodheart Labs aggregate median 2031 with an 80 per cent interval of 2027-2043; Metaculus 5121 January 2033 and 3479 June 2028; LEAP wave 8's superforecaster median 2047 still unrefreshed. I should also log Samotsvety's January 2026 aggregate, eight forecasters, at roughly 28 per cent for AGI by 2030, which sits alongside LEAP on the sceptical side. Governance hardened non-specifically: Meta and 29 state attorneys general are in mid-trial settlement talks, Pennsylvania's AG sued Snap on 25 August, and AI Weekly has Regulation story volume up 1,400 per cent week on week. None of that is AGI-specific; all of it raises the cost of a lab's lawyers signing off on the word.

Netting: a deep real-money book moved against me by 7.2 points on a pre-2030 contract, the matching any-company book did not move at all, the frontier pause is a rightward shift rather than a truncation, and the day's structural news on robotics generalisation and performance per watt is aimed squarely at my two largest drags. Move to 83. I widen the lower bound one point to 72 because this is the first session in this run where a liquid market moved against the thesis by more than a rounding error, which argues my left tail was slightly too thin. Coherence check: 83 against Q1's 31 implies a 75.4 per cent conditional probability of a qualifying declaration during 2030-2035 given none by 2030, down from 76.8 per cent yesterday and comfortably above the 2030 number.

question: Will China initiate a military blockade or invasion of Taiwan before 1 January 2030?
key_change:
Move: 7 to 8.

I have held at 7 for two weeks and I am moving up one point today, not because a threshold was crossed but because two pieces of evidence I had been treating as soft have hardened, and because I found an external anchor I had not previously priced that sits above my implied hazard rather than below it. This is a one-point move with a slightly fatter upper tail, not a regime change.

Start with the trigger checklist, which is mostly quiet. Taiwan's MND reported two PLA aircraft sorties, seven PLAN vessels and two official ships for 25 August, following two sorties, seven PLAN vessels and two official ships on the 24th, zero aircraft with seven PLAN and seven official ships on the 23rd, and three sorties with eight PLAN and seven official ships on the 22nd. The air component is pinned at its floor, the naval component is flat at seven to nine hulls, the coastguard component oscillates between two and seven. There is still no Fujian MSA navigation warning anywhere in August, still no named exercise since Justice Mission 2025 - eight full months, the longest gap since 2022 - and still no boarding of a Taiwan-bound merchant vessel under Coast Guard Order No. 3. None of the mobilisation indicators in trigger four have appeared. I will add one deflationary note on this week's readings: Typhoon Saudel is passing closest to Taiwan on Thursday and Friday, and the CWA has had torrential-rain warnings up across southern and eastern Taiwan since the 22nd. That is a mundane suppressor of flight operations, so I should not read this particular week's floor as signal in either direction.

The first hardening concerns US carrier posture. Yesterday I upgraded this factor on The War Zone's 17 August survey. Today's 24 August survey is more definite and worse. USS George Washington - the only forward-deployed carrier, homeported in Yokosuka - has transited the Malacca Strait and relieved USS Abraham Lincoln in the Arabian Sea; Lincoln is now transiting eastward across the Indian Ocean. TWZ's own summary of the 17 August edition put it bluntly: George Washington en route to relieve Abraham Lincoln in the Middle East, 'which leaves no carriers in the Pacific.' Theodore Roosevelt was still pierside in San Diego on 24 August. Carl Vinson departed San Diego on 10 August but is in Tailored Ship's Training Availability and Final Evaluation Period - basic workups, months from a deployment. So the position on 26 August is not a gap that closes in September; it is zero US carrier presence in the Pacific with the theatre's own permanently assigned carrier committed to CENTCOM. My third update trigger specified Theodore Roosevelt going to CENTCOM with no replacement assigned. Strictly that has not happened, but the functionally equivalent thing - the forward-deployed carrier leaving PACOM for CENTCOM with no replacement - has. I count that as a partial fire.

I should be honest about the counterweight, because it cuts against the confidence I expressed yesterday. TWZ's 11 August edition says Roosevelt's destination - CENTCOM to sustain dual-carrier coverage, or a western Pacific patrol - 'will likely depend on how the negotiations with Iran shake out.' That is a genuinely open question, not the settled CENTCOM assignment the 17 August framing implied. So the direction of the carrier factor is confirmed but its durability is less certain than I said. Those roughly cancel, and on their own would not have moved me.

What moved me is the market evidence. I had been anchoring on Polymarket's invasion markets: 4 percent for an invasion by 31 December 2026 on about forty million dollars of volume, 1 percent by 30 September. Today I looked at two markets I had not been tracking. The first is 'Will China blockade Taiwan in 2026?', trading at 6 percent on 261,491 dollars as of 25 August, and its resolution language is strikingly close to mine: it requires prevention of normal ingress or egress of foreign commercial traffic to Taiwan's main ports or airports by threat or use of force for at least 24 hours, declared or de facto, covering part or whole of the main island, established by broad consensus of credible reporting. It explicitly excludes drills with NOTAMs that do not materially deny access, excludes purely economic or coercive measures without physical interdiction, excludes islet-only incidents, and excludes seizure of a single vessel unless part of an enforced pattern. That is very nearly the question I am forecasting, with a 24-hour rather than 72-hour bar. Six percent for the remaining four months of 2026 is far above my implied near-term hazard, which is roughly one percent for the same period.

I do not take that at face value. The market is thin - 261,000 dollars and 28 comments - and the No side is paying 94 cents for a six-cent return over four months, roughly a 19 percent annualised yield, which is well above risk-free. That spread is the classic signature of long-shot bias and scarce No-side capital rather than genuine crowd belief. Annualising 6 percent over four months would imply something like 18 percent a year and 45 percent over my full window, which I regard as absurd. So I discount it heavily. But I cannot discount it to zero, and it is the closest-matched external estimate I have found for this question.

The second and better-capitalised anchor is 'Will China invade Taiwan by December 31, 2027?', at 12 percent on 3.03 million dollars as of 26 August. Its bar is looser than mine - any military offensive intended to establish control over any portion of ROC-administered inhabited territory, which would include Kinmen, Matsu or Pratas - but the arithmetic is instructive. Take 12 percent through end-2027 on the loose bar, apply the 25-to-35-percent narrowing factor I use for the strict blockade-or-assault-on-Taiwan-proper bar with two-agency confirmation, and you get roughly 4 percent through end-2027 on my terms. Add the 2028-29 period, where I think hazard is materially higher - PLA centenary milestone passed, command layer rebuilt, January 2028 Taiwan presidential election, the projected trough in US hull and munitions availability - and the implied total lands nearer 8 or 9 than 7. The deep market, properly translated, is not below me. It is slightly above me. Notably the invade-2026 market at 4 percent and the invade-2027 market at 12 percent are roughly consistent with a flat hazard, i.e. the crowd applies no term-structure discount at all.

One more item runs upward, and it firmed rather than softened today. The Taipei Times of 26 August reports that Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu opened interparty negotiations on 24 August over the DPP's NT$210 billion special budget act for coastal surveillance drones, coastal attack drones and uncrewed one-way strike boats. The KMT's counter-proposal offers a larger headline number, NT$240 billion, but disbursed at NT$40 billion a year over six years from the annual budget with the Ministry of Economic Affairs as lead agency; the TPP version specifies no funding source at all and explicitly refuses to fund uncrewed ground and surface vehicles. MND Comptroller Bureau head Hsieh Chi-hsien said last Thursday that the opposition bills would not fund the three uncrewed systems the armed forces planned to buy, and the 14 August passage of NT$19.2 billion covered unarmed drones and industry subsidies, not weapon systems. Because this year's and next year's annual budgets are already proposed, and Article 79 of the Budget Act reserves supplementary budgets to the Executive Yuan, the practical effect of the opposition route is that no money reaches the 210,000-drone programme until 2028 - a 17-month delay. That programme is the lynchpin of the hellscape concept, and the delay lands squarely in the years where most of this question's probability mass sits.

Against all of that, one clean piece of downward news. Xi's state visit is now dated and dual-confirmed: arriving Washington late on 23 September, White House talks with Trump on 24 September, departing on the 25th - his first US state visit in eleven years. Polymarket prices it 94 percent by 30 September and 97 percent by 31 December on 738,000 dollars. Yesterday I had only 'expected September'. A confirmed date is worth more than an expectation, and it reinforces the crowded near-term political calendar alongside the October fifth plenum and November APEC in Shenzhen.

Net: the carrier factor confirmed but with its durability more open, the drone-procurement delay firmed, a well-matched but thin market anchor and a deep market anchor both sitting above my number, against a firmer near-term diplomatic floor. Move to 8, interval 4 to 13.

question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
key_change:
Move: 1 to 1. The 80% interval stays at [0, 1]. Today the single largest resolvable input in this question stopped being a forecast and became a published fact, and it landed almost exactly where the analyst community had put it.

Ofgem confirmed the Default Tariff Cap for 1 October to 31 December 2026 at around 7am this morning. The new level is GBP 1,723 a year for a typical dual-fuel direct debit household, a rise of roughly GBP 60, or 3.6%, from the current GBP 1,663. Cornwall Insight's final forecast on 19 August was GBP 1,729.31, or 4.0%; Uswitch reported suppliers converging on about 3.7% after the observation window closed on 19 August. So the outcome came in a touch below consensus, but only by about GBP 6, four tenths of a percentage point on the quarterly change. Neither of yesterday's thresholds fired. I said I would revise up if the cap came in at or below GBP 1,663, which would have removed the administered impulse entirely, and down to zero if it came in at or above GBP 1,747. It did neither, so the arithmetic of the question is unchanged: the cap covering the October, November and December reference months, which is three of the four publishable attempts left, rises rather than falls, and it does so despite the removal of the 5% VAT rate on domestic electricity from 1 October. Martin Lewis's team make the point that from 1 October electricity unit rates under the cap will be restated without VAT, so the headline unit rate will look lower than today's even though the underlying wholesale-driven cost has gone up. That restatement is a genuine CPI-relevant price cut for consumers, because CPI prices goods inclusive of VAT, and on an electricity weight of roughly two and a half per cent a 4.8% reduction is worth on the order of a tenth of a point on the index. But it is already inside the 3.6% headline, already inside every published forecast, and nowhere near the roughly one full percentage point of unexpected disinflation this question requires.

The genuinely new information today came from crude, and it is the largest YES-friendly move I have recorded in this series. Brent ended Tuesday 25 August near USD 87.12 and WTI at USD 82.36, against Monday's close of USD 92.17 and USD 85.01. That is a fall of USD 7.27, or 7.7%, from Friday's close, across two sessions. Trading Economics had Brent as low as USD 86.33 intraday, down 6.33% on the day. Two things did it, and both point the same way. First, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's Operation Economic Outcast, unveiled Monday with Normandy imagery and around sixty designations covering digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping, set no deadline for secondary sanctions and designated no major Chinese bank, and China takes well over eighty per cent of Iran's seaborne crude. Bessent called it a warning shot. Second, Pakistan's army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir spent Monday in Tehran carrying a reported sanctions-relief proposal, meeting President Pezeshkian, negotiator Ghalibaf and General Rezaei, while Oman's foreign minister worked separately on navigation rules for the strait and word circulated that Washington might return evacuated diplomats. The cleanest read is the Murban spread: Abu Dhabi's light grade leaves via the Habshan-Fujairah pipeline and never enters Hormuz, and its premium over Brent, north of USD 11 on Monday, roughly halved by Tuesday afternoon. That is a war premium coming out of the price, and it is coming out fastest where it was thickest. The EIA's August outlook has Brent averaging USD 85 in Q3, USD 78 in Q4 and USD 69 across 2027.

I have taken that seriously and it still does not move the number, for four reasons. First, the physical floor has not moved. Hormuz throughput fell from 21.6 million barrels a day in Q4 2025 to 4.9 million a day in Q2 2026, shut-in production averaged 5.5 million a day in July, global inventories drew 4.2 million a day in Q2 and the EIA projects a further 3.8 million a day this quarter. Not one barrel was released by either Monday's sanctions or Munir's visit; what was removed was fear. Second, the framework Munir invoked, the Islamabad memorandum signed on 17 June, saw its sixty-day window lapse in the middle of this month with neither side extending, and Rezaei and Ghalibaf both told him Washington must move first. A 7.7% repricing resting on an expired framework is exactly the kind of move that reverses. Third, and most important for this question, transmission from crude to consumer prices is currently broken downstream. The US diesel crack touched a record USD 102.20 a barrel on 17 August and is still near USD 100, distillate stocks were around 107.1 million barrels in early August, the thinnest for the time of year since 1996, and US retail diesel rose fifteen cents in the same week that Brent fell 7.7%. When the binding constraint is refining capacity rather than crude, cheaper Brent does not reach the pump, and motor fuels carry only about three per cent of the UK CPI basket in any case. Fourth, the UK-relevant energy price is gas, not oil, and gas barely budged: NBP settled at 163 pence per therm on 25 August, down 3.6% on the day but off a 169 pence high that is the strongest since January 2023, while TTF held above EUR 68 per megawatt hour, also the highest since January 2023, with EU storage around 55% at end-July, some eleven points below a year earlier, and hot weather slowing injections.

One technical item worth logging. ONS confirms it has not been able to update to 2026 CPI and CPIH weights in line with standard methodology because of delays in processing the underlying household final consumption expenditure survey data and the need for further quality assurance; the series is running on 2025 weights and ONS will update when the data allow. A mid-series reweighting is the kind of technical event that can shift a headline print, and it is the sort of thing that keeps me at 1 rather than 0. Historically, though, weight updates move the annual rate by hundredths, occasionally a tenth. They do not deliver a hundred basis points.

The forecaster distribution is untouched. The Bank of England's July Monetary Policy Report has CPI peaking around 3.2% in Q4 2026 with risks tilted to the upside; Pill, Greene and Mann voted for 4.00% at the end of July; a Reuters poll conducted 13 to 18 August found 56 of 64 economists expecting Bank Rate held at 3.75% for the rest of the year and none expecting a change on 17 September, with markets still assigning some probability to a hike rather than a cut. HM Treasury's August comparison of independent forecasts averages 3.4% for Q4 2026, and Deutsche Bank sees the peak at 3.3% to 3.5%. Nobody published has an in-window month near 2.0%.

So: the biggest uncertainty in the window resolved, marginally on the friendly side of consensus but still upward; the biggest disinflationary impulse of the series arrived in crude but is blocked downstream and does not touch the administered gas and electricity prices that dominate the remaining reference months. Those roughly cancel. Four attempts remain, August published 16 September, September 21 October, October 18 November and November 16 December, with December 2026 publishing 20 January 2027 and therefore mechanically outside. I hold at 1.

question: Will Spider-Man: Brand New Day gross over $1.5B worldwide by 31 December 2026?
key_change:
Move: 100 to 100. I hold at the ceiling for a seventeenth consecutive day, and today is the cleanest single day of evidence in this entire series: both named resolution sources refreshed overnight, both moved upward, and both now agree to the dollar on the domestic line for a second consecutive day.

Verification performed today, Wednesday 26 August 2026 at 08:07:15 UTC, by direct raw-HTML request with a desktop browser user-agent, compression enabled and redirects followed. Box Office Mojo (https://www.boxofficemojo.com/release/rl2299756545/) returned HTTP 200, 177,644 bytes on disk, MD5 e4d74e535a9346273b8e4ccff3cf9303, and reports Domestic $858,400,177 (38.6 per cent), International $1,365,000,000 (61.4 per cent) and Worldwide $2,223,400,177, with opening weekend unchanged at $360,091,572 across 4,487 theatres and a release date of 31 July 2026. The Numbers (https://www.the-numbers.com/movie/Spider-Man-Brand-New-Day-(2026)) returned HTTP 200, 138,733 bytes, MD5 0a234229795d42739b74676bc04b0cbf, and reports Domestic Box Office $858,400,177, International Box Office $1,366,115,336 explicitly datestamped 8/26/2026, and Worldwide Box Office $2,224,515,513, alongside Legs of 2.38 and a domestic share of 38.6 per cent. Both worldwide lines reconcile exactly against their own published components: 858,400,177 + 1,365,000,000 = 2,223,400,177, and 858,400,177 + 1,366,115,336 = 2,224,515,513. Taking the LOWER of the two, as I have throughout, the film stands at $2,223,400,177 worldwide. That is 48.2 per cent above the $1.5B threshold, a buffer of $723,400,177, up $3,498,996 on yesterday's buffer.

The day's movement is entirely upward and entirely on the domestic line. Both sources moved from $854,901,181 to $858,400,177, a gain of $3,498,996, which is a plausible Monday-plus-Tuesday actuals ingestion for a film running roughly $3.5M to $4.5M per weekday in its fourth and fifth weeks. Critically, they moved in lockstep and landed on the identical figure to the dollar. Yesterday I flagged as an open question whether the newly exact domestic agreement reflected genuine independent ingestion of the same Comscore actual or one source mirroring the other. Today's evidence leans toward the former for a specific reason: the two sources moved together on domestic but did NOT move together on international, where Box Office Mojo held its round $1,365,000,000 for a third consecutive day while The Numbers held $1,366,115,336 for a second. If The Numbers were simply mirroring Box Office Mojo's feed, the international lines would have converged too. They have not. The feeds are independent; they simply happen to draw domestic from the same reconciled Comscore actual, which is exactly what one would expect and exactly what makes the corroboration meaningful rather than illusory.

The international divergence is therefore stable at $1,115,336, identical to yesterday, rather than growing. Box Office Mojo's flat round number is the signature of a studio-reported international estimate awaiting reconciliation, and it has now been static for three days while the domestic line updated twice. That is a mild staleness on one field of one source, worth noting but not worth a single basis point: it is 0.05 per cent of the cume and 0.15 per cent of the buffer, and the direction of any eventual catch-up is upward, not downward.

External corroboration strengthened materially today. The Hollywood Reporter reports the film has hit No. 2 on the all-time domestic chart, topping Avengers: Endgame, which independently confirms a domestic cume in the $858M region since Endgame's final domestic sits at $858.4M. Forbes on 24 August reported the film passing both Titanic and Ne Zha 2 to become the fourth-biggest film ever worldwide, with subsequent coverage placing it at $2.224 billion and closing on Avatar: The Way of Water at No. 3, less than $100M ahead. That is three independent trade outlets, none of them a named resolution source, all placing the worldwide cume within a rounding error of the two aggregator figures I retrieved directly. When Variety, The Hollywood Reporter, Deadline, Forbes, the Washington Post, Box Office Mojo and The Numbers all place a number in the same $2.22B to $2.23B band, the probability that all seven are wrong by the $723M required to threaten this threshold is not a number I can meaningfully write down.

I also re-ran a targeted search for any correction, re-audit or restatement notice covering this title from Box Office Mojo, The Numbers, Comscore or Sony. Null for a third consecutive day. The only revisions in the published record remain the well-documented upward ones from opening: first Friday including previews restated to $169.8M, the domestic opening weekend from a Sunday estimate of $355M to a final $360,091,572, and the global opening from $927M to $932M. Not one downward restatement of any magnitude exists in this film's entire published history. That directional asymmetry is the single most important structural fact here, because the only mechanism producing a NO is a large, durable, correlated downward restatement, and the empirical record on this title contains zero instances of downward restatement at any size.

Retrieval also improved today. Yesterday's first curl attempt returned HTTP 200 with a zero-byte body and needed a retry. Today both fetches succeeded on the first attempt with full bodies. That does not eliminate instrument risk, which has recurred on 19, 22, 23, 24 and 25 August, but it is the first clean single-pass retrieval of the series and it slightly reduces my concern about a resolution-day fetch failure.

For a NO, both named sources would have to restate the worldwide cume downward by more than $723,400,177, or 32.5 per cent of the lower published figure, simultaneously, and hold that restatement through 31 December. With 127 days to run, a film still in wide release, and a cumulative-by-then rather than snapshot test, the buffer can only widen. I hold central at 100.

I keep the lower CI bound at 99 rather than closing to 100, for reasons unchanged and unrelated to box office. Residual risk is now almost entirely instrument and adjudication risk: the 23 August episode proved a named source can display a materially wrong nine-figure value for a full day with no correction notice, retrieval has failed on five of the last eight days before retry, and resolver mechanics remain unobservable to me. A 1-point floor is the honest price of that residual. Seventeen days of confirmation should not persuade me that a published number is a law of nature.

question: Will OpenAI and Anthropic have a combined ARR exceeding $70B by 31 December 2026?
key_change:
Move: 99 to 99. The 25-26 August window produced no new company-sourced revenue disclosure for either firm, but today's searches did surface one genuinely new class of evidence that I had not previously incorporated in quantified form: third-party alternative-data trackers, which run materially ABOVE the company-reported figures on Anthropic and slightly above on OpenAI. That is a meaningful strengthening of the YES case at the level of the arithmetic, offset by the first clean quantification of deceleration I have seen. Net, I hold at 99 with the interval at [98,99].

The company-sourced anchors are unchanged and were re-verified today. Anthropic's annualised revenue run rate topped $65bn at end-July 2026, reported by Bloomberg on 17 August and corroborated the same day by TechCrunch, Axios and CNBC. That is a more than sevenfold jump from roughly $9bn at end-2025, via $47bn at the May Series H. Preliminary Q2 recognised revenue was $11.6bn against $4.73bn in Q1 and $787m in the year-ago quarter, with positive adjusted operating income. OpenAI's run rate topped $40bn, reported by Bloomberg on 13 August, up from roughly $20bn at the start of the year and having been flat near $25bn through the spring; Q2 recognised revenue was $6.7bn against $5.7bn in Q1, an 18% sequential increase that disappointed some investors. Combined exit run rate is therefore about $105bn against a $70bn bar, roughly 50% of headroom with four months to run.

The new material. TickerTrends is independently tracking Anthropic at $74.1bn and OpenAI at $41.3bn as of July, a combined roughly $115bn, with OpenAI's tracked run rate rising from $33.0bn in May to $41.3bn in July. Yipit separately put Anthropic at $74.3bn as at 22 July, having been at roughly $69bn in early July with average daily ARR adds of about $550m, up from about $400m in May. These are alternative-data estimates, not disclosures, and I weight them well below Bloomberg's investor-update sourcing. But their direction matters: independent bottom-up estimation lands above rather than below the company-reported numbers, which is the opposite of the pattern that would worry me. It also means that on the tracker view Anthropic ALONE ($74.1bn) already exceeds the $70bn combined bar, so the question would resolve YES even if OpenAI's contribution were struck out entirely. Separately, SemiAnalysis's Tokenomics team, which builds these financials bottom-up by SKU and tier and whose accuracy was corroborated by the WSJ's Anthropic reporting, wrote on 8 July that the two labs combine for roughly $100bn of ARR and projected Anthropic above $60bn by Q3 with over $1bn of quarterly GAAP EBITDA. Three methodologically independent sources now converge on a combined figure in the $100-115bn range.

The offsetting new item is deceleration, and I want to be honest that it is real. TickerTrends' headline is explicitly that Anthropic's growth is beginning to decelerate: month-on-month growth cooled from roughly 55% in the spring to mid-single digits by July, with tracked ARR going $10.2bn in January, $35.6bn in April, $69.6bn in June, $74.1bn in July. A move from $69.6bn to $74.1bn is about 6.5% month-on-month. If Anthropic compounds at 6.5% monthly from an August base of roughly $79bn, it reaches about $95bn by December on its own. If it goes to literally zero growth from here, it stays at $74bn. Both clear. OpenAI, meanwhile, is accelerating on the same dataset, up 65.2% since its last reported figure against Anthropic's 57.7%, consistent with Friar's 14 August investor slides showing run rate up 35% quarter to date and enterprise up 50% QTD, and Brockman's report of July run rate up more than 20% month-on-month. The composition is rotating but the aggregate is not at risk.

On resolution mechanics, which remain the entirety of my residual, one detail sharpened today. CNBC's 19 August report of Friar's all-hands has her saying not only that OpenAI "will be a public company in 2027" or sooner, but specifically that "Anthropic is also under file. There is a chance they pull the cover off that confidential file in the coming weeks and become public in September." That raises the odds of an audited Anthropic revenue figure landing inside the forecast window rather than after it. Anthropic's S-1 was confidentially submitted on 1 June 2026 and today's checks still show nothing on EDGAR beyond unrelated small-cap filings. A public S-1 in September would resolve the ASC 606 gross-versus-net branch, which is the only live NO mechanism, one way or the other well before December. The accounting question itself is unchanged: Anthropic books cloud-reseller consumption through Bedrock, Vertex and Azure Foundry on a gross basis on a principal argument, OpenAI has alleged the gross-to-net gap is roughly $8bn, and market pricing has sat at roughly 50% SEC affirmation, 40% disaggregated disclosure, 10% forced restatement. To flip this question a restatement would have to cut the combined figure by 33%, or Anthropic alone by about 54%. The $8bn allegation is about 12% of Anthropic's run rate. Even the aggressive 20-40% haircuts floated in IPO-preview commentary leave $79-92bn.

Background conditions are noisier than the arithmetic. Nvidia reports fiscal Q2 after the close today, 26 August, with consensus at $92.2bn revenue and $2.09 EPS; the stock has fallen for seven straight sessions, its longest losing streak since 2022, and the AI complex has been under sustained pressure. A bad print could extend the drawdown. But this is a capex, sentiment and financing story, and transmission from equity drawdown to reported ARR at firms with contracted enterprise commitments historically runs over years, not four months. The price war likewise continues without visible revenue effect: OpenAI's 30 July cuts took Luna to $0.20/$1.20, a roughly 80% reduction, Terra to $2/$12, and the 21 August Sol cut runs guaranteed through 21 November; Anthropic has made Sonnet 5's $2/$10 permanent rather than raising to $3/$15. Prices for equivalent capability have collapsed 90-97% over 2025-26 while both firms' revenue multiplied. Elasticity has outrun price at every previous step.

No revision. Central 99, interval [98,99].

question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
key_change:
Move: 36 to 35. A one-point trim. Today's information flow contains one genuinely clarifying upward anchor that I had not previously recorded and three modest downward corrections to factors I credited over the past 48 hours, and on balance the corrections outweigh the anchor slightly. The discipline after Sunday's three-point move is to test that move rather than extend it, and testing it today produced more friction than support.

The upward anchor first, because it is the most important thing I found and because it partly rescues my central estimate from drifting lower. The OBR's Fiscal risks and sustainability report, published 7 July 2026 and launched at the Darlington Economic Campus, sets a baseline scenario assuming long-term average productivity growth of 1.4 per cent over the next fifty years which, combined with projected changes in the workforce, implies real GDP growth averaging around one and a half per cent a year across the long run. For the first time the OBR has incorporated an explicit projection of the capital stock, so it now decomposes long-run productivity into capital deepening and total factor productivity rather than assuming a single trend. That is the official long-run anchor for exactly the variable this question resolves on, and it sits at the threshold rather than beneath it. I had been carrying the medium-term EFO numbers as my institutional anchor, where TFP growth reaches only 0.8 per cent in 2030 and potential output growth is around 1.4 to 1.5 per cent, and I had implicitly assumed the long-run projection would be lower still. It is not. The FRS also runs a higher-productivity scenario with TFP at 1.3 per cent a year, 0.3 points above baseline, which the OBR says would cut borrowing by around 50 billion pounds in 2030-31 and push the point at which debt turns unsustainable back nearly twenty years, and a downside scenario in which productivity growth remains at 0.5 per cent, close to its post-financial-crisis average. The existence of a named, quantified downside scenario at 0.5 per cent is itself informative about where the OBR thinks the risk lies.

I do not treat the FRS baseline as implying a fifty per cent probability, and the reason is the shape of the path. The OBR's medium-term forecast has TFP still climbing towards 0.8 per cent in 2030; the 1.4 per cent long-run figure is a convergence assumption reached over subsequent decades. The 2030s are the earliest and therefore the lowest slice of that fifty-year window. Under the OBR's own baseline the decade mean for 2030-2039 is very plausibly 1.3 to 1.4 per cent, not 1.5. So the FRS confirms my central estimate rather than overturning it, and it is a reason to nudge the upper tail of my distribution rather than the central case.

Now the corrections. The first is Andrew Bailey's Mansion House speech of 14 July 2026, which I had cited only through the Monetary Policy Report's quarterly potential-supply figure of 0.3 to 0.4 per cent. Read directly, Bailey decomposes the record: for roughly fifteen years before the financial crisis, UK potential supply grew at around 2.8 per cent a year, of which productivity contributed 2.4 points and labour supply 0.4 points; for the fifteen years since the crisis, potential growth has fallen to 1.3 per cent, of which productivity contributed just 0.4 points and labour supply 0.8 points. That composition is the whole argument in one line. The post-crisis UK bought two thirds of its potential growth from labour supply, and labour supply is precisely the component that ONS demographics take away in the 2030s. Yesterday I credited the Bank's potential-supply estimate as straddling the 1.5 per cent bar. Bailey's own framing puts the Bank's recent-history number at 1.3 per cent, below the bar, with the productivity leg at 0.4 points. To clear 1.5 per cent through the 2030s the productivity contribution has to more than triple from its post-crisis average while the labour contribution roughly halves. That is a harder ask than the quarterly figure alone implied, and I mark down my Bank-of-England factor accordingly.

The second correction concerns business investment, where I gave two points on Monday for the ONS provisional Q2 2026 estimate showing a 1.7 per cent quarterly rise. The EY UK Economic Outlook published this month forecasts UK GDP growth of 0.9 per cent in 2026, up from 0.8 per cent in May, but simultaneously downgrades business investment to a fall of 0.7 per cent across 2026, against the zero growth forecast in May, citing energy costs and inflation staying higher for longer. It has investment returning to growth only in 2027 and 2028, at a downgraded 1.8 and 2.6 per cent, and unemployment rising to 5.3 per cent by end-2026 before easing to 5.1 and then 4.8 per cent in 2028. EY also warns explicitly that the UK faces recession if the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz lasts into 2027, which would cut 2026 growth to 0.5 per cent and shrink the economy 0.2 per cent next year. A forecaster looking at the same Q2 print and still marking down the annual investment path is telling me my two-point credit was too generous for one provisional, bias-adjusted quarter. I keep the factor but shrink it.

The third is subtler and cuts at the foundation of the bull case. The ONS labour market transformation update published this month reports that Labour Force Survey response levels have improved markedly since 2023 following higher incentives and more interviewers, with waves two to five slightly above their pre-pandemic level in January to March 2026, and that the Transformed Labour Force Survey is on track to become the headline measure in 2027. The entire Resolution Foundation and CEP LSE case rests on the LFS denominator being broken. If the LFS is convalescing, the wedge between the survey-based and administrative-data productivity measures should narrow over time, and it is not obvious in which direction. The ONS separately acknowledges it needs to give a clearer steer on which productivity measure to use, which is a fair admission but not a resolution.

Two smaller items lean up and I record them without moving on them. The Resolution Foundation's Q3 2026 Macroeconomic Policy Outlook notes that the 1.1 per cent annual growth in output per hour over the two years to Q2 2026 is faster than the 0.7 per cent rate of the late 2010s, and the Retail Gazette coverage of 24 August confirms retail is among the twelve of nineteen sectors recording gains, which speaks directly to my trigger about the pickup spreading beyond information and communication into large-employment sectors. But note what the bull number actually delivers if projected forward: 1.1 per cent productivity plus 0.2 to 0.5 points of labour input gives 1.3 to 1.6 per cent, centred at about 1.4. Even the optimists' measure, taken at face value and held for a decade, lands just short of the bar. The same Outlook records that ONS output per hour in Q2 2026 is around 5 per cent below the level implied by the OBR's final pre-Covid forecast, roughly 150 billion pounds a year or 4,500 pounds per worker. Separately, analysts now expect gilt yields to fall ahead of the 28 October Budget, potentially restoring the 10 to 12 billion pounds of headroom lost this year, which marginally eases the risk that public capital spending is cut to meet the fiscal rules.

Mechanically I hold the decade mean at roughly 1.30 to 1.35 per cent with a standard deviation near 0.5 points, shading the point estimate a touch down within that range on the Bailey decomposition. That gives 34 to 36 per cent. I take 35. The scheduled events that should move this are unchanged: the quarterly national accounts and revised Q2 business investment on 30 September, the ONS productivity methods article due September, the Healey Budget and OBR EFO on 28 October, the Blue Book revisions article on 30 October, the November Monetary Policy Report and the Q3 productivity flash on 17 November.

question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2030?
key_change:
Move: 29 to 32. This is the first genuine move in this run, and I want to be precise about why, because the temptation today is to move much further than the evidence supports.

Trigger one, the resolving pathway, came closer to firing than on any previous day but did not fire. TIME published its cover story 'Inside OpenAI's Reboot' on 26 August, built on interviews with more than twenty OpenAI executives, employees, investors and rivals. In it Sam Altman says he expects OpenAI to have an internal system he would call AGI by the end of 2026; chief research officer Mark Chen says the company is '80% of the way' to AGI; chief scientist Jakub Pachocki says Astra already meets OpenAI's internal benchmark for an automated research intern, able to take an experimental idea, implement it in OpenAI's codebase, run the experiment and return results, or take a paper and do a week of a human researcher's follow-up work; and co-founder Greg Brockman says this period may be remembered as the point when AGI was created. IBTimes wrote it up the same evening, adding that Astra ran for days at a stretch, operated computers at what insiders call super-human speed, and was demonstrated at OpenAI headquarters this month with sixteen agents collaborating on a research-level mathematics problem. Read against my resolution bar, none of these is an assertion that AGI has been achieved. Altman explicitly says 'not quite yet'; 80 per cent of the way is a statement of incompleteness; an internal research-intern benchmark is not AGI; 'may be remembered as' is not a claim. The article itself notes OpenAI has not said Astra meets its full charter definition and that the internal assessments are unverified. So: not fired. But this is qualitatively different from the five previous senior-figure episodes I have been discounting. It carries a dated, falsifiable forward commitment from the CEO of the most likely declarer, it is corroborated by the two most senior research officers with operational specifics rather than vibes, and it lands while OpenAI is negotiating with Microsoft over a contract in which 'AGI achieved' is a live financial trigger worth 15 per cent of revenue until 2032.

question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
key_change:
Move: 1 to 1. No change. Yesterday's note held that the largest resolvable input had converted from forecast to published statistic, and nothing today reverses that. The ONS bulletin of 19 August 2026 put CPI annual inflation at 2.9% for July 2026, up from 2.6% in June and a four-month high, driven by housing and household services (4.1% against 2.7%) after the 13% Ofgem cap increase, with gas up 14.7% and electricity up 3.6%. Core CPI was 2.6%, unchanged from June; CPIH rose from 2.8% to 3.1%. None of yesterday's triggers fired: no downside energy shock, no ONS revision notice, no fiscal announcement.

The remaining-months arithmetic is the whole question. Reference months January through July 2026 are published and every one is at or above 2.0%, so they are dead. Under the publication-date reading of the resolution criterion, only four reference months can still be published before 1 January 2027: August 2026 (due mid-September), September 2026 (mid-October), October 2026 (confirmed by ONS for 18 November 2026) and November 2026 (mid-December, following the standard four-to-five week lag). The December 2026 reference month is published in mid-January 2027 and therefore cannot resolve this question, so it is excluded regardless of its value. That leaves four draws, each of which requires the annual rate to fall from 2.9% to below 2.0% - a swing of more than 0.9pp - within one to four months.

Every available projection points the opposite way. The Bank of England's July 2026 Monetary Policy Report (30 July) has CPI peaking at around 3.2% in 2026 Q4, having revised the Q3 path to a little under 3% on mid-June energy pricing, and explicitly describes risks to the inflation outlook as tilted to the upside given the Middle East conflict. The HM Treasury comparison of independent forecasts (17 June) averaged 3.7% for Q4 2026, with more recent compilations near 3.4%. The MPC held Bank Rate at 3.75% on 29 July on a 6-3 vote, with Pill, Greene and Mann voting to hike to 4% - a hawkish hold - and a Reuters poll of 64 economists conducted 13-18 August found nearly 90% expect no change for the rest of the year. A central bank whose own forecast has inflation rising through the resolution window, and whose committee contains three hike votes, is not consistent with a sub-2% print in any of the four remaining months.

The mechanical requirement is severe. A 0.9pp fall in the annual rate over one to four months would need month-on-month prints running roughly 0.3-0.4pp below their year-ago equivalents repeatedly. Outside VAT cuts (2008, 2020) and the 2023 energy cap unwind, the UK has essentially never delivered that from a starting point of 2.9% with core at 2.6% and services inflation still elevated. Base effects from autumn 2025 are not favourable enough, and the October 2026 Ofgem cap would need an implausibly large cut to bridge even half the gap.

Net adjustment: zero. The residual probability sits entirely in a statistical-revision or resolution-wording tail, not in an economic path. Central stays at 1 with the interval unchanged at [0, 1].
